0–91 term

5S

Lean workplace organization and maintenance method

5S is a Lean method for organizing and maintaining a workplace through five practices: sort, set in order, shine, standardize, and sustain.

More about this term

The practices remove unneeded items, locate needed ones, keep the area clean, make arrangements consistent, and maintain them over time.

A one-time cleanup is incomplete without standards and sustained use.

CC0 1.0View versioned object
A52 terms

Abnormality

observed process departure in quality control

In process control, an abnormality is an observed condition or pattern that departs from the process's expected or specified state.

More about this term

A sudden spike in waste can signal a cause that needs investigation.

The departure identifies something to examine; it does not by itself establish its cause or prove that the whole process has failed.

CC0 1.0View versioned object

Academic quality

quality of teaching, learning and scholarship in higher education

Academic quality is how well a program or institution's educational and scholarly work serves its relevant academic aims and standards.

More about this term

The judgment may consider teaching, student learning, research, and the conditions that support them.

Different purposes and review schemes emphasize different evidence, so one indicator alone cannot settle every academic-quality claim.

CC0 1.0View versioned object

Academic rigor

higher-education learning demands and demonstrated standards

In higher education, academic rigor is the appropriately challenging standard of learning and demonstrated performance expected in a course or program.

More about this term

It appears in the learning outcomes, tasks, and criteria used to judge what students can do.

A course can support students through difficult work while keeping its academic standard clear; difficulty alone does not establish rigor.

CC0 1.0View versioned object

Accelerated life testing

reliability testing over compressed observation time

Accelerated life testing subjects items to more intensive use or more severe conditions to learn about their failure or lifetime behavior sooner than ordinary use would allow.

More about this term

Continuous use can compress elapsed test time without increasing the operating stress; elevated stress is a different route to acceleration.

When elevated-stress results are used to estimate normal-life behavior, the stress relationship and failure mechanisms need justification.

CC0 1.0View versioned object

Acceptability

people's appraisal of how health care treats and involves them

In health care, acceptability concerns whether people regard the way they are treated and involved in decisions as appropriate.

More about this term

Respectful treatment and attention to patients' views are central to this appraisal.

Being able to reach a clinician does not, by itself, establish that the care is acceptable to those receiving it.

CC0 1.0View versioned object

Acceptable range

permitted interval for an engineering characteristic

In an engineering specification, an acceptable range is an interval of values that satisfies a stated requirement for a specified characteristic.

More about this term

State both limits, the unit, and whether each boundary value is included.

This decision interval is distinct from the spread of values actually observed in production or measurement.

CC0 1.0View versioned object

Acceptance criterion

specified acceptance decision

An acceptance criterion is a condition or decision rule used to determine whether a specified item, result, or process may be accepted for a stated purpose.

More about this term

It can specify a limit, an observable condition, or another checkable basis for the decision. State what is being accepted, how the condition is checked, and who may decide.

A requirement may need one or more acceptance criteria to make its fulfillment assessable. Passing one criterion does not by itself establish the object’s overall quality.

CC0 1.0View versioned object

Acceptance quality limit

sampling-inspection limit for a satisfactory process average over a series of lots

In acceptance sampling over a continuing series of lots, the acceptance quality limit (AQL) is a designated quality level at the boundary of what is treated as a satisfactory process average for sampling inspection.

More about this term

It helps specify a sampling plan's intended performance for a continuing process.

It is not a promise that every accepted lot meets that level or contains no nonconforming units.

CC0 1.0View versioned object

Acceptance sampling

sample-based lot acceptance decision

Acceptance sampling is a method for deciding whether to accept or reject a lot by inspecting a sample under a specified decision rule.

More about this term

The plan identifies the lot, how units are selected, the sample size, what counts as nonconforming, and the number or pattern of findings that triggers rejection.

A sample decision does not establish the condition of every unit. Any plan carries a chance of accepting a poor lot or rejecting a good one, so its risks must fit the intended use.

CC0 1.0View versioned object

Access to care

practical ability to obtain needed health services

In health services, access to care is people's practical ability to obtain needed care when and where they need it.

More about this term

A nearby facility does not by itself establish access: travel, cost, service arrangements, and social or cultural conditions can affect whether people can use it.

An access judgment should specify the population and type of care rather than assume that everyone near a service has the same opportunity to obtain it.

CC0 1.0View versioned object

Accessibility

ease of obtaining appropriate health services

In health services, accessibility is how readily people can obtain appropriate care when they need it.

More about this term

Travel, time, cost, service arrangements, and a person's circumstances can each affect access.

A service can exist in an area yet remain difficult for some people to use.

CC0 1.0View versioned object

Accountability

answerability for conduct or results to an evaluating party

Accountability is a relationship in which a person or organization must give an account of its actions or results to another party able to assess it.

More about this term

The relationship identifies who answers to whom, for what, and under which rules or possible consequences.

Having a responsibility is not the whole relationship: accountability also requires an account that another party can examine.

CC0 1.0View versioned object

Accreditation

higher-education institutional or program recognition

In higher education, accreditation is an accreditor's public recognition of an institution or program based on its standards and requirements.

More about this term

The recognition applies to the institution or program named by the accreditor; a program’s status does not automatically extend to its whole institution.

Accreditation can carry findings or monitoring. Name the accreditor and the status before treating the recognition as evidence that every requirement is fully met.

CC0 1.0View versioned object

Accuracy

closeness of a measurement result to a reference value

In measurement, accuracy is the closeness of a measured result to an accepted reference value for the same quantity.

More about this term

Repeated results can agree closely with one another yet all lie away from the reference value.

State the quantity and reference used before calling a result accurate.

CC0 1.0View versioned object

Action

human agency in social inquiry

In human activity, an action is something an agent does for a reason or purpose, rather than an event that merely happens to the agent.

More about this term

The same outward movement can be different actions depending on intention and context. Describing movement alone may therefore leave out what the person was doing.

CC0 1.0View versioned object

Adequacy

purpose-relative sufficiency of evidence, analysis or other object

Adequacy is being sufficient for a specified purpose or requirement.

More about this term

An analysis can be adequate for one question yet inadequate for another because the data and method must fit the goal.

Adequacy marks a defensible sufficiency judgment; it does not by itself mean the work is excellent or free of limitations.

CC0 1.0View versioned object

Adjustment

change to measuring equipment or an item in metrology

In metrology, adjustment is a deliberate change to a measuring item or system that alters its output or indication.

More about this term

It may bring an indication closer to a desired setting, but the change itself does not establish measurement accuracy.

Record the condition before and after adjustment when that difference matters; calibration and adjustment are distinct operations.

CC0 1.0View versioned object

Administrative justice

fairness and lawfulness of public-agency decisions affecting people

Administrative justice concerns whether public agencies make and apply decisions affecting people through fair and lawful procedures.

More about this term

In the U.S. example, a person facing loss of a benefit or license may have a right to be heard and a route to challenge the agency's decision.

The question is how public power is exercised and reviewed, rather than whether every affected person receives the outcome sought.

CC0 1.0View versioned object

Advanced product quality planning (APQP)

automotive-oriented product and production-process planning

Advanced product quality planning (APQP) is an automotive-oriented approach for coordinating how a product and its production process will meet customer requirements.

More about this term

It links planning, design, risk analysis, process preparation, and evidence of readiness before launch. Methods such as failure mode and effects analysis, measurement system analysis, and production part approval can contribute to that work.

APQP is a planning framework, not a single test or a synonym for product quality. Its particular deliverables depend on the applicable customer and industry requirements.

CC0 1.0View versioned object

Adverse event

patient harm associated with healthcare management

In patient safety, an adverse event is harm caused by health care rather than by the patient's underlying condition alone.

More about this term

It can arise from diagnosis, treatment, or other care; whether care caused the harm must be assessed rather than assumed from timing alone.

A near miss creates a risk of harm but does not meet this harm-based sense of adverse event.

CC0 1.0View versioned object

Aesthetic merit

worth of an object considered aesthetically

Aesthetic merit is the worth attributed to a work, scene, or other object on aesthetic grounds.

More about this term

A claim of merit should say what features or experience support the appraisal, rather than merely name a descriptive property.

Judgments may differ even among informed appreciators, so disagreement calls for reasons instead of an assumed universal score.

CC0 1.0View versioned object

Aesthetic quality

a characteristic ascribed in aesthetic attention

An aesthetic quality is a characteristic ascribed to something when attending to its aesthetic character.

More about this term

Rhythmic, balanced, and beautiful name different kinds of aesthetic qualities; some describe character, while others appraise it.

Identifying one such quality does not by itself establish the object's overall aesthetic merit.

CC0 1.0View versioned object

Affected party

person or group bearing effects of an activity or decision

An affected party is a person or group that may experience consequences from an activity or decision.

More about this term

The effects may concern access, conditions, benefits, burdens, or risks; identify them for the decision at hand.

A party can be affected without participating in the decision or having power over it.

CC0 1.0View versioned object

Aggregation rule

combining multiple component values for an evaluation

An aggregation rule specifies how several component values are combined into a summary value or judgment.

More about this term

It may use a sum, mean, weighting scheme, minimum, or another stated procedure; the choice affects the result.

State whether a strong result on one component may offset a weak result on another.

CC0 1.0View versioned object

AI quality

AI-enabled systems

AI quality is how well an AI-enabled system meets requirements for its intended use, considering the behavior of its software and the data on which it depends.

More about this term

A model's test score alone cannot establish the quality of the whole system; behavior can change with data and operating conditions.

CC0 1.0View versioned object

Algorithmic audit

clinical AI fairness assessment

In clinical AI, an algorithmic audit is a structured examination of a model and its supporting data against stated criteria for fair performance.

More about this term

It can compare results across patient groups and look for biases in training data or outputs; favorable average accuracy does not settle those questions.

CC0 1.0View versioned object

Alignment

AI-system behavior relative to human aims and constraints

In AI, alignment concerns how well a system's behavior follows the human aims, instructions, and constraints specified for its use.

More about this term

An AI system can perform a task capably yet still produce outputs that conflict with intended safety or preference requirements.

An alignment claim needs to identify whose aims matter, the use conditions, and the behavior used to test the claim.

CC0 1.0View versioned object

Alternative

possible action in a framed decision

In decision making, an alternative is a possible course of action that could be chosen within a stated decision frame.

More about this term

The options considered should reflect what can actually be done and the aims of the decision.

An outcome is what may follow a choice; it is not the action available to choose.

CC0 1.0View versioned object

Analyzability

software maintainability subcharacteristic in ISO/IEC 25010:2011

In software quality, analyzability is how effectively and efficiently maintainers can diagnose deficiencies, locate likely causes, and assess the impact of a proposed change.

More about this term

Clear structure, diagnostic information, and documentation can help people identify the parts that need modification.

Finding what should change is distinct from making the change safely; the latter also involves modifiability.

CC0 1.0View versioned object

Appearance quality

visible qualities of a product

Appearance quality is how well a product's visible features suit its purpose and the relevant viewer's expectations.

More about this term

Color, shape, finish, and visible workmanship can influence this judgment. A pleasing appearance alone does not establish the product's reliability or safety.

CC0 1.0View versioned object

Appraisal cost

quality-related spending to evaluate conformity or performance

An appraisal cost is a cost incurred to measure, inspect, test, or audit whether products, services, or processes meet relevant quality requirements.

More about this term

It pays for obtaining and evaluating evidence of conformity, such as a product inspection or process audit. Finding a defect is not the same as preventing it.

In cost-of-quality accounting, appraisal is distinct from prevention and from the costs of correcting failures. Where one activity serves several purposes, the accounting boundary should be stated.

CC0 1.0View versioned object

Appropriateness

fit of clinical care to the patient's condition and evidence

In clinical care, appropriateness concerns whether a proposed service or intervention fits a patient's condition and circumstances in light of evidence about its likely effects.

More about this term

The relevant patient group, clinical indication, and available alternatives affect that judgment.

Care can be delivered skillfully yet still be inappropriate if the intervention is not indicated for that patient.

CC0 1.0View versioned object

Architecture quality

software architecture's support for system requirements

In software engineering, architecture quality is how well a system's high-level structure supports its relevant requirements and quality attributes.

More about this term

Assess it through consequences for properties such as reliability, efficiency, and maintainability in the system's actual context.

A clear architecture diagram alone does not show that those properties will hold.

CC0 1.0View versioned object

Argument quality

informal argument assessment

Argument quality is how well the reasons offered for a claim meet appropriate standards and support that claim.

More about this term

In informal logic, relevance, acceptability, and sufficiency are common tests; persuasive effect alone does not show that those tests are met.

CC0 1.0View versioned object

Artistic quality

artworks and artistic performance

Artistic quality is the merit of an artwork or artistic performance in respects relevant to its artistic character.

More about this term

Formal and expressive qualities can matter, but novelty alone does not establish artistic merit.

CC0 1.0View versioned object

Assessment

purpose-bound examination

Assessment is the process of gathering and interpreting information about a specified subject for a stated question or decision.

More about this term

An assessment may compare evidence with requirements, criteria, or a reference, then report findings or a judgment. Its methods and evidential demands depend on its purpose.

The term is used differently across fields. It often overlaps with evaluation; an assessment need not always conclude with an overall appraisal of merit or worth.

CC0 1.0View versioned object

Assessment moderation

educational assessment

In education, assessment moderation is a process in which assessors review judgments and discuss standards to make grading more consistent and defensible.

More about this term

It can involve discussion of student work before or after grades are assigned; agreement between markers does not by itself prove the standards are sound.

CC0 1.0View versioned object

Assessment of student learning

evidence about student learning relative to expectations

Assessment of student learning is the deliberate collection and interpretation of evidence about what students know or can do in relation to stated learning expectations.

More about this term

Formative assessment uses findings to guide learning while it is underway; summative assessment appraises achievement at a defined point.

The evidence may come from work at the assignment, course, program, or degree level.

CC0 1.0View versioned object

Assurance

systems-engineering support for a claim

In systems engineering, assurance is a reasoned basis for trusting a particular claim about a system's behavior or properties.

More about this term

Name the claim and the grounds supporting it. The justification needed depends on the consequences if the system fails to behave as claimed.

Claims can concern safety, reliability, resilience, security, or privacy; assurance supports confidence without guaranteeing the outcome.

CC0 1.0View versioned object

Attestation

formal signed assertion about specified facts

An attestation is a formal assertion by an identified person or body that specified facts or conditions hold.

More about this term

It should make clear who is making the assertion, what is being asserted, and the scope or time to which it applies.

An attestation records an accountable claim; it does not by itself establish that the claim was independently verified.

CC0 1.0View versioned object

Attribute

descriptive property of an object

An attribute is a feature or property ascribed to, observed in, or recorded for an object.

More about this term

An attribute can be described by a category, a number, or words. Its recorded state is different from the attribute itself.

The label alone does not show that the feature is inherent, quality-relevant, or favorable. State the object and the role the attribute plays in the assessment.

CC0 1.0View versioned object

Audio quality

voice communication and videotelephony

In voice communication, audio quality is how well the received sound supports listening and understanding under stated conditions.

More about this term

Speech transmission can be assessed separately from video, although both contribute to the experience of a video call. A single sound-quality score need not explain which audible problems produced it.

CC0 1.0View versioned object

Audit

management-system audit

In management-system work, an audit is a systematic, independent, and documented examination of evidence against stated criteria to determine how far those criteria are met.

More about this term

The audit's scope identifies the activities, locations, and period covered.

A finding depends on the evidence and criteria examined; an audit is not a guarantee that every instance or future result will conform.

CC0 1.0View versioned object

Audit criteria

requirements used as a comparison basis in management-system auditing

In a management-system audit, audit criteria are the requirements used as the reference for judging audit evidence.

More about this term

They may come from policies, procedures, contracts, or applicable legal requirements.

The criteria state the basis for comparison; findings result from comparing relevant evidence with that basis.

CC0 1.0View versioned object

Audit evidence

verifiable information used in a management-system audit

In a management-system audit, audit evidence is verifiable information relevant to the audit criteria.

More about this term

It may consist of records, observed facts, or statements that can be checked.

Auditors compare it with the criteria to form findings; evidence alone is not an audit conclusion.

CC0 1.0View versioned object

Audit finding

result of evidence evaluation against audit criteria

An audit finding is a result of comparing collected audit evidence with the audit criteria.

More about this term

A finding can record that a requirement is met or identify a gap; it is not synonymous with a defect.

Findings inform the audit conclusion, which considers the audit’s objectives and the findings together.

CC0 1.0View versioned object

Authenticity

genuineness in aesthetic and artistic practice

In aesthetic practice, authenticity is an appraisal that a work, performance, or experience is genuine in a respect that matters to that practice.

More about this term

The relevant respect may concern its origins, recognizable features, or the maker's expression; these are distinct accounts rather than one universal test.

An authenticity claim should state the respect and practice at issue. Authenticity alone does not settle overall merit, and its standards can be applied unfairly.

CC0 1.0View versioned object

Authority

delegated decision and resource power in project governance

In project governance, authority is an assigned power to make decisions or commit resources within a defined remit.

More about this term

A clear assignment identifies who holds that power, which decisions it covers, and its limits.

Expertise or a stake in the decision does not, by itself, confer authority to make it.

CC0 1.0View versioned object

Autonomy

patient decision-making in healthcare ethics

In healthcare ethics, autonomy is a person's authority to make decisions about their own care in light of their values and informed understanding.

More about this term

Respecting autonomy calls for information about the proposed care, material risks, and available alternatives before consent is sought.

It concerns the person's decision-making role, not a guarantee that every requested treatment is available or appropriate.

CC0 1.0View versioned object

Availability

operability of an engineered system when needed

For an engineered system, availability is the probability or proportion of time that it is operable when needed under stated conditions.

More about this term

It can be estimated from uptime or from how often the system works when called upon; those calculations answer related but different questions.

State the observation period and operating conditions before comparing availability results.

CC0 1.0View versioned object

Average outgoing quality

expected outgoing nonconforming fraction under rectifying sampling

Average outgoing quality (AOQ) is the expected fraction of nonconforming units leaving a rectifying acceptance-sampling process at a stated incoming quality level.

More about this term

Accepted lots pass through, while rejected lots are inspected and nonconforming units are replaced under the assumed plan.

AOQ describes a long-run expectation for that plan and incoming quality; it is not the measured quality of one outgoing lot.

CC0 1.0View versioned object

Average outgoing quality limit

maximum expected outgoing nonconforming fraction for rectifying sampling plan

The average outgoing quality limit (AOQL) is the highest average outgoing quality predicted for a rectifying sampling plan across possible incoming quality levels.

More about this term

It is the peak of the plan's AOQ curve when rejected lots are inspected and nonconforming units are replaced as assumed.

AOQL describes a maximum long-run expectation under that plan, not a guarantee about every outgoing lot.

CC0 1.0View versioned object
B15 terms

Balance

representation of perspectives in news reporting

In journalism, balance is the distribution of attention and representation among relevant sides or perspectives in a news account.

More about this term

A balanced account may give each side a chance to be heard, but equal space or symmetrical quotations do not by themselves establish accuracy or fairness.

Judging balance therefore requires attention to what evidence supports each claim and which perspectives are relevant.

CC0 1.0View versioned object

Baseline

starting reference in program evaluation

In program evaluation, a baseline is an initial assessment used as the reference for later comparison.

More about this term

It records a program or population's condition before a later observation, often before an intervention.

A change from baseline shows a difference over time; the comparison alone does not establish what caused it.

CC0 1.0View versioned object

Batch release

EU advanced-therapy medicinal product manufacture

For an advanced-therapy medicinal product under EU GMP, batch release is the controlled step that permits a specified batch to be supplied or used after the required review and certification.

More about this term

The review covers relevant manufacturing records, tests, deviations, and applicable authorization requirements before a qualified person certifies the batch.

Certification and assigning release status are distinct steps; a finished batch remains under control until the release step is completed.

CC0 1.0View versioned object

Bathtub curve

schematic reliability hazard-rate pattern

A bathtub curve is a schematic plot of failure rate against age that falls early, stays roughly level for a period, and then rises.

More about this term

Its three regions are commonly interpreted as early failures, approximately constant-rate failures, and wear-out failures.

It is a possible population pattern, not a rule that every item follows or proof that the changes occur at sharp, universal ages.

CC0 1.0View versioned object

Benchmark

evaluation comparison reference

A benchmark is a reference for comparison.

More about this term

In evaluation, it helps answer “How does this result compare with what a relevant peer has achieved, or with what appears achievable under similar conditions?”

A relevant comparison may use recent performance by similar organizations or a reasoned estimate of what is achievable under similar conditions.

In some uses, a benchmark specifically represents leading practice or performance.

Thus, a benchmark need not mean “the best” in every field.

CC0 1.0View versioned object

Benchmarking

organizational performance and practice comparison for improvement

Benchmarking is a planned comparison of an organization's practice or performance with a relevant reference to identify differences and possible improvements.

More about this term

The reference may be another organization or an appropriate practice or performance level; the basis of comparison should be stated.

A measured gap helps focus inquiry, but it does not show by itself why the gap exists or which change will close it.

CC0 1.0View versioned object

Benefit

favorable change for a specified beneficiary

A benefit is a favorable change or consequence for a specified party, judged against a stated purpose or interest.

More about this term

A planned output may enable a benefit, but delivering the output does not show that the benefit occurred.

Name the beneficiary and period: a gain for one group need not be a gain for everyone.

CC0 1.0View versioned object

Best practice

comparatively strong organizational method

A best practice is a method judged especially effective for a specified purpose compared with available alternatives.

More about this term

The label may reflect recognition by peer organizations and evidence of improved performance.

It is a comparative claim whose usefulness depends on the setting; the label does not guarantee that copying the method elsewhere will work.

CC0 1.0View versioned object

Bias

systematic measurement difference from reference

In measurement, bias is a systematic difference between measured results and the quantity or reference value they are meant to represent.

More about this term

Repeated readings can agree closely with one another yet still be shifted from the reference.

Bias concerns the direction and size of that shift; precision concerns agreement among repeated readings.

CC0 1.0View versioned object

Bioavailability

availability of an active drug after administration

For a drug product, bioavailability describes how quickly and to what extent its active ingredient or active moiety becomes available at the site where it acts.

More about this term

A product's stated drug content alone does not establish its bioavailability; formulation and administration can affect absorption.

Bioavailability may be a desired product characteristic, while dissolution is one laboratory observation that can help assess it for some dosage forms.

CC0 1.0View versioned object

Biodiversity

variety of living organisms in a specified ecological setting

Biodiversity is variation among living organisms within and across species and ecosystems.

More about this term

A count of species describes only one aspect; it does not by itself capture variation within species or among ecosystems.

A biodiversity claim should identify the place, scale, and aspect of living variety being considered.

CC0 1.0View versioned object

Bioequivalence

comparative active-drug availability from products

Bioequivalence is a supported finding that two pharmaceutical equivalents or alternatives make the relevant active ingredient or active moiety available at the site of action at comparable rates and extents, when tested at the same molar dose under similar conditions.

More about this term

The products may differ in inactive ingredients; the comparison concerns drug availability, not every product characteristic.

Specific rules can allow certain intentional rate differences. The study method and decision criteria depend on the products.

CC0 1.0View versioned object

Boundary condition

stated limit on engineering or problem-framing scope

A boundary condition states a limit or assumption within which an engineering task, model, or inquiry is considered.

More about this term

It can specify such limits as available resources, time, relevant functions, or whose interests the inquiry includes.

Changing a boundary condition can change which solutions appear feasible or which concerns the analysis addresses.

CC0 1.0View versioned object

Building performance

building operation relative to stated functional goals

Building performance is how a building functions against stated goals and requirements under its conditions of use.

More about this term

Relevant evidence may include energy use and indoor environmental conditions during occupancy.

Predicted and observed performance can differ because construction quality and occupants' behavior affect the result.

CC0 1.0View versioned object

Burden

adverse load borne by an affected party in an evaluation

A burden is a cost, effort, loss, or other adverse load borne by someone under an activity or condition.

More about this term

Identify who bears it, its form, extent, and time period; a burden can be financial or nonfinancial.

A benefit to one group does not erase a burden borne by another.

CC0 1.0View versioned object
C117 terms

Calibration

metrological relation between reference values and indications

Calibration is an operation that establishes how a measuring instrument’s indications relate to reference quantity values under stated conditions, accounting for their uncertainties.

More about this term

That relation is then used to obtain a measurement result from an indication. A useful calibration record identifies the references, conditions, results, and uncertainties relevant to its use.

Calibration does not necessarily adjust the instrument or make every later result accurate. Adjustment is a separate action, and changes in conditions or the instrument can affect the relation.

CC0 1.0View versioned object

Capability

project outputs that enable an organizational outcome

In project management, a capability is the combined ability created by completed outputs that lets an organization pursue an intended outcome.

More about this term

A new system and trained staff, for example, may create a capability before its intended benefit occurs.

Having the capability does not itself show that the organization has used it or achieved the benefit.

CC0 1.0View versioned object

Care coordination

alignment of services across healthcare participants

Care coordination is the deliberate alignment of care activities among the people and services involved in a patient's care.

More about this term

It includes sharing relevant information and arranging how one service connects with the next, especially when the patient moves between settings.

Its aim is that the parts of care work together for the patient rather than proceed as disconnected episodes.

CC0 1.0View versioned object

Case management quality

health and social care coordination

Case management quality is how well assessment, planning, coordination, and review of services respond to a person's changing needs and preferences.

More about this term

A shared plan and clear coordinator can help prevent gaps between providers. The judgment also depends on whether the person can access and use the support arranged.

CC0 1.0View versioned object

Catchball

iterative participation in hoshin planning and policy deployment

In hoshin planning, catchball is an iterative exchange of proposed goals and plans among organizational levels and functions to reach workable agreement.

More about this term

People expected to carry out a plan can return concerns about resources, timing, or feasibility before the plan is settled.

The proposals move across and back through the organization as conflicts are resolved and action plans are refined.

CC0 1.0View versioned object

Causal claim

empirical inference about causes

A causal claim asserts that a factor helps bring about a specified outcome, beyond merely occurring alongside it.

More about this term

A clear claim names the factor, outcome, and conditions of interest. Supporting it requires a justified account of the causal process or comparison; association alone is insufficient.

CC0 1.0View versioned object

Causal factor

potential or established contributor to a specified effect in quality analysis

A causal factor is a condition or action that contributes to a specified outcome or problem.

More about this term

Name the outcome and the way the factor is thought to affect it; a cause-and-effect diagram can organize candidate factors.

Listing a factor on a diagram proposes a causal explanation, which still needs evidence before it is treated as established.

CC0 1.0View versioned object

Causal hypothesis

empirical causal inquiry

A causal hypothesis is a proposed claim that a specified factor helps bring about a specified outcome under stated conditions.

More about this term

It goes beyond saying that the factor and outcome vary together; its support depends on evidence and assumptions suited to the claimed causal relation.

CC0 1.0View versioned object

Cause-and-effect diagram

diagram of possible contributors to a specified effect

A cause-and-effect diagram arranges proposed causes and subcauses around a defined problem or outcome.

More about this term

Its branching shape gives it the name fishbone diagram; Ishikawa diagram names its creator.

The branches organize possibilities for investigation; drawing them does not establish causation.

CC0 1.0View versioned object

Ceiling effect

upper-limit compression in a score scale

A ceiling effect occurs when a measure's upper limit prevents it from distinguishing higher levels of the attribute it is meant to assess.

More about this term

When many people score at or near the maximum, genuine differences or later improvement may be hidden.

The effect depends on the instrument and population; a high score alone does not establish how far beyond the scale's limit someone might be.

CC0 1.0View versioned object

Certainty of evidence

GRADE confidence in an outcome-specific evidence body

In GRADE reviews, certainty of evidence is a judgment about how much confidence to place in the evidence for a specified outcome.

More about this term

It is rated high, moderate, low, or very low after considering such concerns as bias, inconsistency, indirectness, imprecision, and publication bias.

The rating belongs to an outcome and its supporting evidence, not automatically to an entire study or review.

CC0 1.0View versioned object

Certification

management-system conformity assessment

In management-system practice, certification is a third-party attestation, following an assessment, that an organization's management system meets specified requirements.

More about this term

The certificate identifies the system and standard assessed; it does not certify each product or guarantee every future result.

Certification of an individual professional is a different use of the same word.

CC0 1.0View versioned object

Change

difference between states in project or evaluation work

In project and evaluation work, a change is a difference between an earlier and a later state of a specified subject.

More about this term

For planned organizational change, state the starting condition, intended condition, and what actually became different.

A delivered project output can enable change without showing that the intended outcome occurred.

CC0 1.0View versioned object

Change control

governed change to a controlled product, process or system

Change control is a process for identifying a proposed change, assessing its effects, authorizing it, and recording what was done and the resulting state.

More about this term

The depth of review should fit the change and its potential effects on quality, safety, compliance, and operation. Implementation may require updated procedures, records, or renewed validation.

A record that something changed is not enough: control also requires a decision about whether and how the change may proceed.

CC0 1.0View versioned object

Change control system

arrangements for controlled engineering and software changes

A change control system is the set of roles, procedures, and records used to identify, evaluate, authorize, and document changes to controlled items or processes.

More about this term

It assigns responsibility for reviewing change requests and retains decisions and records of the resulting state.

A change control process is the sequence followed for a particular change; the system supports consistent control across changes.

CC0 1.0View versioned object

Change management

organizational transition in quality improvement

In organizational improvement, change management is the planned work of helping people and processes move from a present way of operating to an intended one.

More about this term

It addresses roles, sponsorship, communication, learning, and the practices needed to make the new way of working take hold.

In software configuration management, the same phrase can instead mean formal control of change requests; that narrower sense should be named when intended.

CC0 1.0View versioned object

Change request

proposal initiating formal change control

In change control, a change request is a documented proposal to alter a controlled product, process, document, or system, submitted for evaluation before implementation.

More about this term

It identifies the proposed change, why it is sought, and what may be affected. Reviewers then assess its effects and decide whether to authorize it.

Submitting a request starts the review; it does not itself permit the change to be made.

CC0 1.0View versioned object

Characteristic

descriptive feature of an object

A characteristic is a distinguishable feature by which an object can be described.

More about this term

It may be observed directly, inferred, or assigned in a description. Naming a characteristic does not say whether it is desirable.

To use one in a quality judgment, identify the object and explain how that feature bears on an applicable requirement or other stated basis.

CC0 1.0View versioned object

Check sheet

structured recording of observations for quality analysis

A check sheet is a structured form for recording observations or occurrences according to defined categories.

More about this term

Its categories and collection conditions should be specified before use so the resulting data can be interpreted.

A check sheet records data for later analysis; a checklist instead prompts actions to complete.

CC0 1.0View versioned object

Checklist

task guidance and verification list

A checklist is an organized list of items to consider, perform, or verify for a defined task.

More about this term

It can prompt actions and record responses such as yes, no, or not applicable.

Completing it does not by itself prove that a process conforms; observations and records may still be needed.

CC0 1.0View versioned object

Citizen satisfaction

citizens' subjective appraisal of public services

Citizen satisfaction is citizens' appraisal of a public service in a specified context.

More about this term

The appraisal can reflect the service process and outcome, expectations, and direct or indirect experience.

A satisfaction score is therefore not an unqualified measure of objective service performance.

CC0 1.0View versioned object

Claim

assertion offered for assessment

A claim is a statement put forward for acceptance that can be supported, qualified, or challenged.

More about this term

Claims can concern facts, values, or proposed actions. State the specific assertion and its scope so the evidence needed to assess it can be identified.

A claim is distinct from the evidence offered for it. Finding similar words in a source does not show that the source supports the same assertion.

CC0 1.0View versioned object

Clarity

comprehensibility of communication for an intended audience

In communication, clarity is the ease with which an intended audience can understand a message and how its parts fit together.

More about this term

Word choice, structure, and needed background can all affect clarity for that audience.

A clear account can still be inaccurate or incomplete; those are separate qualities.

CC0 1.0View versioned object

Classical test theory

observed test scores as true scores plus measurement error

Classical test theory is a measurement framework that models an observed test score as a true score plus error.

More about this term

Here, the true score is the expected score across appropriate hypothetical repetitions of the testing procedure, not a directly observed ability.

The framework helps examine score consistency and measurement error.

CC0 1.0View versioned object

Classification

assignment to a defined category in machine learning

In machine learning, classification assigns an item to one of a defined set of categories using information about that item.

More about this term

A classifier can learn the assignment rule from examples whose correct categories are known.

Good performance on its training examples alone does not show that the rule will work on new cases.

CC0 1.0View versioned object

Cleaning validation

EU ATMP manufacturing equipment cleaning

In advanced-therapy medicinal product manufacture, cleaning validation is documented evidence that a specified cleaning procedure repeatedly reduces relevant residues or contaminants below predefined acceptable limits.

More about this term

The study defines the procedure, sampling approach, and acceptance criteria for the equipment and contamination risks concerned.

It assesses the procedure's repeatable capability; cleaning verification checks a particular batch or campaign after cleaning.

CC0 1.0View versioned object

Client-centered care

health-care service delivery

Client-centered care organizes health services around the needs, circumstances, and participation of the person receiving care.

More about this term

The client must have a real role in decisions; calling a service client-centered is insufficient if provider convenience still controls care.

CC0 1.0View versioned object

Clinical quality

clinical aspects of health care in relation to patient needs and outcomes

Clinical quality is how well clinical care uses appropriate knowledge and practices to serve patients' health needs and desired outcomes.

More about this term

It includes attention to effective care and patient safety; an observed outcome alone may not show which aspect of care caused it.

Access and courtesy matter to patients, but they do not by themselves establish clinical quality.

CC0 1.0View versioned object

Code compliance

conformity to applicable construction regulatory provisions

In construction, code compliance is the extent to which a design or completed work meets the regulatory provisions that apply to it.

More about this term

A defensible check identifies the governing code, the relevant provisions, the project conditions, and the evidence used to assess them.

Meeting a code is a minimum regulatory judgment; it does not by itself show that every project goal or user need has been met.

CC0 1.0View versioned object

Code coverage

software testing

Code coverage is the extent to which specified parts of a program are executed when a test suite runs.

More about this term

Name what is counted, such as statements or branches. Even complete coverage does not show that the tests check the program's behavior effectively.

CC0 1.0View versioned object

Coherence

fit among parts of an argument

In argumentation, coherence is the intelligible fit among an account's claims, reasons, and inferential links.

More about this term

A reader should be able to follow how the parts belong together, including any unstated premises needed to connect them.

An argument can be coherent yet unpersuasive if its premises lack credible evidence or its support is insufficient.

CC0 1.0View versioned object

Commissioning

testing building systems before operational use

In construction, commissioning is a planned process for checking that installed building systems work as intended for the owner's requirements.

More about this term

It can include project-specific functional tests, documentation, and training for people who will operate or maintain the systems.

Commissioning supplements ordinary start-up and balancing tests; completing installation alone does not establish that the systems perform as required.

CC0 1.0View versioned object

Common cause

statistical process control

In process control, a common cause is an ordinary influence within a process that contributes to its ongoing background variation.

More about this term

Common-cause variation is part of the process's usual operation. A special cause is an unusual assignable influence that calls for separate investigation.

CC0 1.0View versioned object

Common-cause variation

routine variation inherent in a process as it currently operates

Common-cause variation is the ongoing variation produced by the recurring influences within a process as it currently operates.

More about this term

When those influences remain sufficiently stable, results vary within a pattern that can be estimated from process data. A single high or low result within that pattern does not by itself identify a new cause.

Reducing this variation generally requires changing the process or its conditions, rather than reacting separately to each observation.

CC0 1.0View versioned object

Communication quality

interpersonal and organizational communication

Communication quality is how well a message or exchange serves the relevant goals of its participants in its setting.

More about this term

Clarity, responsiveness, timing, and sensitivity to the audience may matter; sending more messages does not by itself make communication better.

CC0 1.0View versioned object

Comparison

examining options on a shared stated basis

A comparison examines two or more objects or options on a stated shared basis to identify similarities or differences.

More about this term

When comparing options for a decision, specify the criteria, conditions, and evidence used for each.

Finding a difference does not by itself establish which option is better; that requires a relevant evaluative basis.

CC0 1.0View versioned object

Compatibility

software-system coexistence and interoperability

In software quality, compatibility concerns how well a product or system works with others by sharing an environment or exchanging usable information.

More about this term

Coexistence concerns shared resources without harmful interference; interoperability concerns exchanging information that can be used.

Name the other systems and operating conditions, because compatibility is a relation between them, not an isolated property.

CC0 1.0View versioned object

Competence

ability to perform a specified role or task

Competence is the ability to perform a specified role or task using relevant knowledge and skills under the conditions that matter.

More about this term

Training or a credential may provide evidence of competence, but neither alone shows that a person can perform the work.

A useful competence judgment identifies the task, expected level of performance, and conditions of performance.

CC0 1.0View versioned object

Competitive assessment

comparison with alternatives in a House of Quality

In a House of Quality, competitive assessment compares an offering with relevant alternatives on customer requirements, technical characteristics, or both.

More about this term

A customer-side comparison asks how alternatives satisfy the needs customers care about. A technical-side comparison examines the corresponding design characteristics; the two comparisons should be kept distinct.

The result depends on which alternatives, evidence, and scales are used. It can inform priorities or targets, but it does not by itself determine the best design.

CC0 1.0View versioned object

Completeness

presence of required data for a specified use

For data, completeness is the extent to which relevant expected values are present.

More about this term

Which values count as expected depends on the task and the records being assessed.

Completeness is distinct from accuracy: a field can be filled yet contain an incorrect value.

CC0 1.0View versioned object

Completion

finishing a defined educational course or program

In education, completion is finishing a specified course or program according to its stated requirements.

More about this term

A completion rate depends on which learners are counted, the time period, and what counts as finishing.

Completion need not imply a credential or independently demonstrated learning; those depend on the program and its assessments.

CC0 1.0View versioned object

Compliance

meeting applicable obligations in a governed activity

Compliance is meeting the obligations that apply to an activity, product, or organization.

More about this term

The obligations may come from law, regulation, contract, or an adopted policy or standard; first establish which provisions actually apply.

Evidence of compliance with one requirement does not establish compliance with every other applicable requirement.

CC0 1.0View versioned object

Composite indicator

aggregate-index and constitutive-component technical uses

In one common use, a composite indicator is a single index formed by combining several indicators according to a stated rule.

More about this term

The choice of components, scales, weights, and combination rule affects what the index represents and how cases rank. Its score should be interpreted with those choices in view.

In some measurement models, the same term instead names an item that helps constitute the concept being indexed, rather than merely reflecting it. State which sense is intended.

CC0 1.0View versioned object

Concession

bounded authorization to use or release a nonconforming output

In quality management, a concession is permission to use or release a product or service even though it does not meet a specified requirement.

More about this term

The permission should identify the departure and its limits, such as quantity, time, or intended use.

It authorizes that particular exception; it does not make the product or service conforming or waive other requirements.

CC0 1.0View versioned object

Condition

circumstance or prerequisite affecting the applicability of a claim or result

A condition is a circumstance or prerequisite that determines when a statement, process, or result applies.

More about this term

In measurement, relevant conditions can include the environment, equipment state, user, and timing.

A result obtained under one set of conditions may not support the same claim under another.

CC0 1.0View versioned object

Confidence

strength of trust in an evidence-based estimate or conclusion

In evidence appraisal, confidence is the degree of trust placed in a specified estimate or conclusion given the available evidence and its limitations.

More about this term

It is tied to the outcome and intended use; the same studies may support different levels of confidence for different outcomes.

An evidence-confidence judgment is not the same as a statistical confidence interval or the strength of a recommendation.

CC0 1.0View versioned object

Confidence interval

frequentist interval estimation of a population parameter

A confidence interval is an interval calculated from sample data by a method designed to capture a specified population parameter at a stated rate across repeated samples.

More about this term

For example, under the method's assumptions, a 95% confidence-interval procedure covers the fixed parameter in about 95% of repeated applications.

The stated percentage describes the procedure's long-run coverage, not the probability that the fixed parameter lies in one already calculated interval.

CC0 1.0View versioned object

Configuration

identified selection and versions of software-system components

In software engineering, a configuration is a specified selection of components and versions that together constitute a system at a given point.

More about this term

A baseline records which items belong to a chosen configuration so that later changes can be traced.

A configuration is the identified arrangement; configuration management is the work of controlling and recording changes to it.

CC0 1.0View versioned object

Configuration item

separately identified unit under software configuration management

In software configuration management, a configuration item is a separately identifiable unit of information managed as part of a system.

More about this term

It may be a requirement, design document, source file, or other item whose identity and changes need tracking.

The item is one controlled unit; a configuration specifies a selection of items and their versions together.

CC0 1.0View versioned object

Configuration management

identified components and controlled change in evolving software systems

In software engineering, configuration management identifies a system's components and controls changes to them so its versions and current state remain traceable.

More about this term

It uses identified items, baselines, version records, and change decisions to show what belongs in a particular configuration.

Version control is one part of the work; it does not alone establish which combination was approved, built, or released.

CC0 1.0View versioned object

Confirmability

qualitative research trustworthiness

In qualitative research, confirmability is the extent to which findings can be traced to participants' accounts and the analytic record while the researcher's influence is made visible.

More about this term

Transparent methods, reflexivity, and attention to contrary accounts help others assess it; identical results on repetition are not its defining test.

CC0 1.0View versioned object

Conformance

meeting stated requirements

Conformance is the state or degree to which an object or activity meets applicable requirements or a stated specification.

More about this term

A conformance claim needs to identify the object, the requirements checked, and the evidence used. Meeting a specification establishes only what that specification covers; it may leave a user’s other needs unaddressed.

Conformance and conformity are often used interchangeably. Neither word, by itself, names a distinct kind of quality.

CC0 1.0View versioned object

Conformance quality

realized product or service against design requirements

Conformance quality is the extent to which a produced item or delivered service matches its specified design and requirements.

More about this term

Assess it against the applicable specifications, tolerances, or acceptance criteria for the output.

Strong conformance shows faithful execution of a design; it does not establish that the design itself meets users' needs.

CC0 1.0View versioned object

Conformity

fulfillment of an applicable requirement

Conformity is the condition of meeting an applicable requirement.

More about this term

A claim of conformity should say which object and requirement are involved. When several requirements apply, identify the set covered by the claim and how fulfillment was established.

Conformity to a requirement does not guarantee suitability for every use. In many contexts, conformance names the same relationship.

CC0 1.0View versioned object

Conformity assessment

determining whether relevant requirements are fulfilled

Conformity assessment is the determination of whether an object fulfills relevant specified requirements.

More about this term

The object, requirements, assessment method, and scope must be clear. Depending on the case, assessment may use testing, inspection, or certification.

A conformity result addresses the requirements actually assessed; it does not, by itself, establish overall excellence or fitness for every use.

CC0 1.0View versioned object

Consequence

effect of an event or action on an objective or interest

A consequence is an effect that follows from an event, action, or decision and matters to an objective or interest.

More about this term

A decision may have several consequences, favorable or harmful, immediate or delayed. Specify the effect, who or what bears it, and the period considered.

An outcome after a decision is not automatically caused by that decision. Assess alternative causes and uncertainty before assigning responsibility for the consequence.

CC0 1.0View versioned object

Consistency

similarity of comparable outputs in a specified respect

In quality assessment, consistency is the degree to which comparable outputs or performances remain alike in a specified respect.

More about this term

A useful claim of consistency names the characteristic, occasions, and conditions being compared.

Consistent results can still fail a requirement, so consistency alone does not establish quality.

CC0 1.0View versioned object

Constant failure rate

time-invariant conditional failure rate of surviving items

A constant failure rate is a failure rate that remains the same over a specified interval for items that have survived to each time in that interval.

More about this term

For items alive at a chosen time origin, if the rate lambda stays constant through the next t units of time, the chance of surviving that interval is e^(-lambda t).

The model does not say that every item fails at the same age; an item's chance of surviving from the start still declines with elapsed time.

CC0 1.0View versioned object

Construct

conceptual vocabulary in design research

In design research, a construct is a concept used to describe a problem or solution domain.

More about this term

Constructs provide the vocabulary from which a model can state relationships.

Clarifying what a construct includes helps people use it consistently across a design or inquiry.

CC0 1.0View versioned object

Construct validity

test-score interpretation concerning an intended construct

Construct validity concerns how well evidence supports interpreting test scores as reflecting a specified construct for a stated population and use.

More about this term

The evidence can address the test's content, the behavior of scores, and their relationships with other variables.

Validity belongs to the proposed interpretation and use of the scores; it is not a permanent certificate attached to the test.

CC0 1.0View versioned object

Constructability

buildability of a proposed construction design

In construction, constructability is the degree to which a proposed project can be built as designed using workable methods and resources.

More about this term

Reviewing the design early can reveal site, sequencing, coordination, or method problems before construction begins.

A project's eventual usefulness is a separate question from whether its design can be built.

CC0 1.0View versioned object

Construction quality

project work and built asset against applicable requirements

Construction quality is how well the design and construction work, and the resulting asset, meet applicable project requirements and intended performance.

More about this term

Requirements may concern materials, workmanship, completed characteristics, and performance in use. They must be tied to the particular project and contract.

Passing one inspection establishes only what that check covered, not the quality of the whole asset.

CC0 1.0View versioned object

Consumer surplus

buyer benefit expressed as willingness-to-pay gap

Consumer surplus is the difference between the most a buyer would pay for a good or service and the amount actually paid.

More about this term

For a particular purchase, it expresses the buyer's modeled gain from paying less than that maximum.

Its estimate depends on how willingness to pay is assessed; it is neither the seller's profit nor a complete account of the good's value.

CC0 1.0View versioned object

Consumer test

sensory product evaluation

In sensory product evaluation, a consumer test asks intended consumers to assess a product, often for liking, acceptability, or preference.

More about this term

It captures consumer response under the test conditions; it is different from a trained panel's description of sensory attributes.

CC0 1.0View versioned object

Containment

immediate limitation of a detected quality problem's impact

In quality problem response, containment is immediate action to limit the reach or impact of a detected defect or nonconformity.

More about this term

It may involve identifying affected units, segregating them, or preventing further use or delivery while the issue is assessed.

Containment protects against further effects; corrective action addresses causes so the problem is less likely to recur.

CC0 1.0View versioned object

Content validity

test-content evidence for a specified score use

Content validity concerns whether a test's items and tasks adequately represent the domain it is meant to assess for a specified interpretation and use.

More about this term

Important parts of the domain should be covered without letting irrelevant material dominate.

Reviewing content supplies one kind of validity evidence; it does not establish that every proposed use of the scores is warranted.

CC0 1.0View versioned object

Contestability

ability to challenge and seek review of a consequential decision

Contestability is the practical ability to challenge a decision, claim, or system output and seek a reasoned response.

More about this term

For consequential decisions, it depends on knowing what was decided, having a usable way to raise a challenge, and receiving a review capable of addressing it.

A formal appeal is one way to provide contestability, but the opportunity to question and correct an output can exist outside an appeal process.

CC0 1.0View versioned object

Context

circumstances relevant to interpreting or judging an object or action

Context is the set of circumstances that helps determine what an object, statement, action, or result means and how it should be judged.

More about this term

For a quality judgment, relevant context can include the intended use, users, setting, applicable requirements, and constraints. State the circumstances that could change the interpretation.

Context does not excuse an unsupported claim. It tells the reader which conditions the claim applies to and where its conclusion may no longer hold.

CC0 1.0View versioned object

Continuity of care

coherence of a patient's care across time and settings

Continuity of care is the extent to which a person's care remains connected and coherent over time and across providers or settings.

More about this term

Relevant information and plans should carry across transitions so that each episode can build on what came before.

Coordination is work used to achieve continuity; continuity describes a quality of the care the person receives.

CC0 1.0View versioned object

Continuous improvement

recurring evidence-guided improvement work

Continuous improvement is recurring, organized work to improve how a process or system meets its aims.

More about this term

It starts with a stated need and a proposed change, then checks what actually happened. An unsuccessful test can still produce useful learning.

Effective changes should become part of routine practice and remain open to later review. Continuous does not mean that performance rises without interruption or that every change is beneficial.

CC0 1.0View versioned object

Continuous quality improvement

repeated evidence-informed quality improvement

Continuous quality improvement is an ongoing, organized effort to improve quality through repeated tests of change and learning from their results.

More about this term

Teams can plan a change, try it, examine what happened, and decide whether to adapt, adopt, or abandon it.

One successful fix is a change; sustained improvement requires checking what follows and continuing to learn.

CC0 1.0View versioned object

Control

regulation of process conditions in quality management

In quality management, control is an action or arrangement used to regulate process conditions or activities so results can meet stated requirements.

More about this term

A control arrangement identifies what to monitor, the acceptable range or rule, and who responds when results deviate.

Recording results without a response rule is monitoring, but not a complete arrangement for control.

CC0 1.0View versioned object

Control chart

time-ordered process variation chart

A control chart is a time-ordered display of a process measure with a centerline and statistically derived control limits, used to detect signals of process change.

More about this term

Points beyond a limit or certain nonrandom patterns can prompt investigation of a special cause. Chart type, sampling plan, and signal rules must fit the data and process.

Control limits describe expected process behavior under the chart model. They are different from specification limits, which state what an output is required to meet.

CC0 1.0View versioned object

Control limit

statistical process-control chart boundary

A control limit is a boundary on a control chart, calculated from process data, that helps flag variation needing investigation.

More about this term

Upper and lower limits depend on the chart and the process statistic being tracked.

They describe expected process behavior under the chart's assumptions; they are not specifications for whether an individual product is acceptable.

CC0 1.0View versioned object

Control plan

documented arrangements for monitoring and responding to process variation

A control plan is a document specifying how a defined process and its important characteristics will be monitored and what action follows when results depart from stated conditions.

More about this term

It commonly names what to check, the method and frequency, the acceptable limits, who records results, and what to do when a limit is breached.

A chart or target alone is not a complete control plan: people also need responsibility and response instructions for ongoing operation.

CC0 1.0View versioned object

Convergent validity

evidence from predicted relations among measures of related constructs

Convergent validity is evidence that scores relate to other measures of the same or related constructs as the intended interpretation predicts.

More about this term

The expected relation should be stated in advance and judged alongside other validity evidence.

A strong correlation alone cannot establish that two measures capture the intended construct.

CC0 1.0View versioned object

Correction

immediate fix for a detected nonconformity in quality management

In quality management, a correction is an action that fixes a detected nonconformity.

More about this term

Repairing or reworking the affected output can be a correction.

Correction addresses the present problem; corrective action addresses its cause to reduce recurrence.

CC0 1.0View versioned object

Corrective action

addressing causes of a detected nonconformity

Corrective action addresses the cause of a detected nonconformity or other unwanted situation so it does not recur.

More about this term

Repairing or replacing one affected item corrects that case. Corrective action changes the condition that produced it; the two may both be needed.

The action should follow an investigation proportionate to the problem. Its effectiveness must be checked against later evidence rather than assumed from implementation alone.

CC0 1.0View versioned object

Corrective and preventive action

CAPA approach to actual and potential quality problems

Corrective and preventive action, or CAPA, is a structured approach to addressing actual and potential quality problems through the actions appropriate to each case.

More about this term

It distinguishes correcting a detected case, addressing a cause of recurrence, and addressing a cause of a potential problem. These are different tasks; a case does not automatically require every kind of action.

A CAPA record can connect investigation, planned actions, implementation, and an effectiveness check. Its purpose is to show that the response fits the problem and that the intended change occurred.

CC0 1.0View versioned object

Correlation matrix

technical-interaction roof in a House of Quality

In a House of Quality, the correlation matrix is a roof-shaped grid for assessing how proposed technical characteristics interact with one another.

More about this term

A positive mark suggests that changes may reinforce one another; a negative mark flags a possible conflict or trade-off. The meaning of each mark depends on the method and evidence used.

In this use, “correlation” need not mean a calculated statistical correlation coefficient. The roof records design judgments unless a separate analysis establishes measured relationships.

CC0 1.0View versioned object

Corroboration

additional evidence supporting a particular claim

Corroboration is support for a claim from additional evidence that bears on the same point.

More about this term

A separate observation, record, method, or witness can strengthen a claim when it agrees on a relevant detail.

Repeating one unsupported account does not create independent corroboration, and corroborating one part of a claim does not prove the rest.

CC0 1.0View versioned object

Cost

organizational spending for an activity or option

In organizational planning, a cost is an expenditure or resource commitment attributable to an activity, output, or proposed option.

More about this term

Costs may be direct or indirect, and an estimate should state whose costs, which activities, and what period it covers.

An estimated cost differs from an expense already incurred; cost alone does not establish whether an option is worth pursuing.

CC0 1.0View versioned object

Cost analysis

resource costs in decision evaluation

Cost analysis is a systematic examination of the costs associated with an activity or option to inform a decision.

More about this term

It requires stating which resources and time period count and whose costs are included. Estimating costs alone does not show whether an option achieves a valued outcome.

CC0 1.0View versioned object

Cost of poor quality (COPQ)

costs attributable to defects and other quality failures

Cost of poor quality (COPQ) is the estimated cost attributable to failures to meet relevant quality requirements.

More about this term

It can include scrap and rework found before delivery, and returns, warranty work, complaints, or other consequences found afterward. Some costs are difficult to observe or assign.

An estimate needs a stated accounting boundary, time period, and basis for attributing costs. Prevention and appraisal costs are often reported separately as costs of achieving quality; naming the convention avoids misleading comparisons.

CC0 1.0View versioned object

Cost of quality

costs of achieving and failing to achieve quality

Cost of quality is the set of costs incurred to prevent, assess, and deal with failures to meet quality requirements.

More about this term

A common account separates prevention and appraisal costs from internal failure costs found before delivery and external failure costs found afterward. State which costs are included and the period measured.

The accounting total can reveal where improvement may save resources, but it does not capture every harm or benefit of quality. A low recorded cost is not, by itself, evidence that quality is high.

CC0 1.0View versioned object

Cost-benefit analysis

monetized appraisal of local public project alternatives

For a local public project, cost-benefit analysis compares its expected benefits and costs with those of relevant alternatives, expressing them in money terms to estimate net benefit.

More about this term

It identifies whose benefits and costs count and can discount future amounts so they can be compared on a common basis.

The calculation cannot by itself settle questions about rights or distribution, even when it favors a proposal.

CC0 1.0View versioned object

Cost-effectiveness

specified outcome relative to resources used

In program evaluation, cost-effectiveness is the amount of a specified outcome achieved relative to the resources used to obtain it.

More about this term

It may be expressed as cost per unit of outcome or outcome per unit of cost when comparing alternatives that pursue the same outcome.

The least expensive option is not necessarily the most cost-effective if it produces a smaller effect.

CC0 1.0View versioned object

Cost-effectiveness analysis

comparison of interventions for a stated outcome

Cost-effectiveness analysis compares alternatives by examining both their costs and their effects on a stated outcome.

More about this term

It can show the resources needed for each unit of effect when outcomes are measured comparably. A low cost alone does not make an option cost-effective.

CC0 1.0View versioned object

Cost-utility analysis

health economic comparison using preference-weighted outcomes

In health economics, cost-utility analysis compares alternatives' costs with health outcomes expressed in preference-weighted units, commonly quality-adjusted life-years.

More about this term

It can express the added cost of an option in relation to the added quality-adjusted life-years it is expected to produce.

The result depends partly on how health-state utility is measured, so the outcome unit and comparison must be stated.

CC0 1.0View versioned object

Counterevidence

evidence bearing against a claim or hypothesis

Counterevidence is evidence that bears against a specified claim, hypothesis, or interpretation.

More about this term

For example, a finding inconsistent with an initial diagnosis can prompt reconsideration.

How much it changes the conclusion depends on its relevance, quality, and relation to the other evidence; one contrary finding need not settle the question.

CC0 1.0View versioned object

Coverage

requirement traceability coverage in a defined design set

In a traceability matrix, coverage is the extent to which the requirements in a defined set have the intended links to design outputs and checks.

More about this term

A coverage claim must name the requirements counted, the kind of link required, and any exclusions; it may be stated as a count or proportion.

A filled link shows a documented connection, not by itself that the design or verification is adequate.

CC0 1.0View versioned object

Coverage interval

metrology

In metrology, a coverage interval is a range assigned to a measurand with a stated probability of covering its true quantity values, given the available information.

More about this term

It expresses measurement uncertainty as an interval; it should not automatically be read as a statistical confidence interval.

CC0 1.0View versioned object

Cp

potential process capability index using within-process variation

Cp is a process capability index comparing the width between two specification limits with the process's within-process spread.

More about this term

It indicates potential fit to those limits if the process is centered; it does not use the process mean.

Interpretation requires a stable process, a suitable variation estimate, and attention to the distribution and specification limits.
