CC0 1.0View versioned object

Cpk

process capability index accounting for process mean and specification limits

Cpk is a process capability index that compares within-process spread with the nearer specification limit, taking the process mean into account.

More about this term

It reflects both variation and how the process is positioned between the limits; when a two-sided process is centered, Cpk equals Cp.

A stable process and suitable distributional model are needed before using it to predict future conformance.

CC0 1.0View versioned object

Craftsmanship

quality of skilled making in relation to an object's form and use

Craftsmanship is the quality of skilled making shown in how an object's materials, construction, and details serve its intended form and use.

More about this term

It can matter in ordinary functional objects as well as art, with practical and aesthetic merits considered together.

In a vehicle, fit, finish, tactile feel, sound, and ease of use can shape a judgment of craftsmanship.

CC0 1.0View versioned object

Credibility

believability of a claim or source in argument evaluation

In evaluating an argument, credibility is the degree to which a claim or supporting source is believable on relevant grounds.

More about this term

Those grounds may include the reliability of the data or the relevant expertise behind a claim.

Credible support still has to be relevant and sufficient for the conclusion; credibility alone does not settle the argument.

CC0 1.0View versioned object

Criterion

evaluative basis or consideration

A criterion is a consideration used as a basis for a judgment.

More about this term

In evaluation, it identifies something that matters about the subject being assessed, such as accessibility, safety, relevance, or timeliness.

The evaluator must still establish why that consideration matters and what evidence can support a judgment about it.

The subject being assessed is an evaluand; criteria provide grounds for judging its merit or worth.

CC0 1.0View versioned object

Criterion-referenced interpretation

interpretation of assessment scores

A criterion-referenced interpretation explains a score in relation to a defined performance domain or standard.

More about this term

It addresses what the person can do or whether a specified level was met, rather than where the person ranks among peers. The standard and any cutoff need a defensible basis.

CC0 1.0View versioned object

Criterion-related validity

historical psychometric validity terminology

Criterion-related validity is a historical label for evidence that scores relate to an external criterion in a way relevant to their intended interpretation or use.

More about this term

Predictive and concurrent relationships are common examples. A strong relationship alone does not settle validity if the criterion is unsuitable or the proposed use lacks other support.

CC0 1.0View versioned object

Critical control point

HACCP step for controlling a significant food-safety hazard

In food-safety HACCP, a critical control point is a step where control is necessary to prevent, eliminate, or reduce a significant hazard to an acceptable level.

More about this term

A HACCP plan identifies the point, a limit for the control, and how that limit will be monitored.

Not every routine production check is a critical control point; the designation depends on the hazard and the control available at that step.

CC0 1.0View versioned object

Critical limit

hazard-control boundary at a food-safety HACCP critical control point

In a food-safety HACCP plan, a critical limit is a stated boundary for a monitored parameter at a critical control point, chosen to control a specified hazard.

More about this term

The limit identifies the parameter, direction, and value or observable condition. It needs a justified basis for the food, process, and hazard.

Monitoring checks whether the limit is met. A deviation triggers the plan’s corrective-action procedure; it does not by itself establish that every affected product is unsafe. A critical limit differs from an operating target set only for efficiency or product quality.

CC0 1.0View versioned object

Critical process parameter

pharmaceutical process variable affecting critical quality

In pharmaceutical manufacturing, a critical process parameter is a process variable that needs control because changes in it can alter a product attribute essential to its quality.

More about this term

Product and process understanding is used to identify such variables and set appropriate monitoring or control.

A parameter is critical because of its effect on product quality, not merely because its value happens to fluctuate.

CC0 1.0View versioned object

Critical quality attribute

pharmaceutical product-development CQA

In pharmaceutical development, a critical quality attribute is a material or product characteristic whose acceptable range or distribution matters for the intended product quality.

More about this term

Examples may include purity, strength, drug release, or sterility, depending on the product.

Risk assessment and experimentation help identify which candidate attributes need control as product knowledge develops.

CC0 1.0View versioned object

Critical to quality (CTQ)

assessable characteristic consequential to a customer need

A critical-to-quality (CTQ) characteristic is an assessable feature of a product, service, or process whose performance matters materially to meeting a customer need.

More about this term

CTQ work translates a broad need into characteristics and requirements that can be checked. The link between the need and the characteristic should be made explicit.

Calling a characteristic “critical” does not make every available measure relevant. Its priority and acceptable performance must be justified for the particular customer and use.

CC0 1.0View versioned object

Cronbach's alpha

internal consistency of scores from multiple test items

Cronbach's alpha is a coefficient calculated from responses to multiple test items to assess the internal consistency of their scores.

More about this term

It uses data from one administration to describe how the item scores vary together.

Alpha alone does not show that the test measures only one construct or that scores would remain stable across occasions.

CC0 1.0View versioned object

Cultural competence

responsive public and human services across cultural differences

Cultural competence is the capacity of a person or organization to provide services respectfully and effectively across relevant cultural and linguistic differences.

More about this term

It calls for understanding the people served and adapting communication and practice to their needs and circumstances.

A claim of cultural competence should be judged by what the service actually does for those people, not by a training label alone.

CC0 1.0View versioned object

Curriculum quality

higher-education course of study

In higher education, curriculum quality is how well a planned course of study supports its educational aims through appropriate subject matter, skill development, sequence, and options.

More about this term

Its assessment should consider prerequisites, scheduling, and elective choices as well as topic coverage; a list of subjects alone does not show how students can progress through them.

CC0 1.0View versioned object

Customer

recipient of a product, service or information in quality management

In quality management, a customer is a person or organization that receives a product, service, or information from a supplier.

More about this term

A customer may be external to the supplying organization or an internal recipient of another unit's output.

The end user is the ultimate recipient or user and need not be identical to an intermediate customer.

CC0 1.0View versioned object

Customer effort score

customer-reported effort in a specified service interaction

Customer effort score is a survey-based metric summarizing how much effort customers report needing to complete a specified interaction with an organization.

More about this term

A useful score states the question, response scale, interaction, population, and method for combining responses.

Less reported effort may indicate an easier interaction, but the score alone does not establish overall service quality.

CC0 1.0View versioned object

Customer experience

customer responses to service interactions across a journey

Customer experience is the customer's overall cognitive, emotional, and behavioral response to interactions with a provider.

More about this term

It can form before, during, and after a service encounter, including the search for information and later recollection.

When a customer uses several channels, the experience spans their connected touchpoints rather than a single transaction.

CC0 1.0View versioned object

Customer focus

quality-management orientation toward customer needs and requirements

In quality management, customer focus is an organizational commitment to understand customer needs and use them to shape outputs, decisions, and improvement.

More about this term

It includes learning what customers need, meeting relevant requirements, and acting on evidence about their experience.

Customer focus does not mean adopting every expressed preference without weighing other requirements and affected parties.

CC0 1.0View versioned object

Customer interview

direct customer conversation to elicit needs and experience

A customer interview is a direct conversation used to learn a customer’s needs, experiences, expectations, or judgments relevant to a product or service.

More about this term

An interviewer can ask planned questions and follow up on unexpected answers. The study should identify which customers were approached, the setting, and the purpose of the questions.

An interview provides evidence of what that person reports; general claims about all customers require an appropriate sampling and analysis basis.

CC0 1.0View versioned object

Customer requirement

customer-side need or expectation in QFD

In QFD, a customer requirement is a stated or investigated need or expectation that a proposed product or service should satisfy for a specified customer and use.

More about this term

A broad request may need to be clarified into terms that can guide design and later assessment. An inferred need should be labeled and checked rather than presented as something the customer explicitly said.

The requirement describes the customer-side aim. A technical characteristic is a proposed design response, and a technical target specifies a desired level for that response.

CC0 1.0View versioned object

Customer satisfaction

customer appraisal of an offering or experience

Customer satisfaction is a customer’s appraisal of how well a product, service, or experience meets relevant needs and expectations.

More about this term

It is tied to a particular customer, offering, and time. Expectations and perceptions can change, so a satisfaction result should state who was asked and what experience they judged.

Satisfaction is informative about the customer’s view, but it does not by itself establish conformity to every requirement or the absence of harm to others.

CC0 1.0View versioned object

Customer satisfaction score

summary of surveyed customers' satisfaction ratings

A customer satisfaction score is a summary value calculated from customers' ratings of a specified product, service, or interaction.

More about this term

It may be reported as an average rating or as the proportion choosing designated satisfied categories; the question, scale, cutoff, and sample determine its meaning.

The score reports responses under those conditions, not an objective verdict on every aspect of service quality.

CC0 1.0View versioned object

Customer value

customer-perceived worth of an offering in a use setting

In marketing, customer value is a customer's appraisal of how an offering serves what matters to them in a particular use setting.

More about this term

The appraisal can involve functional, economic, social, or emotional considerations, depending on the customer and the choice.

A supplier's claim about value does not determine what the customer actually values.

CC0 1.0View versioned object

Cutoff

score boundary for test-based classification

In test-based classification, a cutoff is a specified score boundary used to assign results to categories or trigger a decision.

More about this term

For example, a proficiency cutoff separates scores reported as meeting a standard from those below it.

The score scale does not choose the boundary by itself; the cutoff and its consequences require a justified standard-setting decision.

CC0 1.0View versioned object
D69 terms

D-value

microbial inactivation and sterilization kinetics

In microbial inactivation, a D-value is the time needed under specified treatment conditions to reduce a viable microbial population by one decimal order, or 90 percent.

More about this term

The organism and treatment conditions, including temperature when relevant, must be stated. One D-value reduces an expected population by a factor of ten; it does not mean that every organism has been eliminated.

CC0 1.0View versioned object

Data accessibility

discoverability and usable retrieval of data for an intended user

Data accessibility is how readily an intended user can find and retrieve needed data in a usable form.

More about this term

It concerns the path to the data, including whether access is available and the format suits the task, rather than whether the data values are correct.

An authorized user's access needs must be balanced with protection against unauthorized access.

CC0 1.0View versioned object

Data accuracy

correct representation of a real entity, event or condition

Data accuracy is how correctly recorded values represent the entity, event, or condition they describe.

More about this term

Assessing it calls for comparing recorded values with reliable information about the facts represented.

A value can meet a format rule yet still represent the wrong fact.

CC0 1.0View versioned object

Data cleansing

detecting and addressing dataset quality problems

Data cleansing is the process of finding and addressing errors, missing values, duplicates, and inconsistencies in data for a stated use.

More about this term

A response may correct, transform, fill, remove, or flag a problematic value according to the available evidence and intended analysis.

The work may recur when later analysis reveals new problems, and changes should be documented so the dataset's history remains traceable.

CC0 1.0View versioned object

Data consistency

agreement of related values under data rules

Data consistency is the extent to which related values agree with one another under specified rules, within or across records and datasets.

More about this term

The rule must say which values should match or which combinations are permissible.

Agreement alone does not establish accuracy: two records can consistently repeat the same error.

CC0 1.0View versioned object

Data currency

data and information quality

Data currency is how closely a stored value reflects the present state of what it represents.

More about this term

It depends on when the underlying fact changed and when the record was updated; a recently accessed record can still be out of date.

CC0 1.0View versioned object

Data drift

input-feature distribution change in machine-learning monitoring

In machine-learning monitoring, data drift is a change in the statistical distribution of input features relative to a stated training or monitoring baseline.

More about this term

A shift in a feature's frequency, mean, spread, or other properties can challenge assumptions under which a model was trained.

Detecting drift calls for investigation; it does not by itself prove that predictions have worsened or that retraining is needed.

CC0 1.0View versioned object

Data granularity

data analysis

Data granularity is the level of detail at which data are recorded or made available for analysis.

More about this term

An individual transaction has finer granularity than a daily total; aggregation can expose broad trends while hiding variation within the group.

CC0 1.0View versioned object

Data integrity

valid links among related records in relational data

In relational data, data integrity is the extent to which required links among records are present and valid.

More about this term

For example, an order linked to a customer ID that has no corresponding customer record fails this check.

This sense concerns relationships among data; it does not by itself cover every aspect of accuracy, security, or protection from alteration.

CC0 1.0View versioned object

Data lineage

metadata tracing data movement and transformation

Data lineage is metadata showing where data came from and how it moved and changed through systems or processes.

More about this term

It may describe the path at a broad system level or in detail down to particular fields and transformation rules.

Lineage helps investigate surprising results and data-quality problems, but a known path does not by itself prove that the original data were correct.

CC0 1.0View versioned object

Data management

planned handling of study data for reliable analysis and reporting

In research, data management is the planned handling of study data through collection, entry, checking, correction, storage, and transfer so they remain usable for analysis and reporting.

More about this term

A data management plan specifies sources, formats, responsibilities, and quality checks.

Electronic capture can help with those tasks, but it does not by itself guarantee that the underlying data are accurate or complete.

CC0 1.0View versioned object

Data profiling

systematic inspection of dataset structure and contents

Data profiling is systematic inspection of a dataset's structure, values, and patterns to understand its contents and identify possible quality issues.

More about this term

It can summarize data types, value frequencies, and relationships among fields or tables.

Profiling reveals conditions that may need investigation; it describes the data rather than automatically repairing suspect records.

CC0 1.0View versioned object

Data provenance

origin and processing history of data

In data management, data provenance is information tracing a dataset or value to its sources and the processes that produced it.

More about this term

A provenance record can identify contributing inputs and transformations so a user can examine where a result came from.

It can aid quality assessment and reproducibility, but knowing the history of data does not by itself establish that the data are accurate.

CC0 1.0View versioned object

Data quality

suitability of data for a specified use

Data quality is how well data are suited to a specified use and its requirements.

More about this term

Aspects such as accuracy, completeness, consistency, and currency can matter, but their relevance depends on the data, question, and setting. A useful assessment says which aspect was checked and how.

Data that support one decision may be inadequate for another. A quality dimension names a concern; a metric or check specifies how evidence about that concern is obtained.

CC0 1.0View versioned object

Data quality dimensions

assessment of data for a stated use

Data quality dimensions are distinct aspects used to assess how well data serve a stated purpose, such as accuracy, completeness, consistency, and timeliness.

More about this term

The useful set of dimensions depends on the data and the task. Strong performance on one dimension does not establish that the data are suitable overall.

CC0 1.0View versioned object

Data quality issue

data assessment and remediation

A data quality issue is a defect or suspected defect in recorded data that may impair a stated use.

More about this term

Missing, incorrect, or inconsistent values are common examples. An unusual value is a reason to investigate, not proof that the value is wrong.

CC0 1.0View versioned object

Data relevance

data quality and use

Data relevance is the extent to which particular data bear on a stated question or use.

More about this term

Relevant data can still be inaccurate, incomplete, or out of date; relevance must be judged for the purpose at hand.

CC0 1.0View versioned object

Data representativeness

dataset use for population inference

Data representativeness is how well the cases and relevant characteristics in a dataset reflect the population or conditions to which an analysis will be applied.

More about this term

If some groups are over- or underrepresented, an estimate may be biased even when the values recorded for sampled cases are accurate.

CC0 1.0View versioned object

Data specification quality

data models, definitions and standards

Data specification quality is how well the definitions and rules for data describe the meaning, structure, allowed values, and use of a dataset.

More about this term

Clear, complete specifications help people collect and interpret data consistently. A dataset can conform to its specifications yet still be unsuitable if those specifications omit a needed attribute or misstate its meaning.

CC0 1.0View versioned object

Data timeliness

data and information quality

Data timeliness is whether data are current enough and available early enough for a specified use.

More about this term

A record may accurately reflect a recent event yet arrive too late to guide the decision for which it was needed.

CC0 1.0View versioned object

Data uniqueness

absence of unintended duplicates for entities or events meant to appear once

Data uniqueness is the extent to which an entity or event meant to appear once is represented without unintended duplicate records or identifiers.

More about this term

The uniqueness rule depends on what is identified: customer IDs may need to be distinct even though different customers can share a name.

Uniqueness checks require a stated entity and comparison rule; repeated values are not automatically errors.

CC0 1.0View versioned object

Data validity

data-quality conformity to specified definitions and rules

In data-quality management, data validity is the extent to which values or records conform to applicable data definitions and rules.

More about this term

A rule may specify an allowed format, range, or relationship between fields.

A validly formatted record can still misstate the world; validity in this sense does not by itself establish factual accuracy.

CC0 1.0View versioned object

Dataset quality

dataset assessment for a stated analysis

Dataset quality is how well a specified collection of data is suited to a stated use.

More about this term

Assessment can consider coverage, accuracy, completeness, coding, and access. A clean dataset may still omit the people, period, or variables needed to answer the question.

CC0 1.0View versioned object

Decision

choice of a course of action

A decision is a choice among possible courses of action, including whether to act, defer, or seek more information.

More about this term

A defensible decision identifies the options, the aim, the relevant evidence, and the likely consequences and uncertainties. A judgment or evaluation can inform the choice without uniquely determining it.

The decision is the choice made; its supporting inference, criteria, and evidence are distinct parts of its justification.

CC0 1.0View versioned object

Decision criterion

rule used to compare and select among options

A decision criterion is a stated basis or rule for comparing options and choosing among them.

More about this term

It connects the decision maker's aims to the outcomes expected from each option.

Choosing expected value, robustness, or a minimum reliability requirement can lead to different preferred options from the same evidence.

CC0 1.0View versioned object

Decision quality

appraisal of a choice under uncertainty

Decision quality is how well a choice is made in light of its aims, available alternatives, relevant information, uncertainty, and the values at stake.

More about this term

A sound appraisal asks what could reasonably be known and considered when the choice was made. It should identify whose objectives and consequences matter.

The result of a decision is relevant for learning, but it is not the same as decision quality: chance or later events can turn a well-made choice into a poor outcome, or the reverse.

CC0 1.0View versioned object

Decision rule

stated procedure turning evidence and criteria into a disposition

A decision rule specifies how stated evidence and criteria lead to a selection, classification, acceptance, rejection, or other disposition.

More about this term

A rule may use cutoffs, an order of priorities, a weighted combination, or a treatment of uncertainty. The relevant inputs and conditions must be clear enough to apply it consistently.

Different defensible rules can produce different outcomes from the same evidence. The rule and its authority should therefore be stated before treating a result as a decision.

CC0 1.0View versioned object

Decision threshold

classification or detection decision based on a specified quantity

A decision threshold is a specified value or boundary at which a decision rule changes its classification or prescribed action.

More about this term

A complete threshold states the quantity, comparison direction, boundary value, and resulting decision.

Moving the boundary can change the balance between missed cases and false alarms; the threshold is a choice, not a measurement result.

CC0 1.0View versioned object

Declaration of conformity

issuer's formal statement of an identified product's conformity

A declaration of conformity is a formal statement by a responsible issuer that an identified product meets specified requirements.

More about this term

The statement should make the product, issuer, and applicable requirements identifiable.

It is the issuer's claim of conformity, not by itself an independent certification.

CC0 1.0View versioned object

Decreasing failure rate

declining conditional hazard over item age

A decreasing failure rate means that, over a specified period, the instantaneous rate of failure falls as the surviving items age.

More about this term

It can describe an early-life period in which vulnerable items fail and the remaining population has a lower conditional failure rate.

The pattern concerns the population of survivors; it does not mean that every individual item becomes more reliable as it ages.

CC0 1.0View versioned object

Defect

nonconformity related to intended or specified use

In quality management, a defect is a nonconformity related to an intended or specified use.

More about this term

The link to use matters: a departure may violate a requirement without being shown to affect the use in question. Identify the object, the unmet requirement, and the use before applying the narrower label.

A defect may be found through inspection, testing, or use. Finding one calls for a response to the affected case; preventing recurrence may also require corrective action.

CC0 1.0View versioned object

Defect density

identified software defects per specified software-size unit

In software engineering, defect density is the number of identified defects relative to a specified measure of software size.

More about this term

The denominator may be code size or functional size; a result must name its size unit and which defects were counted.

Size adjustment can aid comparison, but differences in detection effort or defect definitions can still make two values misleading to compare.

CC0 1.0View versioned object

Defect opportunity

denominator unit in defects-per-million-opportunities analysis

A defect opportunity is one specified chance for a unit to fail a stated requirement.

More about this term

A unit may have several opportunities, such as distinct required features or checks. Count them consistently before calculating defects per million opportunities.

An opportunity is a possible failure point; a defect is a failure actually found.

CC0 1.0View versioned object

Defect rate

frequency of defects or defective units in inspected output

A defect rate expresses the frequency of defects or defective units relative to a stated amount of output.

More about this term

State whether the numerator counts defects or units with at least one defect, and specify the denominator, such as inspected units; a result may be reported per million units.

The two counts can differ when one unit has several defects.

CC0 1.0View versioned object

Defects per million opportunities

defect frequency normalized by defined error opportunities

Defects per million opportunities is the number of observed defects divided by the total defined opportunities for a defect, then multiplied by one million.

More about this term

When each inspected unit has the same number of opportunities, the denominator is units inspected times opportunities per unit.

Counting opportunities consistently matters: this rate counts defects, so one unit may contribute more than one.

CC0 1.0View versioned object

Definition

reader-facing account of a term's meaning in a stated sense

A definition is a statement that explains what a term means in a specified sense.

More about this term

In a dictionary, it should help readers recognize when that sense applies and distinguish it from nearby meanings.

The wording may be brief or use a fuller sentence, provided it makes the meaning clear to its intended readers.

CC0 1.0View versioned object

Degradation

deterioration of an item's performance over life units

In reliability engineering, degradation is a worsening of an item's performance characteristic over time or use.

More about this term

A specified threshold may mark when that characteristic counts as failed; degradation can occur before the threshold is reached.

Measurements of its path may support an estimate of remaining useful life, subject to the model and conditions used.

CC0 1.0View versioned object

Deliberative quality

political news discourse

In political news, deliberative quality is how well coverage supports reasoned consideration of differing positions on a public issue.

More about this term

Inclusion, justification, responsiveness, and civility can be relevant; adding more voices or social-media posts alone does not establish strong deliberation in an article.

CC0 1.0View versioned object

Dependability

time-related operating quality of an engineered system

In systems engineering, dependability concerns a system's capacity to provide acceptable service over time under stated conditions.

More about this term

Depending on the framework, it can bring together reliability, availability, maintainability, and continuity.

A probability of failure-free operation captures only one part of this broader appraisal.

CC0 1.0View versioned object

Descriptive analysis

sensory profiling of product attributes

In sensory science, descriptive analysis uses assessors to identify and rate product attributes so products can be described and compared.

More about this term

Panel members align the meanings of the attributes and the rating scales before evaluating the product set.

The resulting profile describes perceived qualities; it does not itself say whether consumers like the products.

CC0 1.0View versioned object

Design

forming and specifying a proposed product or service solution

In quality management, design is the work of devising and specifying a solution for an identified purpose or requirement.

More about this term

Its outputs can be plans, specifications, or prototypes that guide making a product or delivering a service.

A proposed design still needs checking against its inputs and intended use; having a specification alone does not show that the finished object works.

CC0 1.0View versioned object

Design for quality

anticipating quality concerns in product and process design

Design for quality incorporates known and foreseeable quality concerns into the design of a product, process, or equipment before routine use.

More about this term

Designers can turn those concerns into specifications, design choices, and checks intended to prevent failures.

Finding a defect later may prompt a redesign, but detection alone does not build prevention into the design.

CC0 1.0View versioned object

Design for Six Sigma (DFSS)

structured quality-focused design of new or substantially redesigned offerings

Design for Six Sigma (DFSS) is a family of structured approaches for designing a new or substantially redesigned product, service, or process to meet specified customer and performance requirements.

More about this term

It brings customer needs into design decisions, develops and tests candidate solutions, and considers how the design will perform under expected variation. Different DFSS roadmaps use different phases and tools.

DFSS addresses quality while designing; improving an established process without substantial redesign is usually framed as a different Six Sigma task.

CC0 1.0View versioned object

Design of experiments (DOE)

planned comparison of factor effects on a response

Design of experiments (DOE) is the planned variation of input factors to learn how they affect a specified response.

More about this term

An experimental design states the factors, their settings, the response to observe, and how runs will be compared. It can reveal interactions that a one-factor-at-a-time check may miss.

The design must fit the question and available resources. A pattern found in the tested conditions needs further support before it is assumed to hold under different conditions.

CC0 1.0View versioned object

Design output

medical-device design-stage deliverable

In medical-device design, a design output is a deliverable from a design stage that expresses the device design or how it will be made and checked.

More about this term

It may be a specification, drawing, manufacturing instruction, or test protocol. An output from one stage can become an input to the next.

Teams relate outputs to relevant design inputs and verify them against applicable requirements; producing a document alone does not show that those requirements are met.

CC0 1.0View versioned object

Design quality

architectural design appraisal

In architecture, design quality is how well a proposed design addresses relevant functional, technical, experiential, and contextual aims.

More about this term

Judgment considers the design as a whole and the criteria relevant to its setting and intended users.

A low price or compliance with one requirement alone does not settle the quality of the design.

CC0 1.0View versioned object

Design review

structured examination of a design against requirements

A design review is a planned, documented examination of a design to judge whether it can meet relevant requirements.

More about this term

It considers the design as a whole against its intended functions and requirements, bringing unresolved questions into view before a decision to proceed or revise.

Review is an examination and judgment. It should not be confused with a test result or with proof that a finished design will succeed in every use.

CC0 1.0View versioned object

Design space

quality-assuring combinations of pharmaceutical inputs and process settings

In pharmaceutical development, a design space is a justified set of combinations of material properties and process settings within which intended product quality can be achieved.

More about this term

Its boundaries account for interactions among inputs rather than treating each setting as an independent acceptable range.

Evidence for the space should show that the relevant combinations deliver the intended quality; results outside its boundary cannot be assumed to have the same assurance.

CC0 1.0View versioned object

Desirability

favorable appraisal of an outcome under specified aims or values

Desirability is how favorable an outcome appears under a person's aims or values.

More about this term

It can change with whose perspective is taken and which goals or circumstances matter.

Some decision models represent subjective desirability numerically, but a number is not required for an ordinary desirability judgment.

CC0 1.0View versioned object

Detection

FMEA estimate of discovering a failure or its cause

In failure mode and effects analysis, detection is the estimated likelihood that a specified failure or its cause will be discovered at a stated stage.

More about this term

The estimate depends on what is being sought and which controls or observers could find it. Some schemes assess discovery before delivery; others assess whether a customer will notice the effect.

A detection rating is separate from the failure’s likelihood and severity. State the scale and its direction: on many FMEA scales, a higher detection number means the problem is harder to find.

CC0 1.0View versioned object

Deviation

observation's difference from a statistical reference

In statistics, a deviation is the difference between an observed value and a specified reference value, often the mean of a data set.

More about this term

A signed deviation preserves direction; its absolute value gives the size of the difference without direction.

A deviation from a mean is not, by itself, evidence that a requirement was violated; that requires a separate decision rule.

CC0 1.0View versioned object

Dignity

human moral standing and respect for persons

In ethics, dignity is a person's standing as worthy of respect in their own right.

More about this term

It grounds a demand to treat people as persons whose interests and agency matter, rather than merely as tools for others' ends.

A dignity claim therefore asks how a person is treated, not only whether an action produces a useful result.

CC0 1.0View versioned object

Dimension

aspect in an evaluative framework

In an evaluative framework, a dimension is a distinguishable aspect used to organize what is described or judged.

More about this term

For data quality, accuracy and completeness can be treated as different dimensions. Which dimensions matter depends on the subject and purpose.

A dimension names an aspect; an indicator or measure supplies information about it. This use differs from mathematical dimensions such as length or time.

CC0 1.0View versioned object

Direct observation

recording observable behavior or events by watching them

Direct observation is a method of recording behaviors or events by watching them as they occur.

More about this term

A recording scheme states in advance which observable actions count and how they will be coded.

The observer can record an action directly, while a conclusion about an unseen state such as motivation requires inference.

CC0 1.0View versioned object

Disability-adjusted life year

population health loss from premature mortality and nonfatal conditions

A disability-adjusted life year is a unit of health loss combining years lost to premature death with time lived in less than full health, weighted by severity.

More about this term

DALYs can be added across conditions or populations to summarize a burden of disease.

The result depends on the reference life expectancy and disability weights used; it is not a direct rating of care quality.

CC0 1.0View versioned object

Discourse quality

public deliberation

In public deliberation, discourse quality is how well participants exchange and justify views while giving others a fair opportunity to contribute.

More about this term

Assessments may consider opportunities to speak, the justification of claims, mutual respect, and constructiveness. Agreement alone does not show that competing views received a fair hearing.

CC0 1.0View versioned object

Discriminability

ability to distinguish sensory stimuli under stated test conditions

In sensory testing, discriminability is how well a person or panel can distinguish specified stimuli under stated conditions.

More about this term

It depends on the difference between stimuli, background variation, and the testing procedure.

A test that finds no difference has not shown the stimuli are identical; its power and the number of participants matter.

CC0 1.0View versioned object

Discriminant validity

distinctness of measured constructs in psychometrics

Discriminant validity concerns whether evidence shows that a measure distinguishes its intended construct from constructs it should differ from.

More about this term

One check asks whether scores have appropriately weak associations with measures of theoretically distinct constructs.

A low association is not automatically favorable; the expected relationship must be specified from theory.

CC0 1.0View versioned object

Disinformation

deliberately deceptive public information

Disinformation is false or misleading material created or circulated with an intention to deceive.

More about this term

It can mix accurate details with false ones, so checking only whether each sentence is literally false can miss the deception.

A person who unknowingly shares it does not necessarily share the original deceptive intent.

CC0 1.0View versioned object

Disposition

recorded treatment or outcome of a reviewed issue

A disposition is the decision about how a reviewed issue or item will be treated.

More about this term

It may direct acceptance, correction, rejection, further investigation, or another specified action by the responsible authority.

A finding describes what was observed; its disposition records the resulting decision.

CC0 1.0View versioned object

Distribution

pattern of benefits and burdens across affected groups in quality evaluation

In quality evaluation, distribution is the pattern of who receives benefits or resources and who bears harms or burdens.

More about this term

Looking across relevant groups or places can reveal differences concealed by an overall average.

This sense concerns how consequences are spread among people; a statistical distribution of values is a separate sense.

CC0 1.0View versioned object

DMADV

five-stage Design for Six Sigma method for new design or major redesign

DMADV is a Design for Six Sigma method whose stages are Define, Measure, Analyze, Design, and Verify.

More about this term

It structures the development of a new product or process, or a substantial redesign, around defined needs and a verified design.

It is a design route; DMAIC is the related sequence typically used to improve an existing process.

CC0 1.0View versioned object

DMAIC

five-stage Six Sigma process-improvement method

DMAIC is a structured process-improvement method whose stages are Define, Measure, Analyze, Improve, and Control.

More about this term

A team frames a problem, establishes a performance baseline, examines causes, tests improvements, and sets up controls to sustain the result.

The stages guide evidence-based work on an existing process; the acronym alone does not establish that a change succeeded.

CC0 1.0View versioned object

Document control

governing approval, access and revision of work documents

Document control governs how work documents are approved, made available, revised, and withdrawn.

More about this term

It lets people identify the version and status of a document and use the appropriate one for their work.

Keeping a file in storage alone does not establish that its content is current, approved, or accessible to the right people.

CC0 1.0View versioned object

Documented information

controlled management-system information and records

In a quality management system, documented information is recorded content that an organization controls for directing work or retaining evidence of what occurred.

More about this term

It can include instructions to be kept current and records retained to show results.

The medium may be paper or digital; the function of the information matters more than its format.

CC0 1.0View versioned object

Donabedian model

health-care quality assessment

The Donabedian model is a framework for assessing health-care quality through structure, process, and outcome: the conditions for care, what is done in care, and its effects.

More about this term

These dimensions organize different kinds of evidence; a measure from one dimension alone cannot describe every aspect of care quality.

CC0 1.0View versioned object

Due diligence

proportionate inquiry before a consequential decision

Due diligence is a reasonable investigation of relevant facts and risks before making a consequential decision or taking action.

More about this term

What counts as reasonable depends on the decision, the available information, and the duties involved.

In a transaction, the inquiry may reveal both reasons to withdraw and opportunities to pursue; it does not require exhaustive knowledge.

CC0 1.0View versioned object

Due process

U.S. constitutional protection against government deprivation

In U.S. constitutional law, due process constrains how government may deprive a person of life, liberty, or property.

More about this term

It calls for legally fair treatment and can concern both the procedure used and the justification for government action.

The protections that apply depend on the legal setting and the interest at stake; the phrase alone does not specify a single hearing procedure.

CC0 1.0View versioned object

Durability

resistance to deterioration of a construction material

For a construction material, durability is its capacity to resist deterioration from use and exposure over a relevant period.

More about this term

The expected conditions matter: a material that lasts indoors may weather poorly outdoors.

Durability concerns performance over time and is distinct from initial strength or hardness.

CC0 1.0View versioned object
E45 terms

E-service quality

service delivered through a digital interface

E-service quality is how well a service delivered through digital channels meets the relevant needs and requirements of its users.

More about this term

Depending on the service, assessment may consider access, ease of use, reliability, information, support, and security.

An attractive interface alone cannot establish quality if the service fails to deliver what users need.

CC0 1.0View versioned object

Ecological integrity

ecosystem condition in ecological assessment

In ecological assessment, ecological integrity is the condition of an ecosystem whose physical, chemical, and living features continue to support its characteristic communities and processes.

More about this term

An assessment needs to identify the ecosystem and a suitable reference condition. Relevant features can include species composition, water conditions, habitat continuity, and ecological interactions.

A forest may retain some tree cover while fragmentation limits wildlife movement; area alone does not establish integrity.

CC0 1.0View versioned object

Ecological validity

applicability of research findings to real-life situations

In empirical research, ecological validity concerns how well findings from a study setting apply to the real-life situations the study aims to represent.

More about this term

It draws attention to the relation between study tasks and surroundings and the corresponding activities outside the study.

Realistic conditions alone do not establish that results generalize to every population or setting.

CC0 1.0View versioned object

Ecosystem services

ecosystem contributions to human well-being

Ecosystem services are aspects of ecosystems that contribute to human well-being.

More about this term

They may provide materials, regulate environmental conditions, or support cultural and recreational experiences.

An assessment should identify who benefits and how; an ecological process, a service, and a final benefit are not always the same thing.

CC0 1.0View versioned object

Education quality

evaluation of educational opportunities, processes and outcomes

Education quality is how well educational opportunities, processes, and outcomes serve justified learning aims and the needs of learners in a stated context.

More about this term

A judgment may consider what learners gain, the teaching and support they receive, access, fairness, and the resources that make learning possible. Which considerations matter depends on the learners, institution, and purpose of the evaluation.

A test score or institutional rating is evidence about selected aspects, not a complete judgment of education quality by itself.

CC0 1.0View versioned object

Educational access

opportunity to enter and participate in higher education

In higher education, educational access is a person's practical opportunity to enter and participate in a program.

More about this term

Admissions rules, prior preparation, resources, and support can all affect that opportunity.

An available place or a transparent application process alone does not establish fair access when people face unequal barriers.

CC0 1.0View versioned object

Educational equity

fairness of opportunity in higher education

In higher education, educational equity is fairness in who can enter, participate in, and benefit from study.

More about this term

It asks how historical and institutional barriers shape the opportunities of different groups.

Equal enrollment totals alone do not establish equal participation or opportunity within institutions.

CC0 1.0View versioned object

Effect

causal effect of a specified intervention

In causal inference, an effect is the difference an intervention makes to an outcome compared with what would have happened under another specified condition.

More about this term

State the intervention, outcome, population, and comparison condition to make the effect interpretable.

An observed change or association alone does not establish that the intervention caused it.

CC0 1.0View versioned object

Effect size

quantitative index of a specified difference or association

An effect size is a quantitative index of the magnitude of a specified difference or association.

More about this term

Examples include a standardized mean difference, a correlation coefficient, and an odds ratio; each uses a different scale and interpretation.

The chosen index must be named; a statistically significant result does not by itself show whether the effect is important in practice.

CC0 1.0View versioned object

Effectiveness

attainment of intended results by an action or process

Effectiveness is the extent to which an action or process achieves the results it was meant to achieve.

More about this term

Judge it by relating the intended results to what happened under the relevant conditions.

Completing the planned steps alone does not establish that the intended result occurred.

CC0 1.0View versioned object

Effectiveness check

corrective and preventive action

In corrective and preventive action, an effectiveness check examines whether an implemented action produced the intended improvement or prevented recurrence.

More about this term

It uses planned evidence after implementation; confirming that an action was carried out is a separate check.

CC0 1.0View versioned object

Efficacy

effect of a clinical intervention under specified test conditions

In clinical research, efficacy is how well an intervention produces its intended effect under specified study conditions.

More about this term

An efficacy claim must identify the population, comparison, outcome, and conditions under which the effect was assessed.

Evidence from a controlled study does not automatically establish how well the intervention works in routine practice.

CC0 1.0View versioned object

Efficiency

useful output relative to process resources

In process evaluation, efficiency is the relationship between useful output and the resources used to produce it.

More about this term

A comparison should specify the output and resources at issue, such as time, labor, energy, or money.

A process can use resources efficiently yet produce the wrong or an inadequate result; effectiveness and quality need separate judgment.

CC0 1.0View versioned object

Emissions

air releases associated with motor vehicles

In transport assessment, emissions are gases or particles released into the air from vehicle use or its fuel supply.

More about this term

An emissions figure needs a specified substance, source, amount or rate, and period of observation.

Tailpipe emissions and emissions from producing fuel are different parts of the same transport system.

CC0 1.0View versioned object

Empathy

understanding another person's experience

Empathy is the capacity to understand another person's perspective or feelings by imaginatively considering their experience.

More about this term

It helps someone respond to what matters to the other person rather than assuming their own experience is the same.

Understanding another person's feelings does not require agreeing with every judgment or sharing the same emotion.

CC0 1.0View versioned object

Empowerment

increased agency in social work and community practice

In social work, empowerment is a process through which people or communities gain practical influence over decisions and conditions affecting their lives.

More about this term

It builds on their own capacities and gives their voices a direct part in identifying problems and solutions.

Providing a service without changing the person's agency does not by itself establish empowerment.

CC0 1.0View versioned object

Enforceability

availability of legal effect and remedy for a contract

In contract law, enforceability is an agreement's capacity to receive legal effect and a remedy if its terms are breached.

More about this term

It depends on formation requirements and on whether a relevant defense defeats enforcement.

The parties may comply voluntarily with an agreement even when a court would not enforce it.

CC0 1.0View versioned object

Enterprise risk management

organizational risk management

Enterprise risk management is a coordinated approach to identifying, assessing, and responding to risks across an organization in light of its objectives.

More about this term

It considers significant risks together and connects their management to organizational decisions. Coordination does not remove uncertainty or make all risks equally important.

CC0 1.0View versioned object

Environmental performance

organizational results in managing environmental aspects

In environmental management, environmental performance is the results of how an organization manages its environmental aspects.

More about this term

Those results can be assessed against its policy, objectives, or other stated criteria using suitable indicators.

Having a management system does not by itself show that environmental results are good; the results and their basis for comparison must be examined.

CC0 1.0View versioned object

Environmental quality

conditions of an environment relative to ecological or human purposes

Environmental quality is how favorable the conditions of a specified environment are for relevant ecological or human purposes.

More about this term

A judgment identifies the place, time, affected living systems or people, and criteria. Air, water, and soil conditions can each matter, but no single indicator describes the whole environment.

An acceptable limit for one pollutant answers a narrower question than whether the environment is good overall. The assessment also depends on the chosen reference condition, exposure, and intended use.

CC0 1.0View versioned object

Environmental quality standard (EQS)

environmental protection and regulation

An environmental quality standard (EQS) is a limit for the concentration of a specified substance in an environment, set to protect people or ecosystems from harm.

More about this term

It concerns the receiving environment, such as a body of water, rather than the amount released from a particular source. Meeting one EQS does not establish that the environment is safe in every respect.

CC0 1.0View versioned object

Epistemic risk

risk of false belief from a specified belief-forming basis

Epistemic risk is the possibility of getting something wrong in forming or relying on a belief.

More about this term

The relevant risk depends on the claim and the way the belief is formed: a belief may happen to be true even though its basis could easily have led to error.

In this sense, reducing risk means seeking more dependable ways of arriving at the truth, not merely counting how often a belief turns out true.

CC0 1.0View versioned object

Equity

fair access, treatment and outcomes across groups

Equity concerns whether people or groups have fair access, treatment, and opportunities in light of relevant needs and barriers.

More about this term

Identical treatment can leave unjustified differences in opportunity intact when starting conditions differ. An equity claim should say which population, benefit, barrier, and standard of fairness are at issue.

In health care, equity includes avoiding differences in care quality attributable to personal or social characteristics that should not determine care. In education, it can concern persistent barriers to access and attainment.

CC0 1.0View versioned object

Error prevention

designing processes or controls to stop foreseeable mistakes

Error prevention is the use of process or product design to stop a foreseeable mistake before it produces an incorrect result.

More about this term

A mistake-proofing device may make the wrong action impossible or reveal it in time for correction.

Checking a completed result for defects is a later control and does not, by itself, prevent the original error.

CC0 1.0View versioned object

Escalation condition

governed assessment and corrective-action workflow

An escalation condition is a specified state or event that requires an issue to move to a more authoritative response process.

More about this term

In an assessment workflow, persistent failure to correct a nonconformity can be such a trigger; the condition should identify what is observed and who must act next.

CC0 1.0View versioned object

Estimate

statistical inference about an unknown quantity

In statistics, an estimate is a value or interval inferred from available data for an unknown quantity.

More about this term

A useful estimate identifies the quantity, the data and method, and the uncertainty relevant to its use.

A point estimate gives one value; it does not make the unknown quantity certain.

CC0 1.0View versioned object

Evaluand

evaluation terminology

An evaluand is the specific thing being evaluated.

More about this term

Depending on the evaluation, it may be a program, policy, product, service, organization, person’s performance, or other subject.

The term names a role in an evaluation: it does not, by itself, say whether that thing is good, effective, or valuable.

CC0 1.0View versioned object

Evaluation

reasoned appraisal of a subject

Evaluation is the process of appraising a specified subject against relevant grounds to reach a conclusion about its merit, worth, significance, or other value.

More about this term

It brings information together with criteria or values and interprets the result for a stated purpose. The word can also name the resulting appraisal.

An evaluation may draw on assessments, measurements, or testimony; none of those alone settles the value judgment. What counts as adequate evidence depends on the question and setting.

CC0 1.0View versioned object

Evaluation basis

grounds for a program-evaluation appraisal

An evaluation basis is the stated set of purposes, criteria, and evidence used to support an appraisal of something being evaluated.

More about this term

It makes clear what is being judged, why the chosen considerations matter, and what observations support the conclusion.

Different participants may disagree about the criteria or how strongly the evidence supports a rating.

CC0 1.0View versioned object

Evaluation design

planned evidence strategy for program evaluation

An evaluation design is the planned arrangement of questions, evidence, methods, and analysis used to assess a specified program.

More about this term

The choices depend on the evaluation's purpose, including whether it seeks to understand implementation or effects.

An experimental comparison is one possible design; a design label alone does not guarantee a sound conclusion.

CC0 1.0View versioned object

Evidence

cross-domain claim-bearing evidence

Evidence is information or material brought to bear on a claim: for example, observations, records, testimony, or a physical object.

More about this term

What it establishes depends on which claim is at issue and how the material was obtained and interpreted.

Evidence can support a claim, count against it, or be too weak to settle it.

There is no single evidence threshold that applies across research, quality audits, and courts.

In quality management, objective evidence is data that supports the existence or truth of something. In U.S. federal evidence law, relevance depends on whether material makes a consequential fact more or less probable.

CC0 1.0View versioned object

Evidence hierarchy

ranking evidence designs for a specified kind of inference

An evidence hierarchy ranks types of evidence by their expected ability to support a specified kind of claim.

More about this term

For a question about intervention effects, study design can provide an initial ordering of evidence types.

The quality of the actual evidence also depends on limitations, relevance, consistency, and precision; the design label alone does not settle its strength.

CC0 1.0View versioned object

Evidence quality

warrant of a body of evidence for a specified conclusion

Evidence quality is the degree of confidence a body of evidence warrants for a specified question or conclusion.

More about this term

Relevant concerns include how the evidence was produced, whether findings agree, how directly they address the question, and how precise they are. A strong individual study does not automatically make the whole body of evidence strong.

The quality of evidence and the strength of a recommendation are separate judgments: a decision also depends on benefits, harms, values, and context.

CC0 1.0View versioned object

Excellence

cross-domain elevated appraisal

Excellence is exceptionally strong merit or performance in a relevant respect, judged by standards appropriate to the activity, object, or person.

More about this term

Calling something excellent therefore requires more than saying that it passed a minimum requirement: the judgment must identify what it excels at and provide a sound basis for the elevated appraisal.

CC0 1.0View versioned object

Exchange value

commodity relation in political economy

In political economy, exchange value is what a commodity can obtain in exchange relative to other commodities.

More about this term

It concerns a relation of exchange, whereas use value concerns what the commodity can do for someone who uses it.

The term does not by itself state an item's personal usefulness or ethical worth.

CC0 1.0View versioned object

Expectation

customer anticipation of a service

In service quality, an expectation is what a customer anticipates or believes a service will provide or how it will perform.

More about this term

Some service-quality approaches compare customers' experiences with their expectations; other approaches assess performance without that comparison.

An expectation is not automatically a contractual requirement; identify whose expectation it is and whether it was adopted as a requirement.

CC0 1.0View versioned object

Expected value

probability-weighted average of numerical outcomes

Expected value is the probability-weighted average of the numerical values assigned to possible outcomes.

More about this term

For discrete outcomes, multiply each outcome's value by its probability and add the products.

It is a model-based average, not a prediction that any one outcome will equal that number; expected utility uses a utility scale rather than necessarily monetary values.

CC0 1.0View versioned object

Experience quality

tourism visitor experience

In tourism research, experience quality is a visitor's appraisal of an encounter with a destination or attraction, including its personal and emotional aspects.

More about this term

Researchers can assess it separately from satisfaction with the visit and examine how the two are related.

CC0 1.0View versioned object

Explainability

audience-relative understanding of AI outputs or behavior

For an AI system, explainability is its capacity to provide information that helps a specified audience understand its outputs or behavior.

More about this term

An explanation may address the model's general behavior or a particular decision, depending on what its users need to know.

Its usefulness and limitations must be assessed for that audience and purpose; an explanation that sounds plausible is not automatically adequate.

CC0 1.0View versioned object

Exposure

human exposure assessment

In human exposure assessment, exposure is contact between a person and a chemical, physical, or biological agent at the body's boundary.

More about this term

It can be described by how much contact occurs, how often, and for how long.

An agent merely being nearby is not exposure; the amount entering the body is a separate dose.

CC0 1.0View versioned object

Expressiveness

perceived affective qualities of artworks

In aesthetics, expressiveness is an artwork's capacity to present qualities that viewers or listeners perceive as akin to human feeling.

More about this term

A painting may seem mournful or music may sound joyful through their perceptible features and the way an audience engages with them.

Philosophers differ about how such qualities arise; an expressive work need not be a direct report of its maker's feelings.

CC0 1.0View versioned object

External failure cost

cost arising from defects discovered during or after delivery

An external failure cost is a cost arising from a defect or nonconformity found during or after delivery of a product or service.

More about this term

Examples include returns, warranty work, complaint handling, and repairs after the customer receives the offering. The cost belongs to the failure category because the problem has occurred.

A cost estimate should state what delivery boundary and consequences it includes. Possible losses of trust or future sales may be relevant, but their monetary attribution needs separate support.

CC0 1.0View versioned object

External quality audit

quality-management auditing

An external quality audit is a second- or third-party assessment of an organization's quality-related activities, processes, or system against stated criteria.

More about this term

A customer may conduct or commission a second-party audit; an independent body may conduct a third-party audit. An organization can outsource its own internal audit without turning it into an external audit.

CC0 1.0View versioned object

External validity

warrant for applying study findings beyond studied cases

In empirical research, external validity concerns whether findings warrant an inference beyond the people or setting studied.

More about this term

The intended target might be another population, place, or time and should be stated explicitly.

Such an inference depends on relevant similarities and differences between the study and target; it does not follow from a large sample alone.

CC0 1.0View versioned object

Externality

effect on others outside an economic decision or exchange

In economics, an externality is a benefit or harm from one party's activity that affects others without being fully accounted for in the decision or exchange that produced it.

More about this term

Pollution affecting neighbors is a negative externality; an activity can also confer benefits on others.

Identify the affected parties and the boundary of the decision before calling an effect external.

CC0 1.0View versioned object
F30 terms

Fact-checking

verification of public factual claims in journalism

In journalism, fact-checking is the examination of a checkable factual claim against available evidence to determine how well the claim holds up.

More about this term

The checker identifies the precise claim, looks for relevant records or other independent evidence, and explains any finding in its context.

Repeating a claim or judging whether it sounds plausible is not itself a check of its factual basis.

CC0 1.0View versioned object

Factor

input or condition studied in a designed experiment

In a designed experiment, a factor is an input or condition studied for its effect on a specified response.

More about this term

The experiment uses particular values, called levels, of the factor and records the response at those levels. The design should say which levels are studied.

A factor is distinct from the response being measured. Calling a variable a factor does not by itself establish that it causes a change.

CC0 1.0View versioned object

Failure

loss of an item's required function

In reliability engineering, failure occurs when an item can no longer perform a required function when called upon.

More about this term

The loss of function may be partial, complete, or intermittent.

A defect is a flaw; it becomes a functional failure when it prevents the required performance.

CC0 1.0View versioned object

Failure consequence

system-level impact considered in reliability-centered maintenance

In reliability-centered maintenance, a failure consequence is what a failure would mean for the system and affected people beyond the immediate physical effect on a part.

More about this term

Consequences may include injury, loss of operation, degraded capability, or cost. Their seriousness helps determine which failures call for preventive action.

A failure effect describes what happens; its consequence expresses why that effect matters for use, safety, or other objectives.

CC0 1.0View versioned object

Failure cost

costs arising from defects or nonconformity

A failure cost is a cost that arises because a product, service, or process fails to meet a relevant quality requirement.

More about this term

Internal failure costs arise before delivery, such as scrap or rework. External failure costs arise during or after delivery, such as returns, warranty work, or complaint handling.

The estimate depends on the accounting boundary: some consequences, including lost trust or delayed work, can be difficult to attribute or price. Prevention and appraisal costs belong to different categories.

CC0 1.0View versioned object

Failure effect

consequence of a specified failure mode for a function or affected party

A failure effect is a consequence that may result when a specified failure mode occurs.

More about this term

Describe the effect at a stated level, such as the affected component, system, service, or user. One failure mode may have several effects at different levels.

The effect answers what happens because of the failure; the failure mode describes how function is lost, and a cause explains why that mode arose.

CC0 1.0View versioned object

Failure mode

specified way an item or process fails

A failure mode is a specified way in which an item, process, or system fails to perform an intended function.

More about this term

Depending on the analysis, it may describe a visible symptom, a functional failure, or a physical mechanism. State the intended level: what one analysis calls a mode may be treated as a cause or effect in another.

The same item can have several failure modes, so a useful description identifies the affected function and the particular manner of failure.

CC0 1.0View versioned object

Failure mode and effects analysis (FMEA)

prospective failure analysis

Failure mode and effects analysis (FMEA) is a structured, prospective examination of how a product, process, or system might fail, what could cause each failure, and what its effects would be.

More about this term

The analysis helps a team choose actions that reduce the likelihood or consequences of significant failures. It should be revisited when the design, process, or evidence changes.

Severity, occurrence, and detectability ratings may help organize priorities, but a combined score does not replace judgment about context, especially when consequences differ sharply.

CC0 1.0View versioned object

Failure mode, effects, and criticality analysis

FMEA extended with formal criticality assessment

Failure mode, effects, and criticality analysis (FMECA) is a failure mode and effects analysis that also assesses the criticality of the identified failure modes.

More about this term

The analysis examines how an item or process could fail, what the effects would be, and which failure modes warrant priority under the chosen criticality method.

Criticality may be assessed qualitatively or calculated quantitatively; the selected method and assumptions should be stated.

CC0 1.0View versioned object

Failure rate

conditional time-to-failure rate for a nonrepairable item

In time-to-failure reliability analysis, the failure rate at a given time describes how rapidly items still functioning then fail.

More about this term

It relates failures during a short interval to the items that had survived to its start and to the length of that interval.

The rate can change with age and operating conditions; it should not be treated as a universal constant or confused with the fraction that has failed since the start.

CC0 1.0View versioned object

Failure rate function

instantaneous conditional failure rate over item age

For a time-to-failure model, a failure rate function assigns each time an instantaneous rate of failure among items that have survived to that time.

More about this term

It describes how the conditional failure rate changes with age or exposure and is often called the hazard function.

Its value at a time is a rate per unit time, not the probability that an item has failed by that time.

CC0 1.0View versioned object

Fairness

justifiability of treatment, process or outcome

Fairness is the quality of treatment, a decision process, or an outcome being justifiable under standards relevant to those affected.

More about this term

In a decision, the procedure and the result can be judged separately. A fair procedure does not guarantee that everyone will regard the outcome as fair, and a favorable outcome does not establish that the procedure was fair.

People’s perceptions of fairness matter for trust and response to a decision. Those perceptions are evidence of reception, not conclusive proof that the decision was justified.

CC0 1.0View versioned object

Family quality of life

family and developmental-disability support research

Family quality of life is how well family members' needs are met and how able they are to enjoy life together and pursue what matters to them.

More about this term

It includes family relationships, each member's well-being, available resources, and support. It cannot be inferred from one family member's health or circumstances alone.

CC0 1.0View versioned object

Fault

nonfunctional item state in fault-tree reliability analysis

In fault-tree reliability analysis, a fault is a state in which an item cannot perform a specified function.

More about this term

A fault may result from a failure event or from a systematic problem introduced in design, production, or operation.

The term identifies the nonfunctional state; a failure event describes the transition into that state.

CC0 1.0View versioned object

Fault tolerance

continued required function despite specified component faults

Fault tolerance is a system's ability to keep providing a required function when a specified component fault occurs.

More about this term

Redundant parts or alternate operating modes can help the system continue working after one part fails.

A fault-tolerance claim must name the faults and minimum performance it covers; it does not promise operation under every possible failure.

CC0 1.0View versioned object

Fault tree

top-down logic model of an undesired system event

A fault tree is a diagram that starts with a specified undesired system event and traces combinations of lower-level events that could produce it.

More about this term

Logical gates show how component faults, human actions, and other conditions combine to reach the top event.

The tree can support qualitative analysis of possible pathways and, with justified input probabilities, quantitative estimates of the top event.

CC0 1.0View versioned object

Fault tree analysis (FTA)

top-down logical analysis of a specified undesired event

Fault tree analysis (FTA) is a top-down method for showing how combinations of lower-level events could produce a specified unwanted event.

More about this term

A tree starts with that top event and connects contributing events through logical gates, such as “and” or “or.” The structure helps identify combinations worth investigating or controlling.

The tree can support qualitative analysis; estimating event likelihoods also requires defensible event data and model assumptions. A diagram alone does not establish that its listed events are the actual causes of an occurrence.

CC0 1.0View versioned object

Finding

quality-management auditing

In an audit, a finding is a documented result of evaluating collected evidence against an applicable audit criterion.

More about this term

It identifies what the evidence shows in relation to the criterion, such as conformity or nonconformity. A finding needs an evidential basis rather than an unsupported opinion.

CC0 1.0View versioned object

First-pass yield

share of units passing a defined process on their first attempt

First-pass yield is the proportion of units entering a specified process step that meet its acceptance criteria on the first attempt, without rework or retesting.

More about this term

Count first-pass conforming units over all eligible units entering the step. State the step, unit, population, and time period so the result can be compared meaningfully.

A unit repaired and accepted later may contribute to final output, but it did not pass on the first attempt. For a multistep flow, a separate rolled yield addresses passing every step without rework.

CC0 1.0View versioned object

Fitness for purpose

suitability for a stated aim

Fitness for purpose is how suitable an object is to achieve a specified purpose under relevant conditions.

More about this term

State the purpose, whose purpose it is, and the conditions that matter. A claim may concern an ordinary intended use or a specially declared one.

The phrase often overlaps with fitness for use. It does not prove that every requirement is met, and meeting listed requirements does not always establish fitness for the intended purpose.

CC0 1.0View versioned object

Fitness for use

suitability in a user’s context

Fitness for use is how suitable an object is for a user’s intended activity under the conditions in which it will be used.
