More about this term

The judgment depends on the user, task, setting, and consequences of failure. An object can meet its written specification yet be unsuitable for the intended use if the specification missed a relevant need.

Fitness for use and fitness for purpose overlap. This wording emphasizes the conditions of actual or intended use, without assigning the phrases mutually exclusive meanings.

CC0 1.0View versioned object

Floor effect

lower-end limit in health-status measurement

A floor effect occurs when a measure's lower limit prevents it from distinguishing values or changes below that limit.

More about this term

When many respondents receive the lowest available score, their underlying states may still differ even though the instrument reports the same value.

A low score alone does not establish a floor effect; the concern is lost discrimination at the lower end of the scale.

CC0 1.0View versioned object

Flourishing

human well-being across several dimensions of life

In human well-being research, flourishing is living especially well across several meaningful dimensions of life.

More about this term

Accounts may consider engagement, relationships, purpose, accomplishment, and positive experience, but they do not all use the same dimensions.

Flourishing means more than the absence of illness; its assessment depends on the stated account of well-being.

CC0 1.0View versioned object

Flow

movement of material, information, or work through a process in lean improvement

In lean process improvement, flow is the movement of work, material, or information through connected steps toward an intended output.

More about this term

A flow analysis looks at how each step passes work to the next, including waiting, interruptions, and buildup between steps.

Coordinating the steps with actual demand helps reduce work in process and avoid sending components onward before they are needed.

CC0 1.0View versioned object

Food quality

fitness of food characteristics for applicable requirements

Food quality is how well a food product's characteristics meet applicable requirements for its intended use.

More about this term

Relevant characteristics may include safety, composition, nutrition, sensory properties, and purity; which matter depends on the product and use.

Appealing taste does not make unsafe food acceptable. Safety needs its own assessment.

CC0 1.0View versioned object

Food safety

adverse-health-effect assurance for food used as intended

Food safety is warranted confidence that a food will not cause adverse health effects when it is prepared or eaten as intended.

More about this term

The intended use and the consumers matter when identifying relevant hazards and controls.

A hygiene program or hazard-control plan can support food safety, but the plan is not itself proof that a particular food is safe.

CC0 1.0View versioned object

Framework

organized conceptual structure for analysis or evaluation

A framework is an organized set of concepts, components, or relations used to guide analysis, design, or evaluation.

More about this term

For example, an educational-quality framework can group teaching components with indicators used to examine them.

A framework makes its chosen structure explicit; its usefulness still depends on how well that structure fits the case and evidence.

CC0 1.0View versioned object

Function

required action of an engineered system

In systems and reliability engineering, a function is an action a system or component must perform to achieve a stated objective.

More about this term

It identifies what is required of the system, rather than naming the hardware or person assigned to do it.

A function becomes testable when the required action and conditions of performance are specified.

CC0 1.0View versioned object

Functional suitability

software functions meeting stated and implied needs in specified use

In software quality, functional suitability is how well a product's functions serve stated and reasonably implied user needs under specified conditions.

More about this term

It includes whether needed tasks are covered, results are correct, and the functions help users complete those tasks.

A feature-rich product can still be unsuitable if it omits an essential task or gives the wrong result.

CC0 1.0View versioned object

Functioning

physical and social activity in health assessment

In health assessment, functioning is what a person is able to do in everyday physical and social life.

More about this term

It includes activities such as moving, dressing, and interacting with others, with the relevant activities chosen for the assessment.

Functioning and felt well-being are related but distinct: a person can report symptoms or distress that an observer cannot infer from activity alone.

CC0 1.0View versioned object
G11 terms

Gage repeatability and reproducibility (gage R&R)

industrial measurement-system variation study

A gage repeatability and reproducibility study estimates how much measurement results vary when the same items are measured repeatedly and by different appraisers.

More about this term

Repeatability concerns variation under repeated use by the same appraiser and equipment. Reproducibility concerns differences associated with appraisers or other stated changes in measurement conditions.

The study helps determine whether measurement variation is small enough for a specified decision. It is one part of measurement system analysis; it does not, by itself, assess bias, drift, or every source of error.

CC0 1.0View versioned object

Gap model of service quality

service-quality model of four provider gaps and a customer experience gap

The gap model of service quality explains differences between customers' expectations and perceived service through gaps in what a provider understands, specifies, delivers, and communicates.

More about this term

The expectations-versus-perceived-performance difference is the final gap; four provider-side gaps are proposed contributors.

The framework helps locate a possible service problem, but a particular gap must be investigated rather than assumed from a low rating alone.

CC0 1.0View versioned object

Gemba

actual place where work occurs in Lean practice

In Lean practice, gemba is the place where the work being examined actually happens.

More about this term

It may be a production floor or another work area where a process is carried out.

A gemba walk is a visit to observe conditions and improvement opportunities there; the walk is an activity, while gemba names the place.

CC0 1.0View versioned object

Generalizability

warranted extension of research findings

In research, generalizability is the extent to which findings from studied cases can reasonably be applied to other people, times, or settings.

More about this term

The intended group or setting beyond the study must be identified before judging whether the extension is warranted.

A study may answer its own question well without aiming to generalize beyond its particular cases.

CC0 1.0View versioned object

Good manufacturing practice

pharmaceutical manufacturing requirements and controls

In pharmaceuticals, good manufacturing practice (GMP) is the body of applicable requirements and controls for consistently making and handling medicines to required quality standards.

More about this term

It addresses manufacturing methods, facilities, equipment, and other controls rather than relying only on testing finished products.

The specific obligations depend on the product and jurisdiction; GMP is a practice framework, not a guarantee that every unit is free of defects.

CC0 1.0View versioned object

Goodness

cross-domain evaluative sense

Goodness is favorable evaluative standing.

More about this term

To understand a particular claim of goodness, ask: What is good, in what respect, for whom if anyone, and by which standards?

This is a usable cross-domain definition, rather than a claim that philosophy has settled on one analysis of every use of good.

The logical status of “good” remains disputed.

CC0 1.0View versioned object

Governance

organizational direction and oversight of decisions

In an organization, governance is how authority and accountability are arranged to direct and oversee consequential decisions.

More about this term

It determines who may decide what, how choices are reviewed, and who is answerable for them.

Managing a particular project takes place within those arrangements; it is not the whole of governance.

CC0 1.0View versioned object

Governance quality

evaluation of public governing arrangements and conduct

In public administration, governance quality is how well governing arrangements and decisions meet relevant standards for exercising public authority.

More about this term

The appraisal may consider accountability, transparency, effectiveness, fairness, and the rule of law, with their relevance made explicit for the case.

Efficient service delivery alone cannot settle the judgment if other governing standards are also at stake.

CC0 1.0View versioned object

Grade

named product or component class with specified performance characteristics

A grade is a named class of products or components distinguished by specified characteristics or performance requirements.

More about this term

A premium resistor grade, for example, can be specified to vary less than an ordinary grade.

The grade label identifies a class; whether a particular item meets its class's requirements still has to be established.

CC0 1.0View versioned object

Graduation rate

cohort-based educational credential completion

A graduation rate is the proportion of a defined entering student cohort that earns a specified credential within a specified time.

More about this term

The cohort, permitted exclusions, credential, and completion window must be stated to interpret the figure.

Changing the denominator or time window can change the rate even when the same students' records are used.

CC0 1.0View versioned object

GxP

umbrella shorthand for regulated good-practice families

GxP is shorthand for families of regulated good practices used in pharmaceutical development, testing, and production.

More about this term

The x stands for the particular practice area, such as manufacturing, laboratory work, or clinical research.

The abbreviation does not name a single rulebook; the applicable requirements depend on the activity and jurisdiction.

CC0 1.0View versioned object
H15 terms

Hallucination

plausible but inaccurate generative-AI information response

In a generative-AI information response, a hallucination is plausible-sounding content that conflicts with the best available evidence.

More about this term

Fluent wording can make the error seem credible, so important factual claims need checking against evidence outside the generated answer.

In this sense, it is an unintentional output error, not deliberately generated disinformation.

CC0 1.0View versioned object

Harm

adverse effect on a person or valued subject

Harm is injury, damage, or other adverse effect on a person, living thing, environment, or valued asset.

More about this term

A useful claim of harm identifies who or what was affected, the kind and severity of the effect, and the relevant setting. Harms may differ even when the same event is involved.

A hazard or unsafe condition indicates a possibility of harm. It does not by itself show that harm has occurred.

CC0 1.0View versioned object

Hazard

potential source of harm in risk assessment

In risk assessment, a hazard is something with the potential to cause harm.

More about this term

It may be present without harm occurring.

Identifying a hazard does not by itself tell how likely harm is or how severe the harm would be.

CC0 1.0View versioned object

Hazard analysis

identifying and evaluating significant food-safety hazards for HACCP

In food safety, hazard analysis is a systematic examination of potential hazards in a food operation to identify which need control.

More about this term

It considers the steps in the operation, the significance of possible hazards, and measures that could control them.

The analysis informs a hazard-control plan; it does not by itself show that controls were implemented or food is safe.

CC0 1.0View versioned object

Hazard analysis and critical control points (HACCP)

preventive food-safety control system

Hazard analysis and critical control points (HACCP) is a preventive food-safety system that identifies significant hazards and controls them at specified steps in a process.

More about this term

A HACCP plan identifies critical control points, sets critical limits, monitors them, specifies corrective action, and records and verifies how the controls work. Prerequisite programs provide basic conditions for the plan.

A critical control point is a step where control can prevent, eliminate, or reduce a food-safety hazard to an acceptable level. HACCP does not mean that testing a finished product alone is sufficient to control the process.

CC0 1.0View versioned object

Hazard rate

instantaneous conditional failure rate in reliability

In reliability analysis, the hazard rate at a specified age is the instantaneous failure rate among items that have survived to that age.

More about this term

It relates failures near that age to the items still operating; for a continuous lifetime model, the rate equals the lifetime density divided by the survival probability.

A hazard rate has units of inverse time or another exposure unit and is not itself the probability of failure over an interval.

CC0 1.0View versioned object

Health-related quality of life

health-linked functioning and perceived well-being

Health-related quality of life is how a person functions and feels in the physical, mental, and social dimensions of health.

More about this term

It includes everyday activities and relationships as well as perceived states such as pain, vitality, and emotional distress.

Assessment commonly asks the person directly, because others cannot fully observe their experience of well-being.

CC0 1.0View versioned object

Healthcare quality

quality of care and its delivery

Healthcare quality is how well care and its delivery meet justified health needs while avoiding preventable harm.

More about this term

Safety, effectiveness, responsiveness to patients, timeliness, efficiency, and equity are distinct aspects of a judgment about care. A favorable result in one aspect does not settle the others.

State the patient group, setting, and purpose of care before judging it. An outcome alone may not show whether care was safe, timely, or fair.

CC0 1.0View versioned object

Hedonic quality

pleasantness of experience

For an experience, hedonic quality is its pleasant or unpleasant character for the person having it.

More about this term

It concerns how the experience feels; whether pleasure is an intrinsic feature or depends on a person's attitude remains disputed.

CC0 1.0View versioned object

Histogram

distribution display for quantitative observations

A histogram is a graph that groups numerical observations into value intervals and shows how frequently observations fall in each interval.

More about this term

The intervals, or bins, follow the variable's numerical scale rather than being sorted by frequency.

The display helps reveal a distribution's shape and spread, but its appearance can change with bin width, especially for small samples.

CC0 1.0View versioned object

Hoshin kanri

strategy deployment through aligned plans and repeated review

Hoshin kanri is a method for turning an organization’s strategic priorities into aligned objectives and action plans across its levels.

More about this term

Plans are developed and adjusted through dialogue among the people responsible for carrying them out. Responsibilities, resources, and measures make the priorities actionable.

Regular review connects results and lessons back to the next planning cycle. A statement of priorities alone is not a deployed plan.

CC0 1.0View versioned object

House of Quality

customer-to-design planning matrix used in QFD

A House of Quality is a planning matrix that maps customer requirements to proposed product or service characteristics, recording how those characteristics could address the requirements to guide design priorities and targets.

More about this term

Its central grid contains assessed need-to-response relationships. Depending on the method, it may also show customer importance, interactions among characteristics, comparisons with alternatives, and technical targets.

The matrix supports design decisions within QFD. Its scores and targets are planning judgments, not evidence that the finished offering performs as intended.

CC0 1.0View versioned object

Human oversight

human review of AI outputs and decisions

In AI use, human oversight is human review of a system's outputs or decisions to bring contextual judgment and identify errors.

More about this term

For consequential decisions, people can review an automated recommendation before it is acted on.

Review can also catch errors after deployment, such as resources misclassified by an automated library system.

CC0 1.0View versioned object

Human service quality

social and human services

Human service quality concerns how well a human service's resources, delivery, and immediate results serve its intended recipients.

More about this term

A recipient's quality of life matters, but it is not interchangeable with service quality: changes in life can also reflect circumstances outside the service.

CC0 1.0View versioned object

Hypothesis test

statistical test of a specified null claim

A statistical hypothesis test uses sample data and a stated model to evaluate a null hypothesis against an alternative hypothesis.

More about this term

A test statistic and decision rule indicate whether the observed data warrant rejecting the null hypothesis at a chosen significance level.

Failing to reject the null hypothesis does not prove that it is true; the test's assumptions and possible decision errors matter.

CC0 1.0View versioned object
I36 terms

Identity, strength, quality, and purity

distinct represented properties of a drug under U.S. drug GMP

In U.S. drug manufacturing requirements, identity, strength, quality, and purity name distinct properties that a drug must possess as represented.

More about this term

Identity concerns what the drug is; strength concerns its concentration or potency.

The four terms form a regulatory grouping, not four interchangeable names for quality; each is judged against applicable requirements and evidence.

CC0 1.0View versioned object

Image quality

image fitness for an intended use

Image quality is how well an image's properties support its intended use or interpretation.

More about this term

Relevant properties can include detail, fidelity, and the ability to distinguish what matters for the task. An image suitable for one purpose may be inadequate for another.

In remote sensing, spatial resolution, geometric alignment, and radiometric information can affect which ground features can be identified or compared.

CC0 1.0View versioned object

Impact

consequential change attributed to a program

In program evaluation, impact is a consequential change in people or conditions attributed to a program beyond its immediate activities.

More about this term

An impact claim should identify the affected group, time period, and basis for attributing the change.

Delivering activities or outputs alone does not establish impact.

CC0 1.0View versioned object

Impartiality

journalistic fairness and independence from factional interests

In journalism, impartiality is fair treatment of relevant facts and viewpoints without serving a faction's interests.

More about this term

It requires independent judgment and attention to interests that could compromise a reporter's work.

Fair treatment does not require presenting claims with unequal evidence as though they were equally supported.

CC0 1.0View versioned object

Improvement

positive result of process change

In process management, improvement is a favorable change in performance in a specified respect.

More about this term

The respect and comparison point matter: a change can improve timeliness while worsening accuracy or cost.

An improvement effort is an attempt to produce that result; its completion alone does not show that performance improved.

CC0 1.0View versioned object

Inclusion

access and meaningful participation in higher education

In higher education, inclusion means arranging access and participation so people from different social groups can take part meaningfully and benefit.

More about this term

It concerns policies, teaching, and the learning environment as well as who enters an institution.

Admission or physical presence alone does not show that barriers to participation have been removed.

CC0 1.0View versioned object

Incoming inspection

check of purchased parts or materials after receipt

Incoming inspection checks purchased parts or materials after receipt against applicable specifications or purchasing requirements.

More about this term

It may examine every item or use a defined sample to decide whether a lot can be accepted.

A passing lot check concerns the received goods; it does not by itself establish the supplier’s overall capability or future performance.

CC0 1.0View versioned object

Independence

auditor separation supporting impartial judgment

In auditing, independence is the auditor's separation from the activity under review and from interests that could compromise impartial judgment.

More about this term

Practical arrangements should keep auditors free of bias and conflicts of interest; internal auditors should be separate from the function audited where practicable.

Independence supports credible conclusions but does not replace sound evidence or competent analysis.

CC0 1.0View versioned object

Index

economic index number comparing aggregate change

In economic measurement, an index is a numerical summary comparing a specified set of prices or quantities with a reference period.

More about this term

A price index combines selected items under a stated formula and, where applicable, weighting rule.

Its result depends on which items are included and how they are aggregated; it is not the price of any one item.

CC0 1.0View versioned object

Indicator

evaluation and monitoring

An indicator is an observable or assessable factor used to track something of interest.

More about this term

It helps answer an evaluation question, but its value requires interpretation: even an accurately assessed indicator is an approximation of the condition or change of interest.

Indicators can be qualitative or quantitative.

CC0 1.0View versioned object

Indoor environmental quality

building indoor conditions relevant to occupants

Indoor environmental quality is the condition of a building's indoor environment as it affects its occupants.

More about this term

An assessment can consider air, temperature, lighting, sound, and other conditions relevant to the building's use.

Indoor air quality is one component of this broader appraisal, not its whole meaning.

CC0 1.0View versioned object

Inference

reasoning from grounds to a conclusion

An inference is a move in reasoning from premises, observations, or other information to a further conclusion.

More about this term

The relation between the grounds and conclusion may be deductive, statistical, causal, or another form. The conclusion is warranted only to the extent that the grounds and the inferential connection support it.

An inference can be made explicit so others can test its assumptions and limits. It is distinct from the observations that start it and the decision that may follow.

CC0 1.0View versioned object

Information governance

organizational rules and responsibilities for information

Information governance is an organization's framework of responsibilities, policies, and controls for managing information through its life cycle.

More about this term

It addresses decisions about access, use, protection, retention, and disposal across records, documents, and other information.

A policy by itself is insufficient if no one has authority or responsibility to apply it.

CC0 1.0View versioned object

Information integrity

risk-study evidence

In a risk study, information integrity concerns whether data and other information accurately represent the properties under study and come from credible sources.

More about this term

It is distinct from whether the information is sufficient or applicable to the study's time, place, and population.

CC0 1.0View versioned object

Information quality

fitness of information for a specified use

Information quality is how well information serves a specified purpose, given what it represents, how it was produced, and its relevant limitations.

More about this term

Assessment may consider accuracy, completeness, timeliness, utility, integrity, and whether the supporting data and analysis fit the question. The choice of criteria depends on the use.

Clear presentation cannot make unsupported information reliable. Identify the source, methods, and uncertainty before using the information to justify a consequential claim.

CC0 1.0View versioned object

Inspection

determining conformity to specified requirements

Inspection is an examination used to determine whether an object meets specified requirements.

More about this term

The object, requirements, and inspection method determine what the result establishes. A passing sample does not by itself establish that every item or future output will conform.

Inspection can supply evidence for quality control or assurance. It does not by itself settle whether the requirements are suitable for the object’s intended use.

CC0 1.0View versioned object

Institutional effectiveness

higher-education achievement of mission-linked goals

In higher education, institutional effectiveness concerns how well an institution achieves goals consistent with its mission across its programs and services.

More about this term

It is examined through planned outcomes, evidence of performance, and decisions about improvement and resources.

Success in one program alone cannot establish effectiveness across the whole institution.

CC0 1.0View versioned object

Institutional quality

performance of public governing rules and institutions

In public governance, institutional quality is how well established rules and organizations fulfill valued governing functions.

More about this term

One assessment may examine how reliably institutions protect property rights and restrain corruption; the chosen functions and standards need to be stated.

Efficient public spending alone does not settle whether the institutions performing it are sound.

CC0 1.0View versioned object

Instructional quality

K-12 teaching practice

In K–12 education, instructional quality is how well teaching practices support specified learning goals for the students concerned.

More about this term

It calls for evidence about instruction and learning; the choice of content or a highly rated textbook alone does not establish it.

CC0 1.0View versioned object

Instrument

tool used to obtain observations in measurement or assessment

In measurement or assessment, an instrument is a tool used to obtain or record observations under a specified procedure.

More about this term

It may be a physical device or a structured questionnaire; its role, conditions of use, and output should be clear.

The instrument is distinct from the property assessed and from the result it produces.

CC0 1.0View versioned object

Instrumental value

value as a means to another valued end

Instrumental value is the value something has as a means to a further valued end.

More about this term

A tool's instrumental value depends on the end it helps achieve and how well it helps achieve it.

Instrumental value is a form of value derived from something else, but not every form of such value is instrumental.

CC0 1.0View versioned object

Integrity

honest and principled professional conduct

In professional ethics, integrity is conduct that remains faithful to one's duties and stated ethical commitments.

More about this term

It involves truthfulness, objective decisions, and handling conflicts of interest openly.

This sense concerns a person's or profession's conduct; the word also has different technical uses for data or physical systems.

CC0 1.0View versioned object

Intended use

stated users, purpose and conditions for a designed product

An intended use is a use for which a product is designed or represented as suitable, with its users, purpose, and conditions stated.

More about this term

It gives design and validation a defined question: can the product serve those users under those conditions?

A foreseeable misuse may still call for risk assessment, but its foreseeability alone does not make it an intended use.

CC0 1.0View versioned object

Inter-rater reliability

relative consistency among raters in an empirical rating task

Inter-rater reliability describes how consistently different raters distinguish among the same targets in a specified rating task.

More about this term

Raters can rank targets similarly while assigning different values; exact matching concerns inter-rater agreement.

To interpret a result, identify the raters, what they rated, the kind of ratings, and the statistic used.

CC0 1.0View versioned object

Interaction

factor-dependent effect in a designed experiment

In a designed experiment, an interaction occurs when the effect of one factor on a response changes with the level of another factor.

More about this term

For example, changing temperature might improve output at one pressure but worsen it at another. The result must therefore be interpreted for the relevant combination of factor levels.

A study that varies one factor at a time can miss this pattern. An interaction is a property of the studied response and setting, not a claim that the factors physically touch.

CC0 1.0View versioned object

Interest

stake in a decision or outcome

In a decision, an interest is something a person or group has at stake because the outcome may affect what matters to them.

More about this term

The interest may concern a possible benefit, burden, valued condition, or protected claim; identify whose interest it is and how it may be affected.

Being interested in an issue does not itself give someone formal authority to decide it.

CC0 1.0View versioned object

Internal consistency

coherence among items in a multi-item measure

In psychometrics, internal consistency is how strongly items in a multi-item measure relate as indicators of the intended construct.

More about this term

Split-half methods and coefficients such as Cronbach's alpha summarize aspects of that relationship, and test length can affect the result.

A high internal-consistency estimate provides reliability evidence, not proof that the measure is valid for a particular interpretation or use.

CC0 1.0View versioned object

Internal failure cost

cost arising from defects discovered before delivery

An internal failure cost is a cost arising from a defect or nonconformity found before a product or service is delivered.

More about this term

Scrap, rework, and review of defective material are typical examples. The failure is discovered within the producing organization’s delivery boundary.

Internal and external failure costs differ by when the problem is found relative to delivery, not by whether the failure is serious. State the boundary for a multistage service or supply chain.

CC0 1.0View versioned object

Internal quality audit

first-party audit of an organization's quality-related work

An internal quality audit is an audit conducted by or on behalf of an organization to assess its own quality-related work against stated criteria.

More about this term

It may examine a product or service, a process, or the quality management system, using collected evidence to identify conformity and gaps.

Auditors should be independent of the activity examined where practicable, even though the audit is internal.

CC0 1.0View versioned object

Internal validity

warrant for causal inference within studied cases

In a study of cause and effect, internal validity concerns how well the evidence supports attributing an observed outcome to the proposed cause.

More about this term

The study must address other explanations for the observed relationship within the cases it examined.

This differs from asking whether the finding also applies to people or settings beyond the study.

CC0 1.0View versioned object

Interoperability

systems exchanging and using information

In systems engineering, interoperability is the ability of systems or components to exchange information and put it to use.

More about this term

Successful transfer alone is insufficient if the receiving system cannot interpret or apply what it receives.

An interoperability claim should specify the systems, information, intended use, and conditions being assessed.

CC0 1.0View versioned object

Interpretability

human understanding of a machine-learning model's outputs

In machine learning, interpretability is the extent to which a person can understand how a model reaches or supports an output.

More about this term

A short decision path may let a reader trace a classification through visible tests; a more complex model may be harder to inspect.

Interpretability depends on the question and audience and does not by itself establish that a model's output is correct.

CC0 1.0View versioned object

Intrinsic value

axiological value grounded in what something is

In axiology, intrinsic value is value something has in virtue of what it is itself, rather than value derived from something outside it.

More about this term

The claim concerns the ground of value; valuing something as an end rather than a means is related but conceptually distinct.

Whether pleasure, nature, or another subject actually has intrinsic value requires a separate argument.

CC0 1.0View versioned object

Item difficulty

difficulty of a scored test item for examinees

In testing, item difficulty describes how challenging a particular question is for the examinees or ability range of interest.

More about this term

In classical item analysis, it is often reported as the proportion who answer correctly, so a higher reported proportion means an easier item.

In item response theory, a difficulty parameter locates the item on the modeled ability scale; the two quantities should not be confused.

CC0 1.0View versioned object

Item discrimination

separation of examinees by a measured trait

In testing, item discrimination is how well a test item distinguishes people at different levels of the trait the test intends to measure.

More about this term

Its value depends on how higher and lower trait levels are established and on the group being assessed.

The term describes a measurement property, not unfair treatment of a protected group.

CC0 1.0View versioned object

Item response theory

statistical models linking latent traits to item responses

Item response theory is a family of statistical models that relates a person's unobserved trait level to the probability of particular responses to test or questionnaire items.

More about this term

The models describe properties of individual items, such as where along the trait scale responses change and how sharply they change.

They can be used for scored questions or rating-scale responses that have no single correct answer.

CC0 1.0View versioned object
J3 terms

Jidoka

production response that stops and exposes abnormal conditions

In production, jidoka is a practice of stopping work when an abnormal or defective condition appears so it can be addressed before production continues.

More about this term

A machine or worker may trigger the stop, making the condition visible for investigation.

It intervenes at the point of production rather than relying only on inspection after output has moved on.

CC0 1.0View versioned object

Journalism quality

professional reporting

Journalism quality is how well reporting fulfills the purposes and standards relevant to journalism.

More about this term

Assessment may consider independence, relevance, context, and audience needs; reach alone does not establish quality.

CC0 1.0View versioned object

Judgment

conclusion drawn from information

A judgment is a conclusion reached about a matter by interpreting information in light of a relevant basis for deciding.

More about this term

The basis may be a rule, criterion, comparison, or informed professional appraisal. A useful judgment makes that basis and any important uncertainty visible.

Judgments may be factual or evaluative. A quality judgment is the narrower case that appraises how well an object meets relevant quality requirements or criteria.

CC0 1.0View versioned object
K3 terms

Kaizen

participatory continual improvement in quality management

Kaizen is a participatory practice of making continuing improvements to work.

More about this term

The word conveys change for the better, with people involved in the work contributing to improvements in quality and safety.

A short team-based kaizen event is one possible activity, not the whole continuing practice.

CC0 1.0View versioned object

Kaizen event

time-limited team improvement activity in lean practice

A kaizen event is a short, focused team effort to improve a defined work process or area.

More about this term

People who do the work join others who can analyze the process and authorize changes.

The team aims to make practical changes within a limited period and assign follow-up work where immediate implementation is not possible.

CC0 1.0View versioned object

KJ method

qualitative synthesis and quality function deployment

The KJ method organizes many qualitative observations or ideas into groups based on their perceived affinities, then develops themes from those groups.

More about this term

In QFD, it can help a team turn raw customer statements into articulated needs. The groupings are interpretive judgments, not numerical measurements.

CC0 1.0View versioned object
L22 terms

Lead time

elapsed time across a defined process or delivery boundary

Lead time is the elapsed time from a specified starting event to completion of a process or delivery of its output.

More about this term

The start and end points should be stated, such as receipt of an order and delivery to a customer. Time spent waiting within those boundaries counts as well as processing time.

Making one activity faster may leave total lead time unchanged if queues or other delays remain.

CC0 1.0View versioned object

Leadership

direction and example in organizational quality management

In quality management, leadership is the work of setting direction, showing commitment through action, and enabling people to achieve and improve shared results.

More about this term

Leaders communicate purpose and values, engage the people affected by the work, and create a focus on action and accountability.

A formal title alone does not establish effective leadership; the relevant evidence is what leaders do and what their direction enables.

CC0 1.0View versioned object

Lean

organizational approach to value, flow and improvement

Lean is an approach to organizing and improving work so that it delivers value with less waste and more reliable flow.

More about this term

Practices may include clarifying value for the user, mapping the work, reducing unnecessary steps, using pull where appropriate, and learning from problems. The practices must fit the setting.

A single tool or cost-cutting exercise does not, by itself, establish a lean system. Look for how the work, people, and continuing improvement fit together.

CC0 1.0View versioned object

Lean Six Sigma

combined Lean and Six Sigma approach to improving processes

Lean Six Sigma is a process-improvement approach combining Lean's attention to waste and flow with Six Sigma's attention to variation and defects.

More about this term

Teams use evidence about customer needs and process performance to select and test changes.

The combined name describes an approach, not a fixed list of tools or a guarantee of a particular result.

CC0 1.0View versioned object

Learning effectiveness

attainment of specified learning outcomes by intended learners

Learning effectiveness is how well a learning activity helps its intended learners achieve specified learning outcomes.

More about this term

The outcomes may involve knowledge, skills, behavior, or attitudes, so assessment must fit what the activity aims to develop.

Participation or satisfaction alone does not establish that the intended learning occurred.

CC0 1.0View versioned object

Learning outcome

intended and assessable learning from an educational experience

An intended learning outcome states what a learner is expected to know, understand, or be able to demonstrate after an educational experience.

More about this term

It describes learning by the student rather than only material covered or an activity performed by the instructor.

The phrase can also name what learners actually achieved, so an assessment should distinguish the intended outcome from evidence of attainment.

CC0 1.0View versioned object

Legal certainty

predictable guidance from law

In rule-of-law discussions, legal certainty is the degree to which people can identify the rules governing their conduct and reasonably anticipate how those rules will be applied.

More about this term

Clear, publicly accessible rules and regular procedures help people rely on the law for guidance.

Legal certainty does not promise that every case has an unambiguous outcome.

CC0 1.0View versioned object

Legal coherence

fit among legal rules and decisions

Legal coherence is the extent to which legal rules and decisions fit together under a defensible interpretation rather than yielding unresolved contradictions.

More about this term

Coherence helps law guide conduct and supports consistent decisions. It does not, by itself, establish that the rules are fair or just.

CC0 1.0View versioned object

Legal quality

rule-of-law qualities of legal rules and official action

In a rule-of-law assessment, legal quality concerns how well rules and official acts are publicly knowable, coherent, and capable of guiding conduct without arbitrary exercise of power.

More about this term

These formal qualities matter, but they do not alone settle whether a law is just; substantive accounts also examine rights and equality.

CC0 1.0View versioned object

Legitimacy

justification of an intervention's framing to affected people

In participatory systems work, legitimacy concerns whether an intervention's aims, boundaries, and decisions can be justified to people affected by it.

More about this term

Ask who sets the aims, whose interests count, and who can question the framing.

Technical expertise or a desired result alone does not settle whether the affected parties were treated justifiably.

CC0 1.0View versioned object

Level of analysis

scale of units addressed by observations and claims in research

In research, a level of analysis specifies the kind or scale of unit about which observations and claims are organized, such as an individual, household, organization, or nation.

More about this term

It helps a reader tell whether a reported pattern concerns people separately or aggregates such as cities or organizations.

A pattern observed for groups does not by itself establish the same pattern for every member of those groups.

CC0 1.0View versioned object

Life cycle

pharmaceutical product life cycle

For a pharmaceutical product, the life cycle spans its initial development, marketing, and eventual discontinuation.

More about this term

Knowledge about the product and its manufacturing process can grow across those phases.

A decision made during development may need review when later evidence or changes affect the product.

CC0 1.0View versioned object

Life-cycle assessment

environmental assessment

Life-cycle assessment is a method for estimating a product's or project's environmental impacts across specified stages of its life cycle.

More about this term

Its boundary and assumptions determine what is counted; it differs from life-cycle cost analysis, which examines financial costs.

CC0 1.0View versioned object

Lifecycle stage

object or information lifecycle

A lifecycle stage is a named phase in an object's progression from creation through use to eventual disposition.

More about this term

Stages organize the work, responsibilities, and handoffs that matter at a given point; their boundaries depend on the lifecycle model and the object.

CC0 1.0View versioned object

Likelihood

risk assessment of a specified event

In risk assessment, likelihood expresses how plausible it is that a specified event will occur under stated conditions.

More about this term

It may be expressed as a numerical probability or a qualitative category such as low, medium, or high.

Likelihood concerns occurrence; assessing risk also requires attention to the event's possible consequences.

CC0 1.0View versioned object

Liking

favorable sensory response to food

In food sensory evaluation, liking is a person's favorable response to the experience of a food.

More about this term

It can be assessed after tasting a product and may differ between people or testing conditions.

Liking differs from preference: someone may enjoy a food but choose another because of price, availability, or other concerns.

CC0 1.0View versioned object

Loss

loss counted in cost-benefit appraisal

In cost-benefit appraisal, a loss is a reduction in a valued resource or condition attributable to a proposed project.

More about this term

A loss can count as a social cost even when it has no market price, as when a project removes a valued natural amenity.

Estimating its monetary value can be difficult; the stated appraisal should make that uncertainty visible.

CC0 1.0View versioned object

Loss function

numerical cost assigned to supervised prediction outcomes

In supervised learning, a loss function assigns a numerical cost to a prediction in light of the outcome that actually occurs.

More about this term

The model can use that function to compare predictions and seek lower expected loss on new cases.

Different loss functions penalize errors differently, so the choice expresses which mistakes matter for the task.

CC0 1.0View versioned object

Lot

defined product quantity for sampling decision

In acceptance sampling, a lot is a defined quantity of product treated as one unit for an accept-or-reject decision.

More about this term

Its units are grouped under conditions regarded as sufficiently uniform for the sampling plan.

The lot is the whole quantity under decision; the sample is the subset inspected.

CC0 1.0View versioned object

Lot acceptance

acceptance sampling

In acceptance sampling, lot acceptance is the decision that a submitted lot meets a sampling plan's acceptance criteria on the basis of inspected samples.

More about this term

It is a decision under sampling uncertainty, not proof that every unit conforms; a lot that is not accepted is not automatically unusable.

CC0 1.0View versioned object

Lower control limit

statistical process control

A lower control limit is the lower statistical boundary on a control chart for values expected from a process showing only routine variation.

More about this term

A point below it can signal a process change that warrants investigation. It is calculated from process behavior and is not the same as a minimum acceptable specification.

CC0 1.0View versioned object

LTPD

lot tolerance percent defective in acceptance sampling

Lot tolerance percent defective (LTPD) is a specified percentage of defective units at which an acceptance sampling plan has a low probability of accepting a lot.

More about this term

It marks a poor-lot quality point on the plan's operating-characteristic curve; the associated probability of acceptance expresses the consumer's risk at that point.

LTPD is a property of the sampling plan, not a measurement of the defective percentage in a particular lot.

CC0 1.0View versioned object
M51 terms

Maintainability

ability to maintain or restore an engineered item

For an engineered item, maintainability is how readily it can be kept in or restored to a required condition through maintenance under stated conditions.

More about this term

The assessment depends on the work, available procedures and resources, and the skills of those performing it.

It concerns carrying out maintenance, not how often the item fails.

CC0 1.0View versioned object

Maintenance task

specified action selected within reliability-centered maintenance

In reliability-centered maintenance, a maintenance task is a specified action, with a basis for when to perform it, intended to preserve or restore an asset’s required function.

More about this term

A condition-based task responds to an observed indicator; a time-directed task is scheduled by elapsed time or use.

A task is chosen in light of the failure mode, its consequences, and whether the action is feasible and worthwhile. Some failures instead call for redesign or an explicit decision to let the part run until failure.

CC0 1.0View versioned object

Management philosophy

guiding principles for managing quality across an organization

A management philosophy is a set of guiding beliefs about what an organization should pursue and how its people should manage work to pursue it.

More about this term

In quality management, such a philosophy can shape priorities, leadership practices, employee participation, and the use of evidence for improvement.

A tool or procedure may put one principle into practice, but it is not the whole philosophy.

CC0 1.0View versioned object

Management response

management action or plan in answer to an audit finding

In an audit, a management response is the audited organization’s account of action taken or planned in answer to a finding.

More about this term

An immediate correction may address a visible problem without eliminating its cause.

For a nonconformity, the response should connect the finding to cause analysis and corrective action; follow-up evidence is needed to establish whether the action was effective.

CC0 1.0View versioned object

Management review

leadership review of a quality management system

Management review is a planned examination by responsible leaders of whether a quality management system remains suitable and effective for its objectives.

More about this term

Relevant inputs can include performance trends, complaints, audits, changes, and follow-up from earlier reviews. The point is to interpret those inputs and make decisions, not merely receive a report.

The resulting actions may change processes, resources, policy, or objectives. Record who is responsible and later check whether the actions had the intended effect.

CC0 1.0View versioned object

Management system

interacting organizational arrangements for objectives and coordinated work

A management system is the connected set of an organization's arrangements for setting objectives and directing work toward them.

More about this term

Those arrangements can include interacting roles, processes, resources, and methods for assessing performance.

It is broader than a set of documents or any single management procedure.

CC0 1.0View versioned object

Manufacturing quality

manufacturing process and output against applicable requirements

Manufacturing quality is how well production processes and their outputs meet applicable requirements.

More about this term

It concerns control of production conditions, repeatability of the process, and whether resulting units meet acceptance criteria.

A correctly manufactured product can still be unsuitable if the design requirements were wrong or incomplete.

CC0 1.0View versioned object

Master data management

governance of shared core entity records

Master data management is the coordinated governance of shared records for core entities, such as customers or products, so their identities and key attributes remain consistent across an organization.

More about this term

It addresses conflicting versions of the same entity in different systems or business units.

Master data describe enduring entities; transaction data record events such as orders or payments.

CC0 1.0View versioned object

Material quality

construction materials

In construction, material quality is how well a material's relevant properties meet the requirements for its intended use.

More about this term

Strength or moisture content may matter for a particular material; inspection and traceability help identify unsuitable supplies before installation.

CC0 1.0View versioned object

Materiality

decision significance of reporting information

In reporting, materiality is the significance of information, an omission, or a misstatement to decisions by the report's intended users.

More about this term

A matter may be material because of its nature, size, or surrounding circumstances.

The judgment depends on the report and its users; the term supplies no universal numerical cutoff.

CC0 1.0View versioned object

Maturity

organizational process development against a model

In capability assessment, maturity is the degree to which an organization's processes meet the practices described by a specified maturity model.

More about this term

A maturity level summarizes performance against that model's staged practices and assessment rules.

The level is model-dependent; it is not a universal grade for every outcome the organization produces.

CC0 1.0View versioned object

Mean time between failures

average operating time per failure in a repairable system

For a repairable system, mean time between failures (MTBF) is the average operating time per failure over a stated observation period.

More about this term

It is commonly calculated as total operating time divided by the number of observed failures.

It excludes counted downtime; mean time to repair describes restoration time. The average does not predict when the next failure will occur.

CC0 1.0View versioned object

Mean time to failure

average first-failure time for items treated as nonrepairable

For items treated as nonrepairable, mean time to failure (MTTF) is the average operating time until first failure.

More about this term

It may be estimated from observed lifetimes or calculated from a fitted lifetime distribution.

The reciprocal of a failure rate gives MTTF only under a constant-rate exponential model; MTBF instead summarizes operation between failures of a repairable system.

CC0 1.0View versioned object

Mean time to recovery

repairable system availability

For a repairable system, mean time to recovery is the average elapsed time required to restore a failed unit to service under a specified counting rule.

More about this term

The start and end of recovery and any excluded waiting time must be stated; shorter recovery generally supports greater availability.

CC0 1.0View versioned object

Mean time to repair

average corrective-maintenance duration for repairable equipment

For a repairable system, mean time to repair (MTTR) is the average counted downtime needed to restore it after a failure.

More about this term

For a set of failures, divide the counted repair downtime by the number of failures; state which delays the downtime includes.

MTTR concerns restoration time, whereas mean time between failures concerns operating time between failures. Neither figure alone fully determines availability.

CC0 1.0View versioned object

Measurand

intended quantity in metrology

A measurand is the particular quantity intended to be measured.

More about this term

A useful specification identifies the subject and property so the intended quantity is clear.

The measurement result attributes a value to that quantity; it is not the measurand itself.

CC0 1.0View versioned object

Measure

program evaluation evidence specification

In program evaluation, a measure is a specified observation or calculation used to produce evidence about an indicator.

More about this term

It tells an evaluator what to record or compute.

A measure may be quantitative or qualitative; an indicator identifies what the measure bears on.

In metrology, measurement names the process, while measurement result names its output; measure is therefore too ambiguous to substitute for either term in a technical record.

CC0 1.0View versioned object

Measurement

metrology measurement process

Measurement uses a defined empirical procedure to obtain a value or set of values for a specified quantity.

More about this term

The procedure involves comparison or counting and may include calculations to obtain the result.

It requires a clear account of what is being measured and how.

A measurement result reports the attributed value or values with relevant information, generally including measurement uncertainty. Deciding whether it satisfies a requirement is a further step.

CC0 1.0View versioned object

Measurement error

metrological difference between result and reference value

In metrology, measurement error is a measured quantity value minus a reference quantity value.

More about this term

Its sign and size depend on the chosen reference and the measurement conditions. The exact error usually cannot be known, because the reference itself may be uncertain.

Systematic and random contributions call for different treatment. Measurement error is a difference, whereas measurement uncertainty expresses the spread of values that can reasonably be attributed to what was measured.

CC0 1.0View versioned object

Measurement invariance

psychometric comparability across linguistic or cultural groups

In psychometrics, measurement invariance is the extent to which a test measures the intended construct comparably across specified groups.

More about this term

It matters when scores from different linguistic or cultural groups are compared.

A faithful translation alone does not establish that scores have the same meaning; evidence of comparability is needed for the intended comparison.

CC0 1.0View versioned object

Measurement model

mathematical relation among quantities in metrology

In metrology, a measurement model specifies the mathematical relationship among the quantities involved in obtaining a measured value.

More about this term

It identifies input quantities and an output quantity; a measurement function can calculate the output from given input values.

Its usefulness depends on whether the modeled relationship and inputs fit the quantity and conditions being measured.

CC0 1.0View versioned object

Measurement quality

fitness of a measurement system and result for intended use

Measurement quality is how well a measurement system and its results serve a stated measurement purpose.

More about this term

Assess it against the intended measurand, method, conditions, and data requirements, including the uncertainty relevant to the decision.

A repeatable number may still be unfit if it addresses the wrong quantity or is too uncertain for the intended use.

CC0 1.0View versioned object

Measurement result

metrological result of measuring a quantity

A measurement result is the value or set of values attributed to a specified quantity by measurement, together with information needed to interpret it.

More about this term

It commonly includes a reported value and its measurement uncertainty.

The result records what the measurement supports; deciding whether it meets a requirement is a separate judgment.

CC0 1.0View versioned object

Measurement scale

representation of measurement values and permitted comparisons

A measurement scale is a system for representing observations as categories or values under stated rules.

More about this term

The scale determines which comparisons are meaningful: a category can distinguish kinds, an ordered scale can also rank them, and a numerical scale may permit further operations.

The number shown by an instrument is a result on a scale, not the scale itself.

CC0 1.0View versioned object

Measurement standard

metrological reference realizing a quantity value

In metrology, a measurement standard is a reference that realizes a specified quantity value with stated uncertainty for use in other measurements.

More about this term

It may take the form of an instrument, material, or artifact used to calibrate or compare measuring equipment.

Here, standard means a measurement reference, not a written rule for how to measure.

CC0 1.0View versioned object

Measurement system

arrangement used to obtain values in metrology

In metrology, a measurement system is the instruments, procedures, people, and operating conditions used together to obtain values for a specified quantity.

More about this term

Its configuration includes the reference, test item, method, and environment where these affect the result.

Variation from the measuring arrangement can be mistaken for variation in the subject being measured.

CC0 1.0View versioned object

Measurement system analysis (MSA)

assessment of a measurement process and its variation

Measurement system analysis (MSA) examines whether a measurement process produces results dependable enough for its intended use.

More about this term

It investigates variation and error arising from the instrument, method, operators, environment, and use over time. Common checks include bias, stability, repeatability, and reproducibility.

Gauge repeatability and reproducibility is one part of MSA, not the whole analysis. Before judging variation in what is measured, determine how much of the observed variation the measurement process itself contributes.

CC0 1.0View versioned object

Measurement uncertainty

metrological uncertainty associated with a measured quantity

Measurement uncertainty describes the dispersion of values reasonably attributable to a specified measurand, given the information used in measuring it.

More about this term

It is not the same as measurement error, which compares a measured value with a reference value. An uncertainty assessment identifies relevant contributors and how they are combined.

When a result is used to decide conformity, the uncertainty and the decision rule both matter. A reported interval or coverage factor must be interpreted under its stated method and conditions.

CC0 1.0View versioned object

Mechanism

causal process linking an antecedent to an effect

In a causal explanation, a mechanism is a process or arrangement through which a proposed cause brings about an effect.

More about this term

A mechanism account addresses how the effect could arise, including the relevant interactions or transmission between steps.

Observing that two events occur together does not by itself identify the mechanism linking them.

CC0 1.0View versioned object

Media literacy

critical understanding and use of news media

In journalism, media literacy is the capacity to interpret and critically assess news and related media messages in light of how they are made and presented.

More about this term

It includes asking who produced a message, what supports it, and whether it presents fact, opinion, or persuasion.

Media literacy also helps people participate in public communication as informed audiences or contributors.

CC0 1.0View versioned object

Media quality

quality of journalistic news coverage

For news coverage, media quality is how well the coverage serves relevant informational and public purposes under stated journalistic criteria.

More about this term

Those criteria can concern accuracy, context, relevance, and the range of perspectives represented.

Audience appeal alone does not establish that coverage meets its informational or public purpose.

CC0 1.0View versioned object

Merit

evaluative goodness in relevant respects

Merit is how good something is in respects relevant to what it is or does.

More about this term

A claim of merit should identify the respects being judged and why they matter for that kind of object.

An object can have merit without thereby being worthwhile for every person or decision.

CC0 1.0View versioned object

Message quality

supportive interpersonal communication

In supportive communication, message quality is how well a message's content and expression help its intended recipient in a particular situation.

More about this term

A polite or detailed message can still be ineffective if its advice is infeasible or does not fit the recipient's needs.

CC0 1.0View versioned object

Metadata quality

information-resource description

Metadata quality is how well descriptive records support finding, understanding, using, and managing the resources they describe.

More about this term

Clear descriptions and consistent subject terms can improve discovery; missing or ambiguous metadata can obstruct it.

CC0 1.0View versioned object

Method

measurement and quality-management process methods

In measurement and process work, a method is an organized approach to carrying out operations to obtain an intended result.

More about this term

The subject, required resolution, environmental conditions, and timing can affect which measurement method is suitable.

A procedure specifies steps for applying a method in a particular setting.

CC0 1.0View versioned object

Methodological quality

fitness of research methods for warranted conclusions

A study's methodological quality is how well its design, conduct, and analysis support the conclusions it is used to draw.

More about this term

Appraisal uses criteria suited to the question and design; in a trial these may include allocation, blinding, and handling of withdrawals.

Clear reporting helps others judge the methods, but it does not by itself remove bias introduced by a weak design.

CC0 1.0View versioned object

Metric

quantitative evaluation performance metric

In quantitative evaluation, a metric specifies what numerical value to obtain and how to obtain it for an aspect of performance.

More about this term

The value produced on a particular dataset is its result.

A separate objective or decision rule says how to interpret that result.

An indicator in evaluation may be paired with a specified measure or metric.

In some quality-management uses, metric has a narrower financial or economic scope; the intended field should therefore be stated.

CC0 1.0View versioned object

Metrological comparability

measurement results

Metrological comparability is the property that allows measurement results for quantities of the same kind to be compared when each result is traceable to a common reference.

More about this term

A shared reference enables comparison; it does not establish agreement. Comparable results can have substantially different measured values and uncertainties.

CC0 1.0View versioned object

Metrological traceability

property of a measurement result related to a reference

Metrological traceability is the property of a measurement result that lets it be related to a reference through a documented, unbroken chain of calibrations, each contributing to measurement uncertainty.

More about this term

The chain identifies how the result connects to the reference and where uncertainty enters. It belongs to a particular result and measurement process, rather than merely to an instrument label.

Traceability makes the basis for comparison inspectable. It does not by itself prove that the result is accurate enough for a particular decision; that requires an uncertainty and fitness-for-use judgment.

CC0 1.0View versioned object

Minimal detectable change

repeated score interpretation

Minimal detectable change is the smallest difference between repeated scores that exceeds expected measurement error at a specified confidence level.

More about this term

It addresses whether a change is distinguishable from measurement noise, not whether the change matters clinically or practically.

CC0 1.0View versioned object

Misinformation

false or misleading information in news and public communication

Misinformation is false or misleading information presented or circulated as if it were sound, whether or not the person sharing it intends to deceive.

More about this term

Intentional deception is one route; mistaken or uncritical sharing can also spread it.

Assess the claim against evidence and context rather than relying on a label such as ‘fake news’.

CC0 1.0View versioned object

Model

selective conceptual representation in research and design

In research and design, a model is a selective representation of a system or problem that identifies relevant concepts and their relationships.

More about this term

A model can help explain a situation or explore a proposed solution, but its conclusions depend on what it represents and assumes.

It is a representation of the subject, not the subject itself.

CC0 1.0View versioned object

Model drift

material change in deployed predictive-model behavior or performance

In deployed machine learning, model drift is a material change over time in a model's output behavior or predictive performance relative to a stated baseline.

More about this term

A shift in input data may contribute to drift, but a changed input distribution alone is data drift and does not prove that the model's behavior has changed.

Monitor outputs and outcome-based measures when available, then investigate a detected change before deciding what response is needed.

CC0 1.0View versioned object

Model performance

predictive results on a specified task and evaluation data

In predictive machine learning, model performance is how well a model carries out a specified prediction task under stated data and evaluation conditions.

More about this term

It is assessed with measures suited to the task, such as classification or prediction-error measures, on data reserved for evaluation.

A performance claim must name the task, measure, and testing conditions; runtime speed is a different possible sense of model performance.

CC0 1.0View versioned object

Model quality

predictive machine-learning model in intended use

For a predictive machine-learning model, model quality is how well it meets the requirements of its intended task and use under stated data and operating conditions.

More about this term

Relevant evidence may include prediction performance, reliability, interpretability, and constraints specific to that use.

A strong test score does not establish continuing quality after the data or operating conditions change.

CC0 1.0View versioned object

Model validation

evidence that a predictive model is fit for stated use

In predictive machine learning, model validation is the evaluation of whether a trained model is sufficiently fit for a specified task and use.

More about this term

Methods can include held-out testing or cross-validation to examine performance beyond the data used to fit model parameters.

A favorable score supports a claim only for the population and conditions the validation design can represent; it does not guarantee future performance.

CC0 1.0View versioned object

Modifiability

software change in response to requirements

In software engineering, modifiability is how readily a system can be changed to meet new or revised requirements.

More about this term

A modifiable design helps people make such changes without disproportionate effort or unintended effects elsewhere.

It is related to maintainability, but it does not promise that every change will be simple.

CC0 1.0View versioned object

Moment of truth

customer encounter in service delivery

In service management, a moment of truth is an encounter at which a customer experiences a provider's service and forms an impression of it.

More about this term

It can arise in booking, delivery, or recovery from a problem, rather than only at the main point of service.

Such encounters can influence satisfaction and future choice, though one contact need not determine the whole relationship.

CC0 1.0View versioned object

Monitoring

systematic checking of a process or condition over time in quality management

Monitoring is systematic checking of a process or condition over time to learn its status or detect change.

More about this term

The subject and checking schedule should be clear enough to interpret what is observed.

Monitoring supplies observations; changing the process in response is a separate action.

CC0 1.0View versioned object

Multi-criteria decision analysis (MCDA)

structured comparison using multiple relevant criteria

Multi-criteria decision analysis (MCDA) is a family of methods for comparing options against several relevant criteria when no single measure settles the choice.

More about this term

An analysis states the options, criteria, evidence about each option, and how tradeoffs are handled. Some methods use weights and an aggregate score; others compare options without reducing them to one number.

The result depends on these modeling choices. Checking how the recommendation changes under plausible assumptions helps show how robust it is.

CC0 1.0View versioned object

Multivariate quality control

statistical monitoring of related characteristics

Multivariate quality control monitors several quality characteristics together to detect changes in their joint pattern.

More about this term

It accounts for relationships among measurements that separate charts can miss or misinterpret. The characteristics and reference process state must be specified before a signal can be judged.

CC0 1.0View versioned object
N9 terms

Near miss

broad patient-safety error without harm; incident-classification boundary varies

In a broad patient-safety use, a near miss is an error that could have harmed a patient but did not, through interception or chance.

More about this term

Some incident-classification systems reserve near miss for an incident that never reaches the patient and call one that reaches the patient without harm a no-harm incident.

Reviewing near misses can reveal hazards before they cause injury.

CC0 1.0View versioned object

Need

current-to-required results gap in needs assessment

In needs assessment, a need is a gap between current results and results judged necessary.

More about this term

Identify whose results are at issue, the required level, and evidence of the current level.

A proposed resource, service, or intervention may address the gap, but it is not itself the need in this sense.

CC0 1.0View versioned object

Net promoter score

recommendation-likelihood survey index

Net promoter score (NPS) is the percentage of survey respondents rating their likelihood to recommend at 9 or 10, minus the percentage rating it from 0 through 6, on a 0-to-10 scale.

More about this term

Ratings of 7 or 8 count in the respondent total but in neither percentage being subtracted.

The score summarizes stated willingness to recommend; it does not alone show actual recommendations or overall product or service quality.

CC0 1.0View versioned object

News quality

news outlet coverage

News quality is how well an outlet's coverage helps an audience understand matters of public concern under relevant journalistic standards.

More about this term

It concerns the choice and range of topics as well as the context, verification, and diversity within reports; one accurate story cannot establish the quality of an outlet's overall coverage.

CC0 1.0View versioned object

Noise factor

nonroutine-controlled variation considered in robust design

In robust design, a noise factor is an input or operating condition whose variation affects a product or process response but is not routinely held at one fixed value.

More about this term

Examples include ambient conditions, material differences, and wear during use. Designers may vary such factors deliberately in experiments to find settings that keep performance stable.

Noise here means an influence that can disturb performance, not necessarily sound or random measurement error.

CC0 1.0View versioned object

Noncompensation

limit on trade-offs among evaluative criteria

In a multicriteria judgment, noncompensation means that strength on some criteria cannot fully offset a specified shortfall on another.

More about this term

A veto threshold is one way to apply such a rule: crossing it can prevent an otherwise favorable overall classification.

The protected criterion, boundary, and authority for the rule must be stated; the label alone does not determine them.

CC0 1.0View versioned object

Nonconformance

unmet applicable requirement in quality management

A nonconformance is a failure to meet an applicable requirement.

More about this term

The requirement may concern a product, process, record, or activity, and it must be identified to explain the judgment.

Documenting a nonconformance records the finding; the condition can exist before it is detected or recorded.

CC0 1.0View versioned object

Nonconformity

failure to fulfill an applicable requirement

A nonconformity is a failure to fulfill an applicable requirement.

More about this term

A useful finding identifies the object, the requirement, and the evidence of the departure. It should not treat a preference or an unstated expectation as a violated requirement without establishing its status.

A nonconformity may call for correction of the current case, investigation of a cause, or both. It is a defect in the narrower technical sense when the unmet requirement relates to an intended or specified use.

CC0 1.0View versioned object

Norm-referenced interpretation

interpretation of assessment scores

A norm-referenced interpretation explains a person's score by comparing it with scores from a defined reference group.

More about this term

It shows relative standing, not whether an independent performance standard was met. The reference group must be suitable for the person and intended use.

CC0 1.0View versioned object
O19 terms

Objective evidence

checkable data bearing on existence or truth in quality management

In quality management, objective evidence is checkable information that supports whether a specified condition exists or a claim is true.

More about this term

It may come from observations, measurements, tests, or records, provided they bear on the matter being checked.

Calling evidence objective does not make its interpretation automatic; the claim and the way the information was obtained still matter.

CC0 1.0View versioned object

Objectivity

journalistic reporting and inquiry

In journalism, objectivity is a disciplined effort to make reporting answerable to evidence and critical scrutiny rather than a reporter's unchecked preferences.

More about this term

It involves checking claims, considering counterevidence and relevant perspectives, and correcting mistakes.

It does not require reporters to have no standpoint or guarantee that every account is complete.

CC0 1.0View versioned object

Observability

software-service operations
