For a software service, observability is how well its internal state and behavior can be inferred from information it emits while running.

More about this term

Related metrics, logs, and traces can help locate causes across components rather than merely flag a symptom.

More telemetry alone does not ensure observability; it must answer the questions that matter for that service.

CC0 1.0View versioned object

Observation

recorded behavior in behavioral research

In behavioral research, an observation is a record of behavior made while watching it under stated conditions.

More about this term

Specify who or what was watched, when, and how the behavior was recorded or coded.

The record can support an inference about a broader condition, but the condition itself may not be directly observable.

CC0 1.0View versioned object

Observed value

value obtained for a characteristic by test or measurement

In measurement and testing, an observed value is the value obtained for a specified characteristic in a particular test or measurement.

More about this term

Repeated measurements of the same item can yield different observed values. The spread of such results helps assess precision.

One observed value alone does not establish the exact true value of the characteristic.

CC0 1.0View versioned object

Open science

research openness and wider participation

Open science is a set of practices that makes scientific knowledge, tools, and processes more accessible and reusable, while opening research to wider participation within justified limits.

More about this term

These practices can include sharing publications, data, software, methods, and protocols with enough context to support scrutiny and reuse.

Open access can support scrutiny, while privacy, security, confidentiality, and rights can justify limits on what is shared.

CC0 1.0View versioned object

Operating characteristic curve

acceptance probability across lot quality levels for a sampling plan

In acceptance sampling, an operating characteristic curve shows the probability that a specified sampling plan will accept a lot at each assumed level of lot quality.

More about this term

For an attribute plan, the horizontal axis commonly gives the fraction or percentage nonconforming and the vertical axis gives probability of acceptance.

The curve shows how the plan balances the risks of rejecting satisfactory lots and accepting poor ones; it is a property of the plan, not a quality score for a particular lot.

CC0 1.0View versioned object

Opportunity

favorable uncertainty in project-risk management

In project-risk management, an opportunity is an uncertain event or condition that, if it occurs, could help achieve an objective.

More about this term

It is the favorable counterpart to a threat: its possible effect on objectives makes it relevant to risk work.

A possible benefit calls for assessment and a response, not automatic pursuit.

CC0 1.0View versioned object

Opportunity cost

value sacrificed when resources are used one way rather than another

Opportunity cost is the value of the best available alternative forgone when a resource is used for one purpose rather than another.

More about this term

Using staff time, space, or money for one option can give up benefits that the same resources could have produced elsewhere.

The cost can exist without a cash payment, and its value may be difficult to express precisely in money.

CC0 1.0View versioned object

Opportunity enhancement

project response to favorable uncertainty

In project risk management, opportunity enhancement is a planned response that seeks to improve the potential upside of an uncertain favorable event.

More about this term

The action makes an opportunity more attractive, but the benefit remains uncertain. Exploitation is a stronger response aimed at securing it.

A team should monitor whether the response produced the intended improvement and whether it created new risks.

CC0 1.0View versioned object

Opportunity exploitation

project risk management

In project risk management, opportunity exploitation is a planned response that seeks to secure the benefit of a favorable uncertainty.

More about this term

It goes beyond identifying an opportunity. Enhancing an opportunity instead aims to increase its likelihood or potential benefit.

CC0 1.0View versioned object

Opportunity sharing

project response to favorable uncertainty

Opportunity sharing is a response to a favorable project uncertainty in which another party joins in pursuing the potential benefit.

More about this term

A partner may contribute complementary capabilities or knowledge while taking part of the potential return. Sharing can improve the chance of a favorable outcome without guaranteeing it.

CC0 1.0View versioned object

Organizational leadership

directing and enabling coordinated organizational action

Organizational leadership is the activity of setting direction and enabling people and structures to work toward an organization's aims.

More about this term

It connects a mission and strategy to decisions about responsibilities, authority, coordination, and support.

Leadership can be exercised by people without a formal management title; a title alone does not establish that someone is leading effectively.

CC0 1.0View versioned object

Organizational learning

collective sharing, testing, and retention of work knowledge

Organizational learning is the development and retention of shared knowledge about an organization's work through experience, inquiry, and feedback.

More about this term

People interpret what happened, share what they learned, and test possible changes to their practices.

A lesson held only in one person's memory may be useful to that person, but the organization has limited means to retain or use it across future work.

CC0 1.0View versioned object

Originality

novelty or difference in an artwork

In art, originality is the extent to which a work differs in significant ways from earlier work or familiar conventions.

More about this term

It may concern the work's features or how they are combined; difference alone does not establish artistic merit.

Original is also used as praise, so an appraisal should say whether it claims novelty, value, or both.

CC0 1.0View versioned object

Outcome

resulting condition or change examined in evaluation

An outcome is a resulting condition or change of interest after an activity, intervention, or event.

More about this term

Specify whose outcome it is, what changed or persisted, and the period being examined.

Observing an outcome after a program does not by itself prove that the program caused it.

CC0 1.0View versioned object

Outcome measure

result measure in health-care quality assessment

In health-care quality assessment, an outcome measure tracks a result of care, such as mortality or readmission rates, for a defined group and period.

More about this term

It describes a result rather than a step in the care process intended to influence that result.

A change in the measure alone does not establish which action caused it.

CC0 1.0View versioned object

Output

tangible or intangible project deliverable

In project work, an output is a tangible or intangible item delivered by an activity.

More about this term

An output can enable a later change, but the delivered item is distinct from that change and any benefit that follows.

Name what was delivered and to whom; delivery alone does not show that it was adopted or useful.

CC0 1.0View versioned object

Oversight

organizational governance of delegated work

In organizational governance, oversight is the review and direction of delegated work by a person or body responsible for its accountability.

More about this term

It draws on performance information to check whether activities remain aligned with objectives and to inform decisions when they do not.

Monitoring supplies information; oversight also involves a defined source of authority and responsibility for decisions.

CC0 1.0View versioned object
P70 terms

Pareto chart

ordered categorical display for prioritization

A Pareto chart displays categories as bars ordered from the largest to the smallest contribution under a stated measure.

More about this term

The measure may be a count or relative frequency, and an added line may show how contributions accumulate.

The chart helps prioritize what to examine; it does not establish a universal 80/20 split or identify causes.

CC0 1.0View versioned object

Participation

affected people in environmental-policy development

During environmental policymaking, participation is the informed involvement of people affected by a proposed policy in developing that policy.

More about this term

Governments can convene interested parties before deciding so they can help formulate policy.

Telling people what was decided afterward does not give them a role in making that choice.

CC0 1.0View versioned object

Patient safety

preventing harm arising from health care

Patient safety concerns protecting patients from harm caused by the health care they receive.

More about this term

It is a dimension of care quality that calls for attention to errors, hazardous conditions, and injuries arising during care.

A patient who was not harmed in one encounter may still have been exposed to a risk that the care system should examine.

CC0 1.0View versioned object

Patient-centeredness

individualized health-care relationship and decisions

In health care, patient-centeredness is the extent to which care responds to a patient's individual circumstances, experience, needs, and preferences.

More about this term

It includes understanding how the person experiences illness, sharing relevant information, and involving the person in decisions about care.

Its components can vary by setting, so a single behavior does not by itself establish that care is patient-centered.

CC0 1.0View versioned object

Patient-reported experience measure

structured patient account of care delivery

A patient-reported experience measure (PREM) is a structured instrument for recording a patient's account of what happened during health care delivery.

More about this term

It can ask about communication, access, coordination, or respect, and concerns care experience rather than the patient's health outcome.

Responses can reveal problems in a service or care pathway, but their meaning depends on the setting and people surveyed.

CC0 1.0View versioned object

Patient-reported outcome measure

structured patient report of health outcome

A patient-reported outcome measure (PROM) is a structured instrument for recording a patient's own report of health or functioning, such as symptoms or ability to carry out daily activities.

More about this term

It concerns an outcome experienced by the patient, without substituting a clinician's assessment for the patient's response.

Some PROMs apply across conditions; others concern a particular disease, and repeated use can show change over time.

CC0 1.0View versioned object

PDCA cycle

Plan–Do–Check–Act improvement loop

The PDCA cycle is a repeatable improvement method: plan a change, do it, check the results against the aim, and act on what was learned.

More about this term

Planning states the problem, proposed change, and expected result. Doing puts the plan into practice; checking examines what occurred; acting adjusts the plan or the routine before the next cycle.

The four labels do not establish improvement by themselves. The comparison between expected and observed results is what makes the cycle useful for learning.

CC0 1.0View versioned object

PDSA cycle

quality improvement

A PDSA cycle is a repeated method for testing and refining a change: plan it, do it, study what happened, and act on what was learned.

More about this term

A small test can inform the next cycle before wider adoption; merely completing the four labels does not establish improvement.

CC0 1.0View versioned object

Peer review

academic evaluation by knowledgeable peers

In academic work, peer review is an appraisal of a submission or proposal by people with relevant knowledge in its field.

More about this term

It is used, for example, in journal publication and research-grant decisions, where reviewers assess the work against pertinent criteria.

Reviewers may differ in which criteria they emphasize and how they combine them; review itself is not a guarantee that the work is sound.

CC0 1.0View versioned object

Perceived quality

person's appraisal of product or service quality

Perceived quality is a person's appraisal of how good a product or service seems for a relevant purpose.

More about this term

The appraisal depends on the person's experience and judgment about the product or service and may differ across users or uses.

It is an assessment made by someone, not a direct measurement of every characteristic or proof of actual performance.

CC0 1.0View versioned object

Perceived value

customer appraisal of service benefit relative to effort

For a service customer, perceived value is an appraisal of the benefits received relative to the effort and costs of obtaining and using the service.

More about this term

Price is one cost; time, search, and the risk of failure can matter too.

Two customers may judge the same service differently because their needs and circumstances differ.

CC0 1.0View versioned object

Perceptual quality

listener's appraisal of synthesized speech

For synthesized speech, perceptual quality is a listener's appraisal of how well the speech they hear matches relevant expectations or requirements.

More about this term

Listeners can attend to features such as naturalness and intelligibility as well as overall sound.

An instrumental score can help assess the signal, but it does not by itself express every aspect of the listening experience.

CC0 1.0View versioned object

Performance

actual functioning or results under specified conditions

Performance is what a person, process, product, or system actually does or achieves under stated conditions.

More about this term

Describe the function or result, the conditions, and the time period when comparing performance.

Capability concerns what can be done; judging whether actual performance is good requires a relevant standard.

CC0 1.0View versioned object

Performance efficiency

software performance relative to resources under stated conditions

In software quality, performance efficiency concerns how a system's speed, throughput, capacity, and resource use meet requirements under stated conditions.

More about this term

A fast response alone does not establish efficiency if it requires excessive resources or fails at the needed load.

Assessment should state the workload, resources, and relevant performance requirements.

CC0 1.0View versioned object

Performance level

degree of demonstrated performance in a rubric

In a rubric, a performance level is a named or numbered category describing a degree of demonstrated performance on a criterion.

More about this term

Descriptions identify features associated with each level; example responses can help raters apply the categories consistently.

Assigning a score or rating places a particular response at a level. The level itself is the category, not the evidence that a particular person attained it.

CC0 1.0View versioned object

Pharmaceutical quality system

ICH Q10 model for pharmaceutical quality management

A pharmaceutical quality system (PQS) is an organized system for directing and controlling a pharmaceutical organization with respect to quality.

More about this term

The ICH Q10 model applies across product development, manufacturing, and other lifecycle stages, alongside applicable good manufacturing practice requirements.

It brings together responsibilities and processes for monitoring performance, managing change, corrective and preventive action, and management review.

CC0 1.0View versioned object

Poka-yoke

production design or device preventing a predictable mistake from producing a defect

In production, poka-yoke is a design feature or device that prevents an inadvertent mistake from producing a defect.

More about this term

It changes the task or equipment so a particular error is blocked or made harder to carry forward.

It addresses a specified error path; it does not guarantee that every kind of defect is prevented.

CC0 1.0View versioned object

Policy

standing organizational guide to decisions and action

In organizational governance, a policy is a standing guide to decisions and action in a defined area.

More about this term

It sets direction that can be applied across cases, such as how an organization will address quality or safety concerns.

A policy may be written or tacit; its authority and practical effect depend on who adopts it and how it is used.

CC0 1.0View versioned object

Policy quality

public policy design, implementation and effects

Policy quality is how well a public policy's aims, design, implementation, and effects meet the standards relevant to the problem it addresses.

More about this term

A policy can be formally adopted yet work poorly in practice. The judgment should consider conflicting aims and who benefits or bears costs, not just whether officials carried out the plan.

CC0 1.0View versioned object

Pollution

environmental contamination harmful to living communities

In environmental assessment, pollution is the presence or buildup of material in a place at a level that can harm organisms or ecosystems.

More about this term

A detectable contaminant is not automatically a pollutant; concentration, exposure, and potential effects matter.

Assessment may involve air, water, soil, and the organisms that take up contaminants.

CC0 1.0View versioned object

Poor quality

quality judgment about an object or work

Poor quality is an unfavorable assessment that an object or work falls short in one or more characteristics relevant to its requirements or intended use.

More about this term

The judgment should name the shortfall and its basis. A defect in one respect does not establish that every characteristic is poor.

CC0 1.0View versioned object

Population

complete set of units to which a statistical question refers

In statistics, a population is the complete set of units specified by the question being studied.

More about this term

The units may be people, products, events, or measurements, and the boundaries of the set must be stated.

A sample is a subset used to learn about that population; changing the scope of the question can change which set counts as the population.

CC0 1.0View versioned object

Portability

transfer of software between operational environments

In software quality, portability is how effectively and efficiently a product or component can be moved to another operating environment.

More about this term

The environments may differ in hardware, software, or conditions of use; adaptation and installation may be part of the move.

Portability concerns moving the product or component, not merely sending data between systems.

CC0 1.0View versioned object

Potency

biological activity of a biological medicine

For a biological medicine, potency is its capacity to produce a specified biological activity, assessed by an appropriate test.

More about this term

Potency and the quantity of active material are assessed separately; amount alone need not establish the required activity.

A potency result needs the assay and acceptance criteria to be interpreted for a particular product.

CC0 1.0View versioned object

Pp

overall process spread against two-sided specifications

Pp is a process performance index that compares the width between two specification limits with the overall spread of observed process output.

More about this term

It describes whether the spread could fit between the limits if centered, but does not account for where the process average lies.

Interpret it with checks on process stability and the output distribution.

CC0 1.0View versioned object

Ppk

overall process performance relative to nearer specification limit

Ppk is a process performance index relating the process average's distance from the nearer specification limit to the overall variation in observed output.

More about this term

Unlike Pp, it reflects how far the process is off center as well as its spread.

Its interpretation still depends on the process's stability, output distribution, and specified limits.

CC0 1.0View versioned object

Practical significance

real-world importance of a statistical difference for a decision

Practical significance is the importance of an observed difference for a real decision in its setting.

More about this term

It depends on the size and consequences of the difference, not only on whether a statistical test rejects a null hypothesis.

With a large sample, a very small difference can be statistically significant while having little practical importance.

CC0 1.0View versioned object

Precision

agreement among repeated measurement results

In measurement, precision is the closeness of agreement among results from repeated measurements under specified conditions.

More about this term

More precise measurements vary less from one another when the relevant conditions are held comparable.

Precision describes their agreement, not by itself how close they are to the true or reference value.

CC0 1.0View versioned object

Preference

comparative favoring in evaluative choice

A preference is a person's comparative inclination toward one option or state rather than another.

More about this term

It can change with the alternatives, information, purpose, and setting.

A preference identifies what is favored; it does not by itself show that the favored option meets a requirement.

CC0 1.0View versioned object

Prevention cost

quality-related spending intended to avert defects or nonconformity

A prevention cost is a cost incurred for an activity designed to keep defects or other quality failures from occurring.

More about this term

Examples include quality planning, training, and changes that reduce opportunities for error. The activity aims to prevent a problem before it arises.

In cost-of-quality accounting, prevention is distinct from appraisal, which checks outputs or processes, and from costs caused by failures. Classify a mixed activity by a stated accounting rule and avoid counting it twice.

CC0 1.0View versioned object

Preventive action

addressing causes of a potential nonconformity

Preventive action addresses a cause of a potential nonconformity or other unwanted situation before it occurs.

More about this term

It responds to an identified risk, whereas corrective action responds to a detected problem and seeks to prevent recurrence. The proposed action should match the plausible cause and the consequence at stake.

Some management systems incorporate prevention into risk-based planning rather than a separately named preventive-action step. The label does not, by itself, show that a risk was identified or reduced.

CC0 1.0View versioned object

Price-quality relationship

pricing and customer assessment of offerings

The price-quality relationship is the connection between an offering's price and its actual or perceived quality in a specified market.

More about this term

Buyers may treat a higher price as a quality signal, and valued features may support a premium. Price alone does not establish better performance.

CC0 1.0View versioned object

Prioritization

ordering competing needs or actions for attention

Prioritization is deciding which competing needs, options, or actions deserve attention first under stated aims and constraints.

More about this term

A priority can reflect importance, expected benefit, urgency, feasibility, or a combination whose basis should be made clear. A numerical weight is one possible aid, not the meaning of priority itself.

In a House of Quality, teams may rank customer needs and proposed technical responses. The ranking guides planning; it does not prove that the chosen response will work.

CC0 1.0View versioned object

Privacy

personal information in digital systems

In digital information systems, privacy concerns appropriate protection against unwanted collection, use, disclosure, or inference of information about people.

More about this term

What is appropriate depends on the information, its purpose, the people affected, and the setting.

Security safeguards can help, but even securely held data may be used in ways that violate reasonable privacy expectations.

CC0 1.0View versioned object

Probability

numerical likelihood assigned to a defined event

Probability is a number from 0 to 1 assigned to a defined event under a probability model, representing how likely the event is within that model.

More about this term

To interpret it, identify the event, conditions, and assumptions behind the number.

It describes an event under the model; an observed outcome is separate evidence about whether that model fits.

CC0 1.0View versioned object

Procedural fairness

fairness in making a public decision

In public decision-making, procedural fairness is fairness in how a decision is reached, including a meaningful opportunity for affected people to be heard and have their views considered.

More about this term

It concerns the decision process; whether the outcome favors a particular person is a separate question.

Timely decisions and clear procedures can matter when delay or uncertainty would undermine that opportunity.

CC0 1.0View versioned object

Procedure

specified way of carrying out an activity

A procedure sets out how a particular activity is to be carried out.

More about this term

It may specify a sequence of steps, responsibilities, conditions, and records needed to repeat the activity.

A procedure can put a method into practice, but a method is the underlying approach and a procedure gives instructions for its use.

CC0 1.0View versioned object

Process

organized work in quality management

In organizational work, a process is a connected set of activities carried out to produce a result.

More about this term

Its inputs, resources, activities, and outputs can be described so that the work can be managed and improved.

The inputs need not be physically transformed: a design process can use information to produce a design.

CC0 1.0View versioned object

Process analytical technology

pharmaceutical manufacturing measurement and control

Process analytical technology (PAT) is an approach to designing, monitoring, and controlling pharmaceutical manufacturing through timely measurement of material and process attributes relevant to product quality.

More about this term

Measurements taken during processing can help reveal variation early enough to guide control of the process.

PAT is broader than a single sensor or test: it joins measurement with process understanding and control.

CC0 1.0View versioned object

Process approach

quality management of interrelated work toward intended results

In quality management, the process approach manages work by identifying processes, their intended results, and how they interact to produce those results.

More about this term

It follows activities, resources, responsibilities, inputs, and outputs across departmental boundaries, then checks whether the resulting work meets its purpose.

A process map can describe the work; using the approach also requires managing and improving how the processes operate together.

CC0 1.0View versioned object

Process capability

stable-process fit to specification limits

Process capability concerns how well a stable process can produce outputs within specified limits, given its typical variation and location.

More about this term

Capability analysis compares the process distribution with the applicable specification limits. It should first establish that the process is sufficiently stable for the comparison to be meaningful.

Indices such as Cp and Cpk summarize different aspects of that comparison under stated assumptions. A favorable index is an estimate, not a guarantee that every future output will conform.

CC0 1.0View versioned object

Process capability analysis

statistical appraisal of process output relative to specifications

Process capability analysis examines the distribution of a process's output against specified limits to estimate how consistently the process can produce acceptable results.

More about this term

It uses information about process location and variation under stated conditions, commonly after checking whether the process is stable.

A capability index can summarize that comparison, but its value has meaning only with the chosen limits, data, and assumptions.

CC0 1.0View versioned object

Process capability index

statistical index comparing process behavior with specification limits

A process capability index is a numerical summary of how a process's output distribution relates to specified limits for one characteristic.

More about this term

For example, Cp compares specification width with process spread, while Cpk also reflects how the process is centered within those limits.

Interpretation depends on a stable process, a suitable distributional model, and the particular index used.

CC0 1.0View versioned object

Process control

keeping a process within specified operational boundaries

Process control is the monitoring and adjustment of a process to keep its behavior and outputs within intended boundaries.

More about this term

It requires stated process requirements, observations of performance, and responses when the process moves away from those requirements.

It addresses how the process operates over time, rather than relying only on inspection of a finished output.

CC0 1.0View versioned object

Process improvement

deliberate beneficial change to recurring work

Process improvement is a deliberate change to how recurring work is carried out to achieve better results against stated aims.

More about this term

It can change methods, handoffs, measurement, capacity, or skills after the present process and its results are examined.

Fixing one defective output without changing the process does not necessarily improve future output.

CC0 1.0View versioned object

Process improvement team

quality management

A process improvement team is a work group, sometimes spanning functions, formed to improve a specified existing process.

More about this term

Its responsibility and duration are tied to the improvements and goals for which it was formed.

CC0 1.0View versioned object

Process measure

measure for a specified process objective

A process measure is a specified way to assess whether a process is operating or producing results in line with its objective.

More about this term

It can track an activity, an operating condition, or an output for which the process is responsible.

Its interpretation requires a defined process, objective, and criterion; a desirable organization-wide result may be too remote to guide that process.

CC0 1.0View versioned object

Process monitoring

repeated observation of a quality-management process

Process monitoring is the repeated observation or measurement of selected process conditions and results to see how a process is behaving over time.

More about this term

Useful indicators relate to the process’s objectives and have a stated collection method and frequency. Trends or departures can prompt investigation and action.

Monitoring supplies evidence for decisions; it does not by itself control the process or prove that every output conforms.

CC0 1.0View versioned object

Process quality

quality of an operational process

Process quality is how well a process is designed and carried out to meet requirements for the work it performs.

More about this term

A judgment should identify the process, its purpose, and the relevant conditions, controls, and performance criteria. Monitoring variation and feedback can show whether it remains fit for that purpose.

Process quality and output quality are related but distinct. One acceptable output does not establish that the process is consistently controlled, and a controlled process still requires checks on what it produces.

CC0 1.0View versioned object

Process stability

time-series behavior under a relatively unchanged process

A process is stable when its pattern of variation remains sufficiently consistent over time to support prediction under stated conditions.

More about this term

Control charts can help distinguish variation from an ongoing system of common causes from signals of special causes that call for investigation. The conclusion depends on the data, time period, and chart assumptions.

Stability concerns predictability, not whether the process meets requirements. A consistently underperforming process can be stable but incapable of producing acceptable results.

CC0 1.0View versioned object

Process step

bounded activity within a mapped process

A process step is a bounded activity in a process that moves work toward an output.

More about this term

A map names the step and its place between the process’s start and end points; the useful level of detail depends on the question being asked.

Step-level yield can show where defects or rework arise, while overall yield reflects the linked process.

CC0 1.0View versioned object

Process validation

evidence that a specified process can repeatedly produce required output

Process validation is the documented evaluation of whether a specified process can consistently produce output meeting its predetermined requirements.

More about this term

It examines the process, its operating conditions, and evidence from its results. In regulated manufacturing, the evidence is developed and maintained across the process life cycle.

Testing a finished item alone cannot establish that the process will continue to perform as intended; the process and its controls also need examination.

CC0 1.0View versioned object

Product quality

quality of a product for intended use

Product quality is how well a product’s relevant characteristics fulfill requirements for its intended use.

More about this term

The requirements and characteristics depend on the product and setting: a medicine and a software system call for different evidence. State the users, conditions of use, and characteristics being judged.

Evidence about how a product was made can support the judgment, but it does not replace examination of the product and its performance against applicable requirements.

CC0 1.0View versioned object

Product specification

documented requirements for deciding product conformity

A product specification is a document stating the requirements a product must meet for a defined use or decision.

More about this term

It may identify characteristics, limits, and test or acceptance conditions used to judge conformity.

A specification says what is required; test results and other evidence show whether a particular product meets it.

CC0 1.0View versioned object

Program review

higher-education academic programs

In higher education, program review is a structured appraisal of an academic program using evidence about its curriculum and student learning to guide improvement.

More about this term

A self-study may bring assessment findings, curriculum maps, and external feedback together; evaluating one course alone does not review the whole program.

CC0 1.0View versioned object

Project quality

fulfillment of requirements for project work and outputs

Project quality is how well a project's work and resulting deliverables fulfill the requirements set for them.

More about this term

A judgment should consider both how the project is carried out and whether its outputs meet the needs they were meant to serve.

Finishing on time or within budget does not, by itself, show that a deliverable meets its quality requirements.

CC0 1.0View versioned object

Property

descriptive feature of an assessed object

A property is a feature that an object has or can be described as having.

More about this term

A property's observed value can vary between objects or over time; identifying the property does not yet judge whether its value is good.

In this sense, property means a characteristic, not legal ownership.

CC0 1.0View versioned object

Proportionality

justification of a restriction on a human right

In human-rights review, proportionality concerns whether a restriction on a right is justified by a legitimate aim in light of the burden it imposes.

More about this term

The reviewer asks whether the interference is necessary and whether the competing rights and interests have been fairly balanced.

The precise test depends on the right and legal system; proportionality is not simply a numerical ratio.

CC0 1.0View versioned object

Protein quality

nutrition and food-protein assessment

In nutrition, protein quality is how well a food protein supplies usable essential amino acids for the body's needs.

More about this term

Assessment considers amino-acid composition and digestibility as well as the amount eaten. Proteins in a mixed diet can complement one another, so a single food's score need not describe the diet as a whole.

CC0 1.0View versioned object

Protocol

preapproved plan for a specified test

In planned testing, a protocol is an approved document that specifies what will be tested, how it will be done, what evidence will be recorded, and how results will be judged.

More about this term

Its objectives, prerequisites, steps, and acceptance criteria should be set before testing begins.

Following the protocol documents the procedure; it does not by itself show that the tested item passed.

CC0 1.0View versioned object

Provenance

traceable origin and history of an item

Provenance is the traceable account of an item’s origin and history, including the people or systems and activities that created, changed, or transferred it.

More about this term

For evidence, a provenance record can show which version was examined, where it came from, and how it passed through later hands or processes.

Good provenance makes an item easier to authenticate and interpret. It does not, on its own, establish that every claim made from the item is true.

CC0 1.0View versioned object

Proxy

observable stand-in for a less accessible evaluative construct

In evaluation and measurement, a proxy is an observable measure used as a stand-in for a condition or construct that cannot be observed directly or readily.

More about this term

Its usefulness depends on how well the measure tracks the intended target in the population and setting where it is used.

A change in the proxy need not equal the same change in the target; other influences and measurement error may affect the observed value.

CC0 1.0View versioned object

Public

people concerned by a public decision

In public decision making, the public is the people and communities who may be affected by a decision or have a legitimate interest in it.

More about this term

The relevant public depends on the decision and may include people who are absent from formal consultation.

The word does not mean that everyone shares one viewpoint, and this sense differs from calling a record publicly accessible.

CC0 1.0View versioned object

Public administration quality

public-sector administration

Public administration quality is how well administrative institutions and processes carry out public responsibilities under relevant standards of effectiveness, accountability, and responsiveness.

More about this term

Efficient service delivery matters, but speed or low cost alone does not establish good administration if accountability and responsiveness are weak.

CC0 1.0View versioned object

Public interest

journalistic justification involving shared civic concerns

In journalism, the public interest is the benefit to a community from information that helps people understand and judge matters affecting their shared life.

More about this term

It can justify investigating or publishing a matter, but the claim should identify whose interests are served and how.

Audience curiosity or likely popularity alone does not establish that a story serves the public interest.

CC0 1.0View versioned object

Public service quality

public-service delivery

Public service quality is how well a public service's processes and results meet relevant requirements and the needs of the people it serves.

More about this term

Users' experiences matter, but a satisfaction score alone cannot describe the quality of the service or its wider outcomes.

CC0 1.0View versioned object

Public value

value of public action for a political community

In public governance, public value is the worth of public action in advancing interests and outcomes that a community has reason to regard as important.

More about this term

Judging it calls for attention to whose interests count and how competing concerns such as effectiveness, fairness, rights, and accountability are weighed.

It cannot be read from a service's financial return or a simple sum of individual preferences alone.

CC0 1.0View versioned object

Publication bias

result-dependent publication of research findings

Publication bias occurs when whether research findings are published depends on the nature or direction of their results.

More about this term

The available studies can then give a misleading picture of the evidence, for example if studies with favorable or statistically significant findings are more likely to appear.

It concerns missing studies or reports and is distinct from selectively reporting outcomes within a published study.

CC0 1.0View versioned object

Purity

impurity control for a pharmaceutical substance

For a pharmaceutical substance, purity is the extent to which the material is free of relevant impurities under specified tests.

More about this term

Which impurities matter and what limits apply depend on the substance, its manufacturing process, and the intended product.

Purity is distinct from identity or potency: knowing what a substance is or how strongly it acts does not show what unwanted substances it contains.

CC0 1.0View versioned object

Purpose

intended end or use guiding an activity or judgment

A purpose is the end or use an action, object, or inquiry is intended to serve.

More about this term

A clear purpose names what someone is trying to achieve and for whom. It helps determine which alternatives, requirements, and evidence are relevant.

Purpose is an intention, not proof of success. An activity can have a clear purpose and still fail to achieve it.

CC0 1.0View versioned object
Q68 terms

QFD matrix cascade

quality function deployment planning

A QFD matrix cascade is a sequence of linked planning matrices that carries customer requirements into product, component, process, and control requirements.

More about this term

Each stage uses outputs from the previous stage to guide the next design or production decision. The first House of Quality matrix is only the beginning of this sequence.

CC0 1.0View versioned object

Qualification

documented suitability of pharmaceutical equipment

In pharmaceutical manufacturing, equipment qualification is the documented demonstration that equipment or a system is suitable for its intended use under stated conditions.

More about this term

It can include checks of design, installation, operation, and performance according to the equipment's role and the qualification plan.

Equipment qualification supports process validation but does not by itself establish that the manufacturing process is reproducible.

CC0 1.0View versioned object

Quality

quality management

Quality is how well an object’s relevant characteristics fulfill the requirements used to judge it.

More about this term

Here, relevant characteristics are inherent characteristics of the object that bear on the applicable requirements. An attribute merely assigned to the object is outside this definition of quality.

In quality management, object can mean a product, service, process, organization, or other subject of assessment.

Requirements may be stated, generally implied, or obligatory; they are not limited to written specifications.

CC0 1.0View versioned object

Quality appraisal

methodological appraisal of studies in evidence synthesis

In evidence synthesis, quality appraisal is a structured assessment of the methodological strengths and limitations of the studies used to support a finding.

More about this term

The criteria should fit the study methods, and the appraisal helps interpret how much confidence to place in the synthesized finding.

A polished report alone does not show that the underlying study methods were sound.

CC0 1.0View versioned object

Quality assessment

examination of quality against a stated basis

Quality assessment is the examination of evidence about an object’s quality against relevant requirements or criteria.

More about this term

It may examine characteristics, performance, processes, or outcomes. State what was examined, the basis of comparison, and the limits of the evidence.

An assessment can report findings that support a later quality judgment, or include that judgment itself. The precise boundary between quality assessment and quality evaluation depends on the field and task.

CC0 1.0View versioned object

Quality assurance

confidence in future fulfillment of quality requirements

Quality assurance is the part of quality management concerned with providing a sound basis for expecting quality requirements to be fulfilled.

More about this term

Planning, assigned responsibilities, checks, and evidence can support that expectation. Earlier results and present checks matter when they bear on future fulfillment; no assurance activity guarantees every result.

A check may serve both assurance and control. Assurance emphasizes warranted confidence in what will happen; quality control emphasizes work that fulfills the requirements.

CC0 1.0View versioned object

Quality attribute

quality-model feature

A quality attribute is a named feature of an object treated as relevant to an account of its quality.

More about this term

In systems and software work, a model may organize attributes such as reliability or performance efficiency into narrower attributes and connect them to measures.

Naming an attribute does not give its measured value or decide whether performance is good. The term overlaps with quality characteristic in some fields; specify the model and sense being used.

CC0 1.0View versioned object

Quality audit

systematic quality-related audit against stated criteria

A quality audit is a systematic, documented, and independent assessment of a quality-related product, process, or system against stated audit criteria.

More about this term

It uses relevant, verifiable evidence to determine where the criteria are met and where findings require attention. The scope and criteria must be named before a finding can be interpreted.

An audit may examine a product, a process, or a management system. Inspection of an output can contribute evidence, but an audit also considers the wider questions set by its scope.

CC0 1.0View versioned object

Quality by design

pharmaceutical product and process development

In pharmaceutical development, quality by design is a systematic approach that starts with intended product quality and uses product and process understanding to build and control that quality.

More about this term

It sets a target product profile, identifies critical quality attributes, and studies the material and process variables that affect them. Those relationships guide development and the controls needed to produce the intended result.

Testing a finished product can check what was produced; quality by design also asks how development and manufacturing choices make the desired quality likely and controllable. Uses of the phrase outside pharmaceuticals require their own scope and evidence.

CC0 1.0View versioned object

Quality characteristic

quality management

A quality characteristic is an inherent feature of an object that bears on an applicable quality requirement.

More about this term

A label merely assigned to an object is outside this technical sense. A characteristic may be specified or assessed without yet knowing whether the object fulfills the requirement.

Keep the characteristic distinct from its observed value, an indicator used to track it, and the judgment made from the evidence.

CC0 1.0View versioned object

Quality circle

recurring employee group examining its own work for quality improvement

A quality circle is a recurring group of employees who examine quality problems in their own work and propose improvements.

More about this term

Members typically choose issues from their work area and develop proposals through group discussion and problem-solving methods.

A proposal still needs implementation and follow-up; the meeting itself is not the improvement.

CC0 1.0View versioned object

Quality claim

assertion about an object's quality

A quality claim is an assertion about how well a specified object satisfies a relevant quality requirement or criterion.

More about this term

A useful claim names the object, the aspect being judged, the basis for judgment, and the evidence that supports it.

A measured value alone is not a complete quality claim until it is related to a requirement or evaluative criterion.

CC0 1.0View versioned object

Quality control

operational fulfillment of quality requirements

Quality control is operational work used to keep processes or outputs aligned with applicable quality requirements.

More about this term

It can include checking results, finding departures, and adjusting or correcting the work. The applicable requirements and the scope of the check determine what a passing result establishes.

Some control activities also provide evidence for quality assurance. An inspection is one possible control activity, not the whole of quality control.

CC0 1.0View versioned object

Quality control inspector

manufacturing occupation

A quality control inspector checks materials or products against specified criteria and records whether they meet those criteria.

More about this term

The work may involve visual inspection, testing, or measurement, with nonconforming items identified for further action. An inspector's check is one part of quality control, not a complete quality-management system.

CC0 1.0View versioned object

Quality culture

shared organizational expectations and practice

Quality culture is the shared expectations and everyday practices through which an organization pursues, examines, and improves quality.

More about this term

It becomes visible in what leaders and staff do: how concerns are communicated, how performance is examined, and whether learning changes routine work.

A stated value or a formal quality procedure is not sufficient evidence of such a culture on its own. Look for consistent behavior across roles and over time.

CC0 1.0View versioned object

Quality dimension

aspect of a quality profile

A quality dimension is a distinguishable aspect under which related quality concerns are organized for describing or assessing an object.

More about this term

For data, accuracy and completeness are possible dimensions; another domain may choose a different set. Name the object and framework before comparing dimension results.

The dimension is an organizing aspect, not a single observation, measure, or required performance level. These may be attached to it separately.

CC0 1.0View versioned object

Quality education

primary and secondary schooling

In schooling, quality education supports students in achieving worthwhile learning aims through suitable teaching, opportunities, and conditions.

More about this term

A quality judgment must state which aims and learners matter and examine evidence of learning and access in context. Test scores alone cannot capture every valued educational outcome.

CC0 1.0View versioned object

Quality engineering

engineering approach to product and process quality

Quality engineering applies engineering and analytical methods across design and production to help products and processes meet intended quality requirements.

More about this term

It can address variation and potential defects before delivery, as well as investigate and improve observed performance.

Its methods depend on the product and setting; software quality engineering, for example, places particular emphasis on requirements, testing, and release.

CC0 1.0View versioned object

Quality Enhancement Plan (QEP)

SACSCOC higher-education accreditation, 2024 edition

Under SACSCOC's 2024 accreditation framework, a Quality Enhancement Plan is an institution's focused plan to improve specified student learning or success outcomes as part of reaffirmation review.

More about this term

The topic arises from institutional planning and requires broad support, committed resources, and a way to assess results. The term here names a particular accreditation instrument, not every plan for improving educational quality.

CC0 1.0View versioned object

Quality evaluation

appraisal of an object’s quality

A quality evaluation is a reasoned appraisal of how well a specified object meets relevant quality requirements or criteria.

More about this term

It identifies the object, the basis for judging quality, the evidence considered, and the conclusion reached. The conclusion may be qualified when evidence is limited or criteria point in different directions.

Quality evaluation and quality assessment overlap in some fields. When a distinction is useful, evaluation emphasizes the warranted appraisal, while assessment emphasizes the work of obtaining and interpreting evidence.

CC0 1.0View versioned object

Quality function deployment

translating investigated customer needs into development decisions

Quality function deployment (QFD) is a structured method for translating investigated customer needs into product or service design and subsequent development decisions across organizational functions.

More about this term

It makes proposed links between what customers need and what a team plans to design, build, and control. The links and priorities should be reasoned through rather than treated as facts merely because they occupy cells in a chart.

The House of Quality is a familiar planning matrix within QFD. QFD can continue into further design and process decisions; completing one matrix does not show that the finished offering meets customer needs.

CC0 1.0View versioned object

Quality gap

SERVQUAL service-quality assessment

In service-quality assessment, a quality gap is a mismatch between what customers expect and what they perceive a service delivered.

More about this term

The SERVQUAL framework compares expectation and performance ratings and also identifies organizational gaps that may contribute to the mismatch. A difference score indicates a discrepancy; it does not by itself establish its cause.

CC0 1.0View versioned object

Quality governance

organizational authority and oversight for quality

Quality governance is the arrangement of authority, accountability, oversight, and decision-making through which an organization directs and checks its work on quality.

More about this term

It identifies who sets direction, who can escalate concerns, who reviews performance, and who decides on action and resources. These responsibilities may be distributed across leaders, functions, and governing bodies.

Management review is one governance mechanism. Governance also depends on whether decisions are carried out and their effects examined; a reporting structure alone does not establish effective oversight.

CC0 1.0View versioned object

Quality growth

export-product quality in development economics

In export analysis, quality growth is an increase over time in the estimated quality of goods within a product category.

More about this term

It concerns changes in product quality, which can differ from growth in the amount sold or in total economic output. Its reported rate depends on the study's quality measure and comparison period.

CC0 1.0View versioned object

Quality improvement

deliberate beneficial change in quality

Quality improvement is deliberate change aimed at making an object, process, or system better at meeting relevant quality needs or requirements.

More about this term

An improvement effort should identify what is to change, the desired result, and evidence that could show whether the change helped. A revised procedure alone does not show that performance improved.

Improvement can address recurring failures, strengthen a process, or add capabilities that meet changing needs. Evidence of the resulting effect distinguishes an achieved improvement from an intended one.

CC0 1.0View versioned object

Quality improvement team

organizational process improvement

A quality improvement team is a group formed to investigate a defined quality problem and carry out a coordinated improvement effort.

More about this term

Members combine relevant knowledge, examine the process and its results, and plan changes. Such a team may be temporary and cross-functional; it is not the same as a standing inspection role.

CC0 1.0View versioned object

Quality in use

software or system quality experienced in specified use

In software and systems evaluation, quality in use is how well specified users achieve their goals with a product or system in a specified context of use.

More about this term

Common assessment dimensions include effectiveness, efficiency, satisfaction, freedom from risk, and coverage of intended contexts. Assessing these requires attention to users, tasks, and conditions of use.

A product can meet a technical specification yet perform poorly in use. A claim of quality in use therefore needs evidence from the relevant context, not only a list of product features.

CC0 1.0View versioned object

Quality indicator

quality assessment across domains

A quality indicator is a specified sign used to gather evidence about one aspect of quality.

More about this term

It can describe a feature of an object, how a service is provided, or a result experienced by its users.

Its interpretation depends on the quality question, the population and setting, the data, and the relationship between the sign and the aspect being judged.

In health care, quality indicators may concern structure, process, or outcome.

CC0 1.0View versioned object

Quality judgment

cross-domain evaluative conclusion

A quality judgment is a reasoned conclusion about how well an object meets relevant requirements or evaluative criteria.

More about this term

It identifies the object and the basis for judging it, interprets pertinent evidence, and states the resulting appraisal.

The conclusion may be qualified when evidence is incomplete or criteria conflict.

CC0 1.0View versioned object

Quality level

degree of service quality relative to stated expectations or standards

In service management, a quality level is the degree of service quality achieved or sought relative to customer expectations and service standards.

More about this term

Calling a level high or low requires stating the features being assessed and the basis for comparison.

An economically optimal quality level is a separate business judgment about costs and benefits, not a universal target.

CC0 1.0View versioned object

Quality loss function

modeled loss associated with a quality characteristic departing from a target

A quality loss function relates the value of a quality characteristic to the loss associated with its departure from a stated target.

More about this term

It makes the target and the assumed consequence of deviation explicit. Under a continuous loss model, a result can impose some loss even while it remains inside specification limits.

The shape and scale of the function are assumptions to justify for the particular use; a familiar quadratic model is one possible choice, not a universal law of quality.

CC0 1.0View versioned object

Quality management

organizational direction and operation concerning quality

Quality management is the coordinated work by which an organization sets quality aims and directs its activities toward meeting and improving them.

More about this term

It connects policies and objectives with responsibilities, processes, resources, and evidence about results. Planning, assurance, control, and improvement are related functions within this work.

Managing quality does not itself mean that every output is good. Its effectiveness must be judged by relevant results and needs.

CC0 1.0View versioned object

Quality management maturity

appraisal of pharmaceutical manufacturing-site quality-management practice

For a pharmaceutical manufacturing site, quality management maturity is an appraisal of how developed and consistently applied its quality-management practices are under a specified assessment framework.

More about this term

The framework determines which practices and evidence count and how maturity is characterized.

A maturity assessment concerns the management system; it does not directly measure the quality of every product the site makes.

CC0 1.0View versioned object

Quality management plan

quality-management component of a project plan

A project quality management plan explains how the project will apply its quality policies, methods, roles, and resources to achieve stated quality objectives.

More about this term

It connects the objectives to responsibilities, planned activities, and the checks used to manage quality across the project.

The plan governs the project's approach; a product-specific quality plan may set out controls for one deliverable.

CC0 1.0View versioned object

Quality management system

organizational system for managing quality

A quality management system is the connected organizational arrangement through which quality objectives are set, pursued, checked, and improved.

More about this term

It joins roles, processes, resources, information, and review across the organization. Documents and software may support the system, but neither alone constitutes it.

The system’s value depends on whether those connected activities help meet quality objectives; a collection of documents alone is not sufficient.

CC0 1.0View versioned object

Quality management system planning

quality management

Quality management system planning is the work of arranging a quality management system to meet its objectives and applicable system requirements.

More about this term

It includes planning how changes will be made without disrupting the system's ability to function as a whole.

CC0 1.0View versioned object

Quality manual

management-system overview document

A quality manual is a document that describes an organization's quality management system and how its parts fit together.

More about this term

It may state the system's scope and point readers to the policies, processes, and controlled documents that govern work.

Its use and form depend on the organization and applicable requirements; the term alone does not make one mandatory.

CC0 1.0View versioned object

Quality maturity

organizational quality management

Quality maturity is the extent to which an organization has developed sustained practices for managing and improving quality.

More about this term

A maturity model can describe stages of management practice; a high stage is not direct proof that every product or service meets its requirements.

CC0 1.0View versioned object

Quality measure

specified quality assessment across services

A quality measure specifies how to obtain evidence about one aspect of quality.

More about this term

It identifies what is assessed, the eligible population or events, the data and calculation or observation method, and the direction in which results should be interpreted.

In health care, quality measures may address care processes, outcomes, patient perceptions, or organizational structures.

In broader quality management, the aspect assessed should be tied to relevant characteristics and requirements.

For other services, the specification must fit the service, its users, and the decision it will inform.

CC0 1.0View versioned object

Quality measurement

obtaining values for specified quality-related quantities

Quality measurement is the use of a specified procedure to obtain values for quantities that bear on a stated quality question.

More about this term

Identify what is measured, the subject and conditions, the method, and the resulting value. A quality model or requirement explains why that quantity matters.

The measurement result is evidence. Deciding whether the result is good, sufficient, or compliant requires a further interpretive rule or judgment.

CC0 1.0View versioned object

Quality metric

cross-domain quantitative quality metric

A quality metric specifies how to turn observations into a numerical assessment of one aspect of quality.

More about this term

Its specification identifies the subject, relevant characteristic, data, calculation, unit or scale, and conditions of use.

The calculated value is a result; a requirement, target, or other interpretive rule is needed to decide what that result means.

The relevant quality aspect, calculation, and interpretation depend on the field; a numerical result has no universal grade on its own.

CC0 1.0View versioned object

Quality model

organized representation of quality aspects

A quality model is an explicit scheme for organizing the aspects of quality considered for a class of objects.

More about this term

It may define characteristics, narrower subcharacteristics, and their relationships to measures. Its categories and boundaries depend on the objects and use for which it was made.

A model helps select what to examine; it does not itself set a requirement or establish that a particular object is good. Software and systems quality models are one domain example.

CC0 1.0View versioned object

Quality objective

organizational intended quality result

A quality objective is a result an organization intends to achieve concerning quality.

More about this term

It gives practical direction to a quality policy. A useful objective identifies the subject, desired result, responsibility, and evidence by which progress will be assessed.

An objective states an aim; an indicator or measure tracks progress, and a target can state the level sought by a particular time. The existence of the objective does not show that the result was achieved.

CC0 1.0View versioned object

Quality of care

evaluation of health-care services

Quality of care is how well health services meet justified clinical aims and the needs of the people receiving them.

More about this term

A full judgment can consider whether care is safe, effective, centered on the patient, timely, efficient, and equitable. The relevant evidence and trade-offs depend on the service and population.

A favorable outcome alone does not settle whether the care was good. The way care was delivered, foreseeable risks, and the patient’s circumstances also matter.

CC0 1.0View versioned object

Quality of experience

user experience of communications applications and services

In communications services, quality of experience (QoE) is how pleasing or frustrating an application or service is for its users.

More about this term

Expectations and the context of use can affect that experience.

A network performance measure alone cannot establish how users experience the service.

CC0 1.0View versioned object

Quality of legislation

rule-of-law assessment of enacted rules

Quality of legislation is how well enacted rules are made and stated so they can guide conduct and meet relevant rule-of-law standards.

More about this term

Public availability, clarity, consistency, workable demands, and a valid enactment process matter; good drafting alone does not settle a law's justice or effects.

CC0 1.0View versioned object

Quality of life

person-centered appraisal of life circumstances

Quality of life is a person’s appraisal of how life is going in the circumstances and values that matter to them.

More about this term

Health and functioning may matter, alongside relationships, psychological experience, and features of the surrounding environment. The relevant mix can differ across people and settings.

A clinical measure or an income figure can inform this appraisal, but neither alone stands for the whole of a person’s quality of life.

CC0 1.0View versioned object

Quality of life assessment

health and social-care assessment

Quality of life assessment is a structured appraisal of how a person or group is doing across life domains relevant to the assessment's purpose.

More about this term

It may combine people's own reports with observations of their circumstances. The chosen domains and methods determine which aspects of life the assessment can describe.

CC0 1.0View versioned object

Quality of Life Inventory (QOLI)

named positive-psychology self-report instrument

The Quality of Life Inventory (QOLI) is a self-report instrument that combines how important life areas are to a person with how satisfied the person is in those areas.

More about this term

It produces an individualized profile of perceived life satisfaction. Its named instrument and scoring method should not be confused with every measure of quality of life.

CC0 1.0View versioned object

Quality of life measures

health-related quality-of-life measurement

Quality of life measures are instruments or indicators used to describe specified aspects of people's perceived health and everyday life.

More about this term

Different measures ask about different domains, populations, and experiences. A score must be interpreted in light of what the instrument covers; it cannot alone represent every aspect of a person's life.

CC0 1.0View versioned object

Quality of service

specified technical characteristics of web-service delivery

For a web service, quality of service (QoS) describes specified characteristics of its delivery, such as performance, reliability, or accessibility.

More about this term

A QoS model identifies which characteristics matter and how they are assessed for the service.

Technical QoS results can inform, but do not alone settle, a user's judgment of the wider service experience.

CC0 1.0View versioned object

Quality plan

quality planning for a specified product, project, or contract

A quality plan states how quality requirements will be addressed for a specified product, project, or contract.

More about this term

It identifies the relevant activities and controls and, where needed, who will carry them out and what records will show the result.

It may be a separate document or part of a broader project plan, depending on the work.

CC0 1.0View versioned object

Quality planning

arrangements for quality objectives

Quality planning is the work of setting quality objectives and arranging what is needed to achieve them.

More about this term

The arrangements may identify applicable requirements, processes, responsibilities, resources, checks, and responses to foreseeable failure. A quality plan records such arrangements for a particular product, service, or project.

Planning specifies intended work and criteria; later control, assurance, and evaluation show what was done and what the evidence supports.

CC0 1.0View versioned object

Quality policy

organizational direction on quality

A quality policy is an organization’s stated direction and commitments concerning quality.

More about this term

It provides a basis for setting quality objectives and communicating what leaders expect. Its scope and commitments should be clear enough to guide choices about work and resources.

A written policy does not establish that people follow it. Its effect must be judged from decisions, practices, and results in the organization.

CC0 1.0View versioned object

Quality premium

relative price of higher-quality product output

In product markets with defined quality grades, a quality premium is the higher price of a higher-quality grade relative to a lower-quality comparison grade.

More about this term

The grades, price basis, and method of comparison must be specified. A price difference alone does not establish a difference in quality.

CC0 1.0View versioned object

Quality profile

structured multi-aspect representation

A quality profile is a structured view of how an object fares across specified aspects of quality.

More about this term

It identifies the object and the aspects represented, with observations, assessments, or values for each. A profile can preserve differences that a single overall score would conceal.

In data and information quality, profiles can be computed at the level of an item, flow, process, or organization. Extending the term beyond that domain requires a stated framework and evidence.

CC0 1.0View versioned object

Quality record

retained quality-management evidence

In quality management, a quality record is retained information that shows what was done or what result was obtained.

More about this term

Completed inspection results and training records are examples when they are kept as evidence of quality-related activity.

A blank procedure tells people what to do; it does not record what actually happened.

CC0 1.0View versioned object

Quality requirement

quality management

A quality requirement is a need or expectation concerning an object’s quality that is to be fulfilled.

More about this term

It may concern a characteristic, a level of performance, or the conditions under which the object is used. Like other requirements, it can be stated, generally implied, or obligatory.

Identify the object, the applicable condition, and the basis for deciding fulfillment. The requirement is the expectation; an observed result is evidence about whether it has been met.

CC0 1.0View versioned object

Quality review

learning-and-development content production

In learning and development, a quality review is a structured examination of a product or work in progress against stated quality guidelines.

More about this term

Reviewers record issues that can guide correction, and reviews can occur during development as well as before delivery. Passing a review depends on the applicable criteria, not the label alone.

CC0 1.0View versioned object

Quality risk management

organized handling of risks to quality

Quality risk management is the organized assessment, control, communication, and review of risks that could affect quality.

More about this term

It starts with a clear risk question, considers possible harms and their likelihood or uncertainty, chooses proportionate controls, and revisits the judgment when evidence or conditions change.

The formal term is established in pharmaceutical guidance, where protecting patients and maintaining product quality are central. Applying the same pattern elsewhere requires stating the object, applicable requirements, and who could be affected.

CC0 1.0View versioned object

Quality standard

documented quality reference within a stated scope

A quality standard is a documented reference for specifying, managing, or evaluating quality within a stated scope.

More about this term

Its provisions may set requirements or provide a model or guidance. Identify the document, edition, subject, and which provisions apply before claiming that something conforms to it.

Conformity to a quality-management reference does not by itself show that every product or service is good for its intended users. A separate judgment must connect the applicable requirements to the object and evidence.

CC0 1.0View versioned object

Quality System Regulation

former U.S. medical-device regulatory name

Quality System Regulation (QSR) was the former U.S. FDA name for the medical-device quality-system requirements in 21 CFR Part 820.

More about this term

Since February 2, 2026, the revised Part 820 is called the Quality Management System Regulation (QMSR). The older name remains useful for reading historical guidance and records.

CC0 1.0View versioned object

Quality target product profile

prospective quality characteristics for a pharmaceutical product

In pharmaceutical development, a quality target product profile is a prospective outline of the characteristics a drug product should ideally have to achieve its intended quality, taking safety and efficacy into account.

More about this term

It helps guide development choices and the identification of potential critical quality attributes.

The profile states a target for development, not proof that a finished product already meets it.

CC0 1.0View versioned object

Quality tools

methods and representations used in quality control, planning and improvement

Quality tools are methods and representations used to examine, plan, control, or improve aspects of quality.

More about this term

Examples include a check sheet for collecting observations, a histogram for displaying their distribution, and a cause-and-effect diagram for organizing possible causes.

The seven basic quality-control tools are one named set; planning and management use additional tools.

CC0 1.0View versioned object

Quality trilogy

Juran's quality-management model

The quality trilogy is Juran's model of three linked management processes: quality planning, quality control, and quality improvement.

More about this term

Planning prepares a process to meet quality goals, control manages performance during operation, and improvement reduces persistent shortcomings.

The model treats improvement as additional work beyond keeping an existing process within its current operating pattern.

CC0 1.0View versioned object

Quality-adjusted life expectancy

population-health summary measurement

Quality-adjusted life expectancy estimates expected years of life after weighting those years by valuations of the health states people are expected to experience.

More about this term

Its units are quality-adjusted life years. Unlike unadjusted life expectancy, the result depends on how health states are described and valued.

CC0 1.0View versioned object

Quality-adjusted life year

health-economic unit combining survival and health-state value

A quality-adjusted life year (QALY) is a unit that combines time lived with a weight for health-related quality of life during that time.

More about this term

One year at a weight of 1 contributes one QALY; two years at a weight of 0.5 also contribute one.

The weights require a stated valuation method, and QALYs alone do not settle a treatment or resource-allocation decision.

CC0 1.0View versioned object

Quality-adjusted price

economic price comparison

A quality-adjusted price accounts for differences in relevant features of the goods or services being compared, so price changes are not confused with changes in what is provided.

More about this term

The adjustment depends on which features are counted and how their contribution is estimated; it is not simply a lower advertised price.

CC0 1.0View versioned object
R73 terms

Randomization

chance-determined run order in experimental design
