In experimental design, randomization uses a chance procedure to determine the order of experimental runs.

More about this term

It helps prevent unmeasured influences that change over time from consistently favoring one factor setting or treatment. The procedure and any restrictions on it should be recorded.

Random order does not fix an unsuitable sample, missing controls, or every source of bias. Random assignment of treatments to units is a related use of the word and should be specified separately when intended.

CC0 1.0View versioned object

Rank

ordinal position in a stated ordering

A rank is an item's position in an ordering made under a stated comparison rule.

More about this term

Ranks show which items come before others, but the gap between positions does not by itself measure the size of the underlying difference.

For example, first and second place may be much closer in performance than second and third place.

CC0 1.0View versioned object

Rating

assigned level on an itemized assessment scale

A rating is a selected level on a defined scale used to assess a specified attribute.

More about this term

The scale must identify what is being rated and what its levels mean.

Ordered ratings do not, by themselves, show that the numerical distances between levels are equal.

CC0 1.0View versioned object

Rating scale

ordered appraisal response categories

A rating scale is a set of ordered response categories or anchored levels used to express an appraisal of a specified attribute.

More about this term

A person might select one of several levels of agreement or performance.

The selected level is a rating; numerical labels alone do not show that the distance between neighboring levels is equal.

CC0 1.0View versioned object

Recoverability

software and system restoration after interruption or failure

In software reliability, recoverability is a system's ability after interruption or failure to restore affected data and return to a desired operational state.

More about this term

Assess it against specified failure scenarios, acceptable data loss, and restoration time.

Having a backup alone does not establish that the full system can recover.

CC0 1.0View versioned object

Recovery

organizational response to a service failure

In service management, recovery is an organization's response to a service failure to address its effects and restore the customer's experience.

More about this term

It can begin when staff notice a failure, before a customer complains.

Effective recovery may also identify the cause of the failure so similar problems become less likely.

CC0 1.0View versioned object

Recovery point objective

system recovery and continuity

A recovery point objective is the maximum acceptable time interval of data loss when a system is restored after a disruption.

More about this term

It sets a data-loss tolerance; a recovery time objective instead concerns how long the service may remain unavailable.

CC0 1.0View versioned object

Recovery time objective

digital service continuity

In service continuity, a recovery time objective is the maximum downtime an organization plans to allow before a disrupted service is restored.

More about this term

It is a recovery target, not a record of actual restoration time; a recovery point objective instead concerns tolerable data loss.

CC0 1.0View versioned object

Redundancy

reliability engineering provision of additional means

In reliability engineering, redundancy is the provision of additional means to perform a function if a primary means fails.

More about this term

The added means may be spare components, alternative paths, or enough time to repeat an operation.

Its reliability benefit depends on the arrangement and failure behavior; extra parts alone are not a guarantee.

CC0 1.0View versioned object

Reference level

comparison point for model-performance results

In performance comparison, a reference level is a stated comparison value that helps interpret a result from a model or measure.

More about this term

A shared reference level can make results from different performance measures easier to compare.

It need not be a target to be achieved or a threshold that triggers an action.

CC0 1.0View versioned object

Reference material

material fit for a specified measurement or examination use

In metrology, a reference material is a material shown to be sufficiently uniform and stable for specified properties to serve an identified measurement or examination purpose.

More about this term

It can support calibration, checking a method, assigning values to other materials, or quality control; its usefulness depends on the property and intended use.

A certified reference material additionally has documented property values with stated uncertainty and traceability.

CC0 1.0View versioned object

Reference standard

measurement standard used to calibrate other local standards

In metrology, a reference standard is a measurement standard designated by an organization or at a location for calibrating other standards of the same kind of quantity.

More about this term

It serves as a reference in that calibration chain; the designation does not by itself make it a primary or international standard.

Its use should be identified by the quantity and the standards it is intended to calibrate.

CC0 1.0View versioned object

Referential integrity

relational database

In a relational database, referential integrity is the condition that required references between records point to records that exist.

More about this term

A foreign key expresses such a relationship; enforcing it prevents an orphan record whose required parent is absent.

The rule protects the declared link, but does not establish that the linked facts are accurate.

CC0 1.0View versioned object

Regulatory compliance

applicable binding rules

Regulatory compliance is meeting the binding regulatory requirements that apply to a specified product, service, activity, or organization.

More about this term

The judgment depends on the jurisdiction, the rule, and the part of the operation to which it applies.

Compliance with a rule does not, by itself, establish overall quality.

CC0 1.0View versioned object

Regulatory quality

Worldwide Governance Indicators usage

In the Worldwide Governance Indicators, regulatory quality concerns perceptions of a government's ability to formulate and carry out policies and regulations that enable private-sector activity.

More about this term

It is a governance indicator, not a finding that a particular organization complies with a regulation.

CC0 1.0View versioned object

Relationship matrix

customer-to-technical grid in a House of Quality

In a House of Quality, the relationship matrix is the grid that pairs customer requirements with proposed technical characteristics and provides a cell for each assessed link.

More about this term

The rows represent customer-side needs and the columns represent design-side responses. A mark or score expresses an assessed relationship under a stated convention; different methods may use different scales.

The grid helps a team consider which responses address which needs. Its entries are planning judgments and should not be mistaken for measurements of the finished product or service.

CC0 1.0View versioned object

Relative contribution

category share of an observed total in a Pareto analysis

In a Pareto analysis, relative contribution is the share of the observed total represented by one category.

More about this term

For counts, divide the category count by the count across all included categories and state the population and period being counted.

A large share identifies where observations concentrate; it does not, by itself, establish the cause of those observations.

CC0 1.0View versioned object

Relevance

bearing of a reason or evidence on a claim

In an argument, relevance is the bearing a reason or piece of evidence has on the particular claim it is offered to support.

More about this term

A fact can be accurate yet irrelevant if it does not help establish the claim at issue.

Relevance is distinct from sufficiency: a reason may bear on a claim without providing enough support to settle it.

CC0 1.0View versioned object

Reliability

test-score consistency and engineered-item performance

Reliability concerns whether a specified result or required performance holds consistently under the conditions that matter.

More about this term

Its technical meaning depends on what is expected to remain dependable:

For test scores, reliability or precision concerns consistency across appropriate repetitions of the measurement procedure. The repetitions, population, sources of error, and intended score use must be specified.

For an engineered item or system, reliability concerns performing as required without failure over a specified interval and under stated conditions. When modeled probabilistically, R(t) is the probability that the item survives beyond time t.

CC0 1.0View versioned object

Reliability block diagram

logical component-success model for a system function

A reliability block diagram is a model showing which components must function, alone or in alternative paths, for a specified system function to succeed.

More about this term

Each block represents a needed function or component state; a complete path of functioning blocks represents system success.

The diagram expresses functional dependence, not necessarily physical wiring, and reliability calculations require stated assumptions about component behavior.

CC0 1.0View versioned object

Reliability coefficient

psychometric test scores

In psychometrics, a reliability coefficient is a numerical estimate of how consistently scores from a specified testing procedure behave under a stated model or repetition condition.

More about this term

Different coefficients address different sources of score variation, such as items, occasions, or alternate forms.

A high coefficient alone does not establish that the scores support their intended interpretation.

CC0 1.0View versioned object

Reliability-centered maintenance

selection of maintenance actions from functions, failure modes and consequences

Reliability-centered maintenance is a structured way to choose maintenance actions by examining what an asset must do, how it can fail, and the consequences of those failures.

More about this term

The operating context, available ways to detect deterioration, and safety and economic consequences shape the choice. An action may be condition-based, scheduled, or another justified response.

It does not mean maintaining every component as often as possible; some failure modes call for redesign or a decision to let a low-consequence item run to failure.

CC0 1.0View versioned object

Repair

disposition making a nonconforming output acceptable for use

In quality management, repair is action on a nonconforming product or service to make it acceptable for its intended use.

More about this term

A repair can restore usability without necessarily meeting every original requirement.

This differs from rework, whose aim is to bring the output into conformity with those requirements.

CC0 1.0View versioned object

Repeatability

precision of repeated measurement under repeatability conditions

In measurement, repeatability is the closeness of results from repeated measurements made under specified, closely matched conditions.

More about this term

These conditions commonly include the same procedure, operator, measuring system, location, and a short time interval.

A repeatable method can still yield results systematically displaced from a reference value.

CC0 1.0View versioned object

Replicability

empirical research

In empirical research, replicability is the capacity for an independent investigation to follow a reported method and obtain a sufficiently similar finding.

More about this term

A clear account of the procedure makes the attempt possible; whether findings are sufficiently similar depends on the question and the variation expected.

CC0 1.0View versioned object

Reporting quality

journalistic news reporting

In journalism, reporting quality is how well a news account informs its audience under relevant editorial and public-interest standards.

More about this term

Context, source transparency, diversity of perspectives, and clear presentation may matter; counting sources alone cannot establish factual accuracy.

CC0 1.0View versioned object

Reproducibility

agreement of measurement results under changed conditions

In measurement, reproducibility is the closeness of results for the same quantity when specified measurement conditions change.

More about this term

State which conditions changed, such as operator, time, or instrument, when reporting reproducibility.

Repeatability concerns measurements made under the same conditions, so the two properties answer different questions.

CC0 1.0View versioned object

Reproducibility conditions

measurement precision

In measurement, reproducibility conditions are specified circumstances for repeated measurements in which relevant factors may change, such as operator, location, or measuring system.

More about this term

The specification says which factors change; repetitions with the same operator, instrument, and location instead exemplify repeatability conditions.

CC0 1.0View versioned object

Reputation

organizational public regard

An organization's reputation is how an audience regards it, including what the organization is known for and the esteem attached to it.

More about this term

Being widely recognized is different from being well regarded; the audience and the attributes at issue should be named.

CC0 1.0View versioned object

Requirement

quality management and technical specifications

Requirement is a need or expectation used to specify what an object, process, or action is expected to satisfy.

More about this term

In quality management, it may be stated, generally implied by established practice, or obligatory; it need not be written down to apply.

To judge whether a requirement is fulfilled, identify what is expected, of what, and under which conditions.

In a technical specification, state it clearly enough to check fulfillment without prescribing a particular solution unless that solution is itself required.

CC0 1.0View versioned object

Research integrity

responsible conduct and reporting of research

Research integrity is responsible conduct and truthful reporting of inquiry so that its methods, evidence, and conclusions can be trusted.

More about this term

It calls for sound methods, honest handling of data, and transparency about relevant limitations.

When people take part in research, respecting their rights and welfare is also part of responsible conduct; avoiding fabrication alone is insufficient.

CC0 1.0View versioned object

Research quality

merit of inquiry and its outputs for a stated purpose

Research quality is how well an inquiry and its outputs meet justified standards for their purpose and field.

More about this term

Assessment may consider rigor, originality, significance, and whether the evidence warrants the conclusions; their weight depends on the research question and context.

A journal label, citation count, or attractive result does not by itself settle the quality of a particular study.

CC0 1.0View versioned object

Residual risk

risk remaining after selected controls

Residual risk is the risk that remains after measures to reduce or control an identified risk have been applied.

More about this term

Its acceptability depends on the harm, context, and decision rule rather than on the mere fact that controls were used.

Controls can reduce a risk without eliminating it and may introduce new risks that also need assessment.

CC0 1.0View versioned object

Resilience

organizational response to disruption

Organizational resilience is the capacity to anticipate threats, respond to disruption, and continue or restore essential activities.

More about this term

It includes adapting before harm occurs as well as recovering after an event.

A quick recovery from one incident alone does not establish resilience against other threats.

CC0 1.0View versioned object

Resolution

metrology of a measuring system or display

In metrology, resolution is the smallest change in a quantity that a measuring system or display can meaningfully distinguish.

More about this term

On a digital display, it may appear as the step represented by the last displayed digit.

Finer resolution does not by itself establish greater accuracy or lower measurement uncertainty.

CC0 1.0View versioned object

Resource

usable means for carrying out work or achieving an aim

A resource is something available for use in carrying out an activity or pursuing an aim.

More about this term

Time, people, skills, money, equipment, materials, space, and information can all serve as resources, depending on the task.

Some resources can be reused, while others are consumed or depleted; identifying a resource does not establish that enough of it is available.

CC0 1.0View versioned object

Resource efficiency

building design and operation

In building design, resource efficiency is providing a needed service while using less material, energy, water, or other resources for that service.

More about this term

The comparison must say which service, resource, and life-cycle boundary it covers.

Reducing one input alone does not establish a lower overall environmental impact.

CC0 1.0View versioned object

Respect

health-care delivery

In health care, respect is treating a person so that their dignity, privacy, and expressed preferences matter in how care is given.

More about this term

It is shown through considerate communication, protection of bodily privacy, and appropriate room for the person's choices.

A favorable clinical outcome alone does not establish respectful care.

CC0 1.0View versioned object

Response surface

modeled expected response over combinations of input levels

A response surface represents how the expected value of a response varies across combinations of two or more input variables.

More about this term

It may be expressed as a model and shown as a three-dimensional surface or contour plot. Such views can help locate promising operating conditions.

A fitted surface estimates behavior in a studied region; predictions beyond that region or claims of an optimum require further justification.

CC0 1.0View versioned object

Responsible AI

AI-system development, deployment, and operation

Responsible AI is the practice of developing, deploying, and operating AI systems with explicit attention to their benefits, risks, and effects on people.

More about this term

It calls for examining data and model limitations, testing relevant performance and fairness, making system behavior understandable where needed, and monitoring effects in use.

The label alone does not show that a system meets any particular requirement; the responsibilities and evidence must be specified.

CC0 1.0View versioned object

Responsiveness

timely helpful response in service delivery

In service quality, responsiveness is a provider's readiness to help customers and respond promptly to their requests.

More about this term

It concerns the response when help is needed, such as how quickly staff address a service request.

Responsiveness differs from reliability, which concerns delivering the service as promised.

CC0 1.0View versioned object

Result

what an activity or measurement produces or obtains

A result is something produced or obtained through an activity, process, observation, or calculation.

More about this term

A measurement result may be a value; a project result may be a delivered output or an observed change.

The result itself does not say whether it is good or satisfies a requirement; that requires interpretation against a stated basis.

CC0 1.0View versioned object

Retention

student continuation through a defined interval in higher education

In higher education, retention is the continuation of students in a program or institution through a specified period or checkpoint.

More about this term

A retention rate compares the number still enrolled at the end of a defined interval with the number in the starting group.

State the cohort, interval, and whether continuation means staying in the same program or institution; graduation and transfer may be treated separately.

CC0 1.0View versioned object

Return on quality

quality-management economics

Return on quality relates benefits attributed to quality management to the costs of achieving them.

More about this term

The calculation depends on how benefits and costs are estimated and attributed; the ratio alone is not a complete cost-benefit analysis.

CC0 1.0View versioned object

Review

quality-management examination of performance and evidence

In quality management, a review is a deliberate examination of performance and evidence to judge suitability, effectiveness, and the need for action.

More about this term

A management review can bring together objectives, indicators, product or process results, and emerging problems.

The scope, reviewer, and decision authority should be specified; conducting a review does not itself mean that the subject passed.

CC0 1.0View versioned object

Revision

changed version of a controlled document

In document control, a revision is a changed version of a document identified in relation to an earlier version.

More about this term

Record what changed and which version applies; an annotation or proposed change is not necessarily a released revision.

A revision identifier distinguishes versions, but it does not itself prove that the new version was reviewed or approved.

CC0 1.0View versioned object

Rework

disposition to make a nonconforming output conform

Rework is action on a nonconforming product or service intended to bring it into conformity with its requirements.

More about this term

The result must be checked against the applicable requirements before it is treated as conforming.

Repair has a different immediate aim: making the output acceptable for its intended use, which may leave an original requirement unmet.

CC0 1.0View versioned object

Rhetorical quality

public-facing persuasive communication

Rhetorical quality is how well a communication uses facts, reasons, language, and form to address a particular audience and purpose responsibly.

More about this term

Persuasive effect alone does not establish it; the message also needs a sound factual and ethical basis for the choices it invites.

CC0 1.0View versioned object

Right

protected claim or freedom in a human-rights instrument

In a human-rights instrument, a right is a protected claim or freedom held by a person under that instrument.

More about this term

To understand a particular right, identify who holds it, what it protects, the duties it creates, and any lawful limits.

A person's preference alone does not establish a legal right.

CC0 1.0View versioned object

Rigor

research methods, with systematic reviews as exemplar

In research, rigor is disciplined care in designing, conducting, analyzing, interpreting, and reporting a study so its conclusions are warranted by the method and evidence.

More about this term

Its demands depend on the research question and approach; transparent reporting lets others inspect what was done and where the conclusions are limited.

CC0 1.0View versioned object

Risk

common adverse-outcome sense

Risk is the possibility of an unwanted event or outcome under uncertainty, considered in light of its consequences.

More about this term

A useful risk statement says what could happen, what would be affected, and which conditions make the outcome more or less likely. Probability and severity can help analysis, but a single score need not capture the whole concern.

Uses of risk differ across fields. This entry names the common adverse-outcome sense; frameworks that include favorable departures require an explicitly broader sense.

CC0 1.0View versioned object

Risk acceptance

organizational risk treatment

Risk acceptance is an informed decision to retain a specified risk after evaluating it, with responsibility for the possible consequences.

More about this term

It may include monitoring or a contingency plan; accepting a risk does not make it disappear.

CC0 1.0View versioned object

Risk appetite

organizational willingness to take risk for objectives

In organizational risk management, risk appetite is an organization's overall willingness to take risk in pursuit of opportunities or objectives.

More about this term

It guides whether and how far the organization will venture into uncertainty.

Risk tolerance addresses how much of a particular risk it is prepared to bear, often after treatment.

CC0 1.0View versioned object

Risk assessment

hazard-focused assessment for a decision

Risk assessment is a structured examination of what could cause harm, how likely and consequential the harm may be, and what uncertainty remains.

More about this term

The assessor identifies the setting, people or assets exposed, credible scenarios, and the goals against which risk will be judged. Methods may be qualitative or quantitative.

A risk score is a method-specific aid, not the risk itself. State the assumptions, evidence, and criteria behind any conclusion or decision threshold.

CC0 1.0View versioned object

Risk avoidance

organizational risk treatment

Risk avoidance is deciding not to start, or to stop, an activity that would create a specified unwanted risk.

More about this term

It removes exposure from that activity, but may forgo its benefits or leave other risks to manage.

CC0 1.0View versioned object

Risk management

organized response to risks affecting objectives

Risk management is the organized work of identifying, assessing, and responding to risks that could affect stated objectives.

More about this term

It connects possible events and their consequences to decisions about prevention, reduction, acceptance, or other responses. The response should fit the setting and the significance of the risk.

Risk management continues after an initial decision: responsible people monitor what changes, review whether controls work, and revise actions when needed.

CC0 1.0View versioned object

Risk mitigation

organizational downside-risk treatment

Risk mitigation is action to reduce the likelihood or impact of an unwanted risk while continuing the activity that creates exposure to it.

More about this term

The result should be assessed as remaining risk; adopting a control does not by itself show that the risk is acceptable.

CC0 1.0View versioned object

Risk of bias

intervention-study result

In intervention research, risk of bias is the possibility that a study's estimated effect is systematically shifted from the effect being estimated because of how the study was designed, conducted, analyzed, or reported.

More about this term

An assessment identifies plausible sources of bias for a specified result; it is not a judgment that every result of the study is wrong.

CC0 1.0View versioned object

Risk priority number

FMEA product of severity, occurrence, and detection ratings

In failure mode and effects analysis, a risk priority number (RPN) is a score used to help order possible failure modes for attention.

More about this term

A common calculation multiplies ratings for severity, occurrence, and difficulty of detection under a specified rating scheme.

Because the component ratings are judgments and different combinations can yield the same product, an RPN is a screening aid rather than a direct measure of loss or a universal action threshold.

CC0 1.0View versioned object

Risk response

organizational risk treatment and response planning

A risk response is a selected action or strategy for addressing an identified risk.

More about this term

Depending on the risk, a response may avoid, reduce, transfer, or accept it; responses to opportunities can differ.

A response plan states how the choice will be carried out and checked for effectiveness.

CC0 1.0View versioned object

Risk threshold

organizational risk decision rule

A risk threshold is a specified boundary in a risk scale or rule at which the interpretation of a risk or the required response changes.

More about this term

Its meaning depends on what risk is assessed, how it is assessed, the direction of comparison, and the action assigned to each side of the boundary.

No single cutoff applies to every product, activity, or setting.

CC0 1.0View versioned object

Risk tolerance

readiness to bear specified residual risk

In organizational risk management, risk tolerance is the level of a specified risk that an organization or stakeholder is prepared to bear while pursuing an objective.

More about this term

It can be assessed after available risk treatments and may differ among the people who own different risks.

It is a more particular acceptance judgment than an organization's broad risk appetite; it need not be a single numerical maximum.

CC0 1.0View versioned object

Risk transfer

organizational risk treatment

Risk transfer is an arrangement in which another party assumes or shares specified consequences of a risk, often through insurance or a contract.

More about this term

It reallocates those consequences; it does not eliminate the underlying event or necessarily transfer every form of loss.

CC0 1.0View versioned object

Risk treatment

selecting and implementing responses to assessed risks

Risk treatment is the selection and implementation of a response to an assessed risk.

More about this term

Responses can include avoiding an activity, reducing a risk, sharing or transferring it, or knowingly retaining it with a plan.

The choice should account for remaining risk and the costs and effects of the response; treatment does not imply that every risk disappears.

CC0 1.0View versioned object

Robust design

design choices that reduce sensitivity to anticipated variation

Robust design is an approach to choosing product or process characteristics so performance changes less when anticipated sources of variation change.

More about this term

A design may be tested across relevant materials, manufacturing conditions, environments, or patterns of use. The aim is to keep important performance characteristics near their intended values despite such “noise.”

Robustness is relative to the variation considered. A robust design is not immune to every condition, and performance outside the tested range needs separate evidence.

CC0 1.0View versioned object

Robustness

performance sustained under specified variation

Robustness is the ability to maintain acceptable performance when specified inputs or conditions vary.

More about this term

A robustness claim names the variation tested and the performance that must be preserved.

One successful test at ordinary conditions does not show how the object will behave when those conditions change.

CC0 1.0View versioned object

Role

expected function and responsibilities in an organization

An organizational role is a defined part a person or group is expected to play in carrying out work.

More about this term

It may specify tasks, responsibilities, relationships, and decision authority.

A person can hold several roles, and a role is distinct from the particular person currently filling it.

CC0 1.0View versioned object

Rolled throughput yield

share or estimated probability of passing all process steps without defects or rework

Rolled throughput yield is the proportion, or estimated probability, of units that pass every step of a defined process flow without a defect or rework.

More about this term

For consistently defined step-level first-pass yields, multiply the step yields to estimate the chance of first-pass success through the full flow. State the steps and counting rules.

This differs from final yield: a process can deliver many acceptable units after repair while having a much lower rolled throughput yield.

CC0 1.0View versioned object

Root cause

cause of a nonconformance targeted for corrective action

A root cause is a condition or mechanism that produced a defined problem and can be addressed to reduce its recurrence.

More about this term

In quality improvement, identifying a root cause connects a nonconformance to a corrective action directed at why it occurred.

A proposed cause remains a hypothesis until evidence supports the causal link; a problem may have more than one contributing cause.

CC0 1.0View versioned object

Root cause analysis

investigating causes of a quality problem

Root cause analysis is a structured investigation of the causal conditions behind a problem, undertaken to identify changes that could prevent it from recurring.

More about this term

Begin with a clear account of what happened, then examine the process and test plausible explanations against evidence. A cause-and-effect diagram or repeated “why” questions can generate hypotheses; neither proves a cause by itself.

Several conditions may have contributed. An action aimed only at the visible symptom may contain the immediate problem without addressing why it arose.

CC0 1.0View versioned object

Root cause failure analysis

equipment and facility maintenance

Root cause failure analysis is a structured investigation of an equipment or facility failure to find the underlying conditions that produced it.

More about this term

The aim is to correct causes that could lead to recurrence, rather than only repair the immediate damage. Conclusions should follow evidence about the particular failure.

CC0 1.0View versioned object

Rubric

structured guide for evaluating specified work or performance

A rubric is a structured guide for judging a specified kind of work or performance against stated criteria.

More about this term

It may describe levels of performance, give examples, assign points, or set out scoring rules. These details help reviewers apply the criteria and make the basis of a judgment visible.

A rubric organizes judgment; it does not establish that the criteria are appropriate or that different reviewers will apply them consistently. Those questions require separate justification and checking.

CC0 1.0View versioned object

Rule of law

legal and political constraint on public power

The rule of law is a governance ideal in which public power is exercised under knowable laws that also bind officials, rather than through arbitrary will.

More about this term

It calls for legal accountability and ways to challenge official action through fair institutions.

Accounts differ on whether the ideal also requires particular substantive rights or outcomes.

CC0 1.0View versioned object
S90 terms

Safeguarding

child and family social work

In child and family social work, safeguarding is the continuing work of identifying and responding to threats to a child's safety and welfare.

More about this term

It includes listening to the child, assessing risks in and beyond the home, and checking whether care arrangements protect them.

It extends beyond investigating a single allegation of abuse.

CC0 1.0View versioned object

Safety

control of harmful consequences under stated conditions

Safety is the condition in which a person, activity, or system is protected from unacceptable harm under specified conditions.

More about this term

A safety judgment should say which hazards and affected parties matter, and in what setting. It need not imply that all risk has been eliminated.

A system may operate without failure yet still cause harm in normal use. Reliability and safety therefore require related but distinct judgments.

CC0 1.0View versioned object

Sample

selected units or observations from a defined population

In statistics, a sample is a selected subset of units or observations from a defined population.

More about this term

Its results may inform a judgment about that larger population.

What can be inferred depends on how the units were selected and how well they represent the population of interest.

CC0 1.0View versioned object

Sampling

selection of units or cases for examination

Sampling is selecting some units or cases from a defined population or set to examine.

More about this term

A sampling account identifies the population or case boundary, selection method, and number selected.

Probability and purposive samples serve different purposes; conclusions must fit how the cases were chosen.

CC0 1.0View versioned object

Sampling error

sample-estimate difference arising from sampling variation

In estimation, sampling error is the difference between a value calculated from a sample and the corresponding value for the full population that arises because only part of the population was observed.

More about this term

Different well-drawn samples can produce different estimates even when measurements and calculations are correct.

This is sampling variation, not a mistake in collecting or entering the data; a standard error describes how an estimator varies across samples.

CC0 1.0View versioned object

Sampling plan

lot-acceptance inspection decision

In acceptance sampling, a sampling plan specifies how a sample from a lot will be inspected and how its results determine whether to accept the lot.

More about this term

A single-sample plan states a sample size and the maximum number of nonconforming units allowed for acceptance.

Its decision rule carries risks of rejecting a satisfactory lot or accepting an unsatisfactory one.

CC0 1.0View versioned object

Satisfaction

appraisal of a product or service experience

In a product or service experience, satisfaction is a person's appraisal of how well the experience met their needs or expectations.

More about this term

It reflects the person's perception and can change as needs, expectations, or experience change.

A satisfaction report alone does not establish that every applicable requirement was met.

CC0 1.0View versioned object

Scalability

software and computing workload growth

In computing, scalability is a system's ability to handle a growing workload while maintaining required performance.

More about this term

Growth may involve more users, larger datasets, or more complex tasks.

A scalability claim should name what grows, the conditions, and the level of performance that must be sustained.

CC0 1.0View versioned object

Scale

extent of implementation or reach

In implementation, scale is the extent of an activity's reach across people, sites, units, or area.

More about this term

Moving from a local pilot to broader coverage increases scale; state the unit and time period used to describe that increase.

A larger scale does not by itself show that the activity works equally well in each setting.

CC0 1.0View versioned object

Scale-up

manufacturing process development

In manufacturing development, scale-up is the planned transfer of a process from laboratory or pilot operation to a larger production scale.

More about this term

It may proceed directly or through a pilot plant. Equipment and process conditions must be checked at the new scale to keep the intended product characteristics.

CC0 1.0View versioned object

Scatter diagram

quality and process analysis

A scatter diagram plots paired observations of two variables as points on horizontal and vertical axes to make their pattern of association visible.

More about this term

Its shape may suggest a trend, clusters, or unusual observations; the plot alone does not show that one variable causes the other.

CC0 1.0View versioned object

Scope

boundary of an approved project plan

In project management, scope is the agreed boundary of what a project will deliver and the work included to deliver it.

More about this term

An approved plan and its product descriptions make that boundary inspectable.

A proposed addition changes scope if it adds work or deliverables outside that agreement.

CC0 1.0View versioned object

Score

value from educational or psychological assessment

In educational or psychological assessment, a score is a value produced from a person's responses or performance by a specified scoring rule.

More about this term

A raw score may count correct responses. Other scoring rules may weight responses or transform a raw score.

What the score means depends on the instrument, the comparison used, and the decision for which it is interpreted.

CC0 1.0View versioned object

Scrap

disposition preventing a nonconforming output's original use

In quality management, to scrap a nonconforming product or service is to dispose of it so it cannot be used for its originally intended purpose.

More about this term

Scrap is a disposition of the affected output, rather than work to make that output conform.

It prevents the original use; it does not by itself correct the cause of the nonconformity.

CC0 1.0View versioned object

Security

protection and authorized use of organizational information

In information management, security is the protection of information from inappropriate access, use, alteration, or loss while allowing authorized use.

More about this term

Controls depend on what information needs protection, who may use it, and the applicable privacy, contractual, and business requirements.

Restricting all access would defeat legitimate use; security must protect the information while permitting the right people to work with it.

CC0 1.0View versioned object

Selective reporting

empirical study results

Selective reporting occurs when some study outcomes or analyses are reported and others are omitted in a way that depends on the nature or direction of the results.

More about this term

It can distort the evidence available to a review; an outcome never measured is different from a measured result that is left unreported.

CC0 1.0View versioned object

Semantic consistency

data and information management

In data management, semantic consistency is agreement in the meanings assigned to related data elements across data sets or systems.

More about this term

Elements intended to represent the same concept should use compatible definitions and names or an explicit mapping; matching formats alone does not establish matching meanings.

CC0 1.0View versioned object

Sensitivity

sensitivity of a diagnostic test for a target condition

For a diagnostic test, sensitivity is the proportion of people with the target condition who receive a positive result under a stated test rule.

More about this term

It is the probability of a positive result given that the condition is present.

It is not the probability that someone with a positive result has the condition; that also depends on other factors, including how common the condition is in the tested population.

CC0 1.0View versioned object

Sensitivity analysis

dependence of modeled results on uncertain inputs or assumptions

Sensitivity analysis examines how an analysis's results or conclusions change when specified inputs or assumptions are varied.

More about this term

State which inputs vary, the ranges or scenarios used, and the outputs compared.

It reveals dependence on those choices but does not, by itself, establish that the model or chosen ranges are correct.

CC0 1.0View versioned object

Sensory acceptability

consumer sensory evaluation

Sensory acceptability is whether and to what degree a product's sensory properties are acceptable to a specified consumer group for a specified use.

More about this term

Consumer liking tests can inform it, but trained-panel descriptions or expert judgments cannot simply replace the intended users' responses.

CC0 1.0View versioned object

Sensory attribute

food sensory analysis

In food sensory analysis, a sensory attribute is a distinguishable characteristic of a food as perceived through the senses, such as an aspect of its appearance, aroma, flavor, texture, or sound.

More about this term

A descriptive assessment names the attribute and may rate its intensity; liking the food is a separate judgment.

CC0 1.0View versioned object

Sensory evaluation

food sensory science

In food science, sensory evaluation is a systematic assessment of a food's perceptible characteristics or of people's responses to them under stated conditions.

More about this term

A trained panel may describe attributes and their intensities, while consumer testing may ask whether people like the food; those are different questions.

CC0 1.0View versioned object

Sensory profile

food descriptive sensory analysis

A food's sensory profile is an organized description of its perceived attributes and their intensities obtained through a specified sensory assessment.

More about this term

It shows how the food is perceived on those attributes; consumer liking requires a separate judgment or test.

CC0 1.0View versioned object

Sensory quality

sensory characteristics of food

In food assessment, sensory quality is how well a food's perceivable features meet relevant sensory expectations or criteria.

More about this term

Appearance, aroma, flavor, and texture may matter; trained panels can describe or compare them under specified test conditions.

A favorable sensory judgment does not settle the food's safety or nutritional quality.

CC0 1.0View versioned object

Sentinel event

Joint Commission safety-event classification

In Joint Commission usage, a sentinel event is a safety occurrence that meets its serious-harm criteria or is designated for investigation regardless of that outcome.

More about this term

A patient-reaching event can qualify when it causes death, severe harm of any duration, or permanent harm of any severity, apart from the natural course of illness.

Certain listed events qualify even without these outcomes. They call for prompt investigation and response; reporting them to the Joint Commission is voluntary.

CC0 1.0View versioned object

Service assurance

customer-perceived service quality

In SERVQUAL-based service-quality assessment, service assurance refers to the assurance dimension: customers' confidence inspired by a provider's knowledge, courtesy, and competence.

More about this term

Applied service-quality studies use this compound for the established assurance dimension, rather than an additional dimension.

CC0 1.0View versioned object

Service encounter quality

particular provider-recipient interaction

Service encounter quality is how well a particular interaction between a service provider and recipient meets the relevant needs and expectations of that encounter.

More about this term

It can involve both what was delivered and how the interaction occurred; one encounter should not stand in for the quality of the whole service.

CC0 1.0View versioned object

Service integration

health and social care

Service integration is the process of bringing services, professionals, and organizations together so that people can receive coordinated support.

More about this term

The process is distinct from integrated care: the connected experience people actually have when services work together to support their goals.

CC0 1.0View versioned object

Service level

specified or observed values of service characteristics

A service level states values for specified characteristics of a service, such as response time or availability, within a defined scope and period.

More about this term

The level may be required, agreed between parties, or actually achieved; these are different descriptions of the service.

A target service level does not by itself establish that the service delivered met it.

CC0 1.0View versioned object

Service level agreement

documented provider-recipient commitment for a service

A service level agreement (SLA) is a documented agreement between a service provider and a recipient about the service to be provided and the levels of performance expected.

More about this term

It can specify scope, indicators, reporting, responsibilities, and what happens if an agreed level is missed.

An SLA records a commitment; measured service results show whether that commitment was met.

CC0 1.0View versioned object

Service level indicator

site reliability engineering

In site reliability engineering, a service level indicator is a defined measurement of a service's behavior, such as availability, request error rate, or response time.

More about this term

The indicator supplies an observed value; a service level objective states the target against which it is assessed.

CC0 1.0View versioned object

Service level objective

site reliability engineering

A service level objective is a target for a specified service level indicator over a stated period.

More about this term

It expresses the performance the service aims to achieve; a service level agreement is a separate provider-customer commitment that may carry consequences for falling short.

CC0 1.0View versioned object

Service quality

service performance and user experience

Service quality is how well a service performs in respects that matter to its users and its intended purpose.

More about this term

The result delivered and the way the service is provided may both matter. A service judgment should identify whose experience is considered and the conditions under which the service was provided.

Expectation-gap and performance-only measures are different ways of studying perceived service quality. Neither formula is a universal definition of the service’s quality.

CC0 1.0View versioned object

Service quality gap model

service marketing and customer-perceived quality

The service quality gap model explains customer-perceived quality through mismatches between expected and perceived service and gaps within the provider's design and delivery process.

More about this term

It directs attention to where expectations, specifications, performance, or communications diverge. SERVQUAL is an associated measurement scale, not the whole model.

CC0 1.0View versioned object

Service recovery

response to a service failure

Service recovery is the action a provider takes to address a service failure and its effects on the people receiving the service.

More about this term

It may involve correcting the immediate problem, making amends, and learning why the failure occurred so it is less likely to recur.

Recovery can begin before a customer complains; handling a complaint is only one possible route into it.

CC0 1.0View versioned object

Service recovery quality

provider response after service failure

Service recovery quality is how well a provider recognizes and remedies a service failure from the affected customer's standpoint.

More about this term

A useful response addresses the immediate problem and its causes where possible. Speed alone is insufficient if the remedy does not meet the customer's need or the failure recurs.

CC0 1.0View versioned object

Service reliability

dependable delivery of a promised service

In service-quality assessment, service reliability is the extent to which a provider delivers a promised service dependably and accurately across relevant occasions.

More about this term

A booking that is honored once is one result; reliability concerns whether the provider can be counted on to honor comparable bookings.

The promise, conditions, and occasions of service must be clear before reliability can be assessed.

CC0 1.0View versioned object

Serviceability

ease of scheduled inspection and servicing of an item

In equipment maintenance, serviceability is the ease with which an item can undergo scheduled inspection and servicing.

More about this term

Accessible inspection points and clear servicing procedures can improve serviceability.

This sense concerns planned upkeep; repairability concerns restoring an item after failure.

CC0 1.0View versioned object

SERVQUAL

service quality research

SERVQUAL is a customer questionnaire and model for assessing perceived service quality, commonly by comparing reported service performance with customer expectations.

More about this term

Its familiar dimensions are tangibles, reliability, responsiveness, assurance, and empathy.

The instrument has variants and limits; a score should be interpreted for the service and respondents studied.

CC0 1.0View versioned object

Seven tools of quality

traditional basic quality-tool grouping

The seven tools of quality are a traditional group of simple methods for displaying process information and investigating quality problems.

More about this term

Common members include the check sheet, histogram, Pareto diagram, cause-and-effect diagram, scatter diagram, and control chart.

The name identifies a toolkit, not seven required stages; published lists differ over whether the remaining tool is a flowchart, run chart, or another display.

CC0 1.0View versioned object

Shelf life

food safety and quality

For a food product, shelf life is the period during which it remains acceptably safe and of acceptable quality when handled and stored under specified conditions.

More about this term

The end point depends on the product and relevant safety, sensory, chemical, or microbial limits; a change in packaging or storage can change the period.

CC0 1.0View versioned object

Sigma level

Six Sigma process performance

In Six Sigma practice, a sigma level is a process-performance index derived from its rate of defects per defined opportunity; a higher level indicates fewer such defects under the chosen calculation.

More about this term

The defect and opportunity definitions, observation period, and conversion convention matter, so the level alone does not say which improvement is most valuable.

CC0 1.0View versioned object

Signal

control-chart indication for process investigation

In statistical process control, a signal is a chart result or pattern that meets a stated rule for investigating a possible change in the process.

More about this term

A point beyond a control limit is one example; patterns among plotted points can also be assessed under the chart’s rules.

A signal calls for investigation. It does not prove a particular cause, and even a stable process can occasionally produce a false alarm.

CC0 1.0View versioned object

Six Sigma

process-improvement family and statistical capability use

Six Sigma is a family of data-guided methods for improving processes by reducing unwanted variation and defects.

More about this term

Improvement projects define a problem, examine how the process performs, test causes, make changes, and monitor whether gains persist. Different roadmaps apply to an existing process and to a new design.

The phrase also has a statistical use concerning a process’s modeled performance. A claimed sigma level needs a stated defect definition, opportunity unit, measurement method, and calculation assumptions; the name alone does not demonstrate performance.

CC0 1.0View versioned object

Social care quality

social care services across public, voluntary and private providers

Social care quality is how well support services meet their purposes and serve recipients through their resources, delivery, and immediate effects.

More about this term

Recipients' experience belongs in the judgment. Longer-term changes in quality of life matter too, but they must not be attributed to the service without considering outside influences.

CC0 1.0View versioned object

Social inclusion

public and educational participation

Social inclusion is the opportunity for people, including those usually excluded, to participate meaningfully in social life and decisions that affect them.

More about this term

It concerns access to resources and institutions, as well as whether people can contribute and are treated as participants once present.

CC0 1.0View versioned object

Social service quality

social care and support services

Social service quality is how well social care and support services respond to the needs and goals of the people they serve.

More about this term

People's experience of access, coordination, and support matters, but a satisfaction rating alone cannot establish the quality of the service or its outcomes.

CC0 1.0View versioned object

Social value

benefit to people or communities in construction and procurement

In construction and public procurement, social value is a benefit to people or communities arising from a project or purchasing decision beyond its immediate deliverable.

More about this term

Its content depends on whose benefit counts and the setting; employment and training opportunities may be relevant.

A project can seek social value before a benefit occurs, so stated aims and realized outcomes should be distinguished.

CC0 1.0View versioned object

Software configuration management

identification and control of changing software-system items

Software configuration management is the organized identification, recording, and control of software items, versions, and configurations as a system changes.

More about this term

It lets a team trace approved changes and reconstruct which components made up a particular system state.

Version control is one part of this work; configuration management also coordinates item selection, builds, and change requests.

CC0 1.0View versioned object

Software quality

software product and quality in use

Software quality is how well a software product satisfies relevant stakeholder needs and requirements in its intended contexts of use.

More about this term

Product properties can include functional suitability, reliability, security, usability, and maintainability. Which properties matter, and to whom, should be specified for the system being judged.

Quality in use concerns the outcomes of interaction in a particular context. It is related to, but distinct from, a list of product properties or the quality of the development process.

CC0 1.0View versioned object

Software quality assurance

systematic confidence-building activities across software development

Software quality assurance is the planned set of activities that builds justified confidence that software will meet its requirements and work as intended.

More about this term

It begins with understanding and reviewing requirements and continues through design, coding practices, testing, and use feedback.

Testing examines implemented behavior, but software quality assurance reaches beyond testing alone.

CC0 1.0View versioned object

Sound quality

perceived product sound

Sound quality is how well a sound's audible character serves the purpose or experience for which it is judged.

More about this term

A crisp bite may be desirable in a snack, while quietness may matter in a car cabin; loudness alone cannot settle either judgment.

CC0 1.0View versioned object

Source

origin of information used for a claim

In an inquiry, a source is a person, record, dataset, or other origin from which information relevant to a claim is obtained.

More about this term

Identify the particular source and the version or location used so someone can inspect the same material. Testimony, documents, and other records can play different evidential roles.

A citation identifies where information came from; it does not by itself show that the source is accurate or that it supports the claim made from it.

CC0 1.0View versioned object

Source diversity

journalism sourcing

In journalism, source diversity is the variety of distinct sources and perspectives represented in a report or body of coverage.

More about this term

A high source count is insufficient when the voices share one standpoint. Diversity also does not, by itself, establish accuracy.

CC0 1.0View versioned object

Special cause

statistical process control

In statistical process control, a special cause is a distinct influence that produces variation outside a process's usual pattern.

More about this term

A control-chart signal can prompt a search for that influence; the signal alone does not identify it. Special-cause variation differs from routine fluctuation within the process's established pattern.

CC0 1.0View versioned object

Special-cause variation

nonroutine variation beyond the established process pattern

Special-cause variation is variation associated with a specific, nonroutine influence outside a process’s usual pattern.

More about this term

A suitable control-chart signal can prompt investigation of such an influence. The signal is evidence to examine, not identification of the cause by itself.

A special cause may be removable, but first establish what changed and whether the observed departure reflects a real change rather than a false alarm.

CC0 1.0View versioned object

Specification

documented technical requirements

A specification records requirements for an object, process, or service in a form intended to guide its creation or assessment.

More about this term

It may describe characteristics, limits, methods, or acceptance criteria. To support consistent decisions, its applicable requirements need to be clear enough to check.

A specification states what is expected; test results or other observations show whether the expectation was met. Conforming to it does not establish that it captured every relevant need.

CC0 1.0View versioned object

Specification limit

required boundary for a quality characteristic

A specification limit is a stated boundary for acceptable values of a specified characteristic.

More about this term

An upper limit, lower limit, or both may be set by a customer or another applicable requirement.

A specification limit judges an output against a requirement; a control limit instead helps assess process behavior.

CC0 1.0View versioned object

Specificity

diagnostic-test classification of people without the target condition

In diagnostic testing, specificity is the proportion of people without the target condition who test negative.

More about this term

It shows how well the test avoids false positives among people who do not have the condition.

It is not the probability that a person with a negative result is free of the condition; that is negative predictive value.

CC0 1.0View versioned object

Stability

statistical stability of a monitored process

In statistical process control, stability is a condition in which a process varies over time without detected signals of special causes.

More about this term

A stable process still varies through common causes; a suitable control chart helps detect departures from that pattern.

Stability does not by itself mean that results satisfy specifications.

CC0 1.0View versioned object

Stability testing

pharmaceutical products

In pharmaceuticals, stability testing examines how a drug substance or product's quality changes over time under specified storage conditions.

More about this term

A planned program tests relevant attributes at stated intervals to support storage conditions, a retest period, or a shelf life.

CC0 1.0View versioned object

Stakeholder

party affected by or able to influence a decision or activity

A stakeholder is a person, group, or organization that can affect, be affected by, or reasonably see itself as affected by a decision or activity.

More about this term

Stakeholders may include users, workers, suppliers, regulators, and others beyond the immediate customer. Which ones matter for a particular judgment depends on the decision and its likely effects.

Identify whose interests are at stake and how they may be affected. Being a stakeholder does not mean having the same role, authority, or claim as every other stakeholder.

CC0 1.0View versioned object

Stakeholder value

what a stakeholder values in project planning

In project planning, a stakeholder value is something a person or group regards as important in relation to a proposed project or decision.

More about this term

Different stakeholders may assign different importance to the same concern.

Identifying a value can guide a decision, but it does not show that the completed project delivered a benefit.

CC0 1.0View versioned object

Standard

evaluative reference; documentary and measurement uses distinguished

In an evaluative use, a standard is a reference or expected level used to judge performance or acceptability in a stated context.

More about this term

A criterion identifies a consideration for judgment, while a standard can specify the level or condition expected for it; the terms overlap in some fields.

An indicator supplies an observable or assessable sign relevant to the judgment, but its result alone does not establish that the chosen standard is appropriate.

A standard can be communicated through descriptions, exemplars, or numerical limits; a defensible judgment names whose standard applies and what decision it governs.

The word also has other uses: a documentary standard may specify terminology, procedures, tests, or requirements, while a measurement standard is a reference for quantity values.

CC0 1.0View versioned object

Standard error

sampling variability of a statistical estimate

A standard error is the standard deviation of an estimate's sampling distribution under a specified sampling procedure or model.

More about this term

It describes how much the estimate would tend to vary across repeated samples from the same population.

A small standard error indicates greater precision under those assumptions, but it does not show that the estimate is free of bias.

CC0 1.0View versioned object

Standard error of measurement

test-score interpretation

For test scores, the standard error of measurement describes the spread of score differences attributable to measurement error under a specified model.

More about this term

It helps interpret the precision of a score; a conditional standard error can differ across score levels.

CC0 1.0View versioned object

Standard work

Lean description of current repeatable work sequence and timing

In Lean production, standard work is an agreed description of the current sequence and timing of a repeatable task and the work-in-process needed to perform it.

More about this term

It specifies how the task is ordinarily performed so deviations and improvement opportunities can be seen.

The standard is a present way of working that can be revised when a better method is established.

CC0 1.0View versioned object

Standardization

common procedures and specifications for repeated use

Standardization is the development or use of common specifications, rules, or procedures for repeated activities or products.

More about this term

It can make practices more consistent and results more comparable or compatible.

A standard is a reference produced or applied through this process; standardization does not require every resulting object to be identical.

CC0 1.0View versioned object

Standing

recognized claim to consideration in an evaluative decision

In an evaluative decision, standing is a recognized basis for a person's or group's interests or claims to be considered.

More about this term

Being affected by a decision can give someone a reason to be heard, without giving that person sole authority over the result.

Legal standing is a separate, more specific question about who may bring a matter before a court.

CC0 1.0View versioned object

Statistic

quantity calculated from sample observations

In statistics, a statistic is a quantity calculated from sample observations.

More about this term

A sample mean is a statistic; it summarizes the observed sample and may help estimate a population mean.

The statistic is calculated from the data, while the population quantity being estimated is a parameter.

CC0 1.0View versioned object

Statistical control

process variation consistent with common causes

A process is in statistical control when its observed variation is consistent with common causes and shows no supported signal of a special cause under the chosen monitoring rules.

More about this term

Points beyond control limits or a nonrandom pattern can prompt investigation of a possible process change.

Statistical control does not by itself show that the process outputs meet their specifications.

CC0 1.0View versioned object

Statistical power

probability a test rejects the null under a specified alternative

Statistical power is the probability that a specified test will reject its null hypothesis when a particular alternative is true.

More about this term

For that alternative, power equals one minus the probability of a Type II error, often written 1 − β.

Power must be considered for a stated effect and test design; a low-power test may miss a difference that matters.

CC0 1.0View versioned object

Statistical process control (SPC)

statistical monitoring of process behavior

Statistical process control (SPC) uses process data and statistical rules to monitor variation over time and identify signals that warrant investigation.

More about this term

A control chart is a common SPC tool. It compares observed behavior with limits based on the process, helping distinguish routine variation from evidence of a change or special cause.

A process can be statistically stable yet fail to meet specifications. Stability and capability answer different questions, so an SPC signal is not a pass-or-fail judgment on every output.

CC0 1.0View versioned object

Statistical quality control

statistical methods for quality analysis and improvement

Statistical quality control is the use of statistical methods to understand variation and support decisions about the quality of processes and outputs.

More about this term

It can include process control, acceptance sampling, and designed experiments.

The methods provide evidence and decision rules; the phrase does not mean that every output has been inspected.

CC0 1.0View versioned object

Statistical significance

null-hypothesis test decision under a stated threshold

A result is statistically significant under a specified hypothesis test when its data meet the stated rule for rejecting the null hypothesis.

More about this term

A common rule compares the p-value with a chosen significance level, such as 0.05, under the test's assumptions.

Statistical significance does not establish that an effect is large, important in practice, or caused by the factor under study.

CC0 1.0View versioned object

Sterility assurance

sterile pharmaceutical manufacture

In sterile pharmaceutical manufacture, sterility assurance is justified confidence that the production process yields units without viable microbial contamination.

More about this term

It depends on a validated sterilization or aseptic process and control of each batch; testing a small sample of finished units cannot establish that every unit is sterile.

CC0 1.0View versioned object

Strategy

organizational direction and chosen means for pursuing aims

An organizational strategy is a coherent choice of direction and means for pursuing an organization's aims.

More about this term

It guides priorities and aligns the actions of different parts of the organization.

Because conditions change, a strategy needs review against results and changes in the organization's environment.

CC0 1.0View versioned object

Structure

settings and organizational arrangements through which healthcare is provided

In healthcare quality assessment, structure means the settings, personnel capabilities, and organizational arrangements through which care is provided.

More about this term

It includes features such as facilities, clinician qualifications, and administrative systems.

Structure describes the conditions for care; process describes the care delivered, and outcome describes its effects.

CC0 1.0View versioned object

Structure measure

health-care quality measurement

In health care, a structure measure specifies how to assess a feature of the setting or resources available for care, such as staffing, facilities, or information systems.

More about this term

It describes capacity or arrangement, rather than what clinicians did or what happened to patients.

CC0 1.0View versioned object

Student engagement

higher education

In higher education, student engagement is students' active participation in learning activities and interactions that matter for their education.

More about this term

It can include working through challenging material, collaborating with peers, and discussing learning with faculty; attendance alone captures only a small part of it.

CC0 1.0View versioned object

Student experience

higher education

In higher education, student experience is what students encounter and perceive while studying, including teaching, assessment, and their interactions with the institution.

More about this term

A satisfaction survey reports aspects of that experience but does not by itself show what students learned.

CC0 1.0View versioned object

Student success

achievement of educational learning and progression goals

In education, student success is students' progress toward and attainment of relevant learning and progression goals.

More about this term

Evidence may include demonstrated learning, persistence, completion, or later placement, depending on the program's aims.

No single indicator, including graduation rate, captures every student's educational success.

CC0 1.0View versioned object

Study quality

qualitative evidence synthesis

In qualitative evidence synthesis, study quality concerns the methodological strengths and limitations of a study that affect how its findings can be used.

More about this term

Assess the relevant domains and their effect on particular findings; a single total score can conceal important differences between them.

CC0 1.0View versioned object

Supersession

controlled documents and standards

Supersession is the replacement of an earlier rule, document, or version by a later one for a stated scope.

More about this term

The earlier item can remain a historical record; the later item does not necessarily replace other rules that it merely complements.

CC0 1.0View versioned object

Supplier evaluation

assessment of supplier capability and performance for a purchasing relationship

Supplier evaluation is an assessment of whether a supplier can meet, and is meeting, requirements relevant to a purchasing relationship.

More about this term

Before selection or during a contract, it may examine capability, product quality, delivery, compliance, and performance trends through records, surveys, or audits.

Its criteria depend on the product and its risks. Unlike incoming inspection, it assesses the supplier across a relationship rather than only a received lot.

CC0 1.0View versioned object

Supplier quality

supplier outputs, controls and performance for an intended relationship

Supplier quality is how well a supplier’s outputs and relevant processes meet the requirements of an intended customer relationship.

More about this term

Assessment may consider delivered conformity, consistency, process controls, timeliness, and response when problems occur. The importance of each depends on the purchased item or service and the consequences of failure.

A single delivery score cannot establish the quality of every supplier activity. State the requirements, period, and evidence behind the judgment.

CC0 1.0View versioned object

Surveillance

continuing or periodic assessment of a process in quality management

In quality management, surveillance is continuing observation or periodic assessment of a process to see whether it still performs to a specified standard.

More about this term

It looks for changes or emerging problems after a process has been put in use.

A surveillance check observes the process over time; it is not a one-time demonstration that every output conforms.

CC0 1.0View versioned object

Survey

questionnaire-based collection of responses from a group

In evaluation research, a survey is a planned collection of responses from a specified group using a set of questions.

More about this term

A survey design states whom the questions are meant to represent, how respondents are selected, and how answers are collected.

Answers report respondents' views or experiences; they do not automatically prove how people behave.

CC0 1.0View versioned object

Sustainability

maintaining valued activity within enduring limits

Sustainability is the capacity of an activity or system to continue over time without undermining the conditions on which it and others depend.

More about this term

An assessment should identify what is to continue, over what time horizon, and which ecological, social, or other limits and affected people matter.

Sustainable development asks how present needs can be met while preserving the possibility of meeting future needs. Sustainability claims can be contested when they conceal unequal burdens or treat a single resource measure as the whole judgment.

CC0 1.0View versioned object

System quality

quality of a software-intensive computer system

For a software-intensive computer system, system quality is how well the system meets the relevant needs of its stakeholders.

More about this term

Assessing it calls for a stated context and relevant characteristics of the system, such as reliability, usability, or security.

The needs of different stakeholders may differ, so one score or characteristic cannot establish the system's overall quality without a stated basis for judgment.

CC0 1.0View versioned object
T37 terms

t-test

t-statistic hypothesis test for a mean or mean difference

A t-test is a hypothesis test that uses a t statistic to assess a claim about a population mean or a difference between means.

More about this term

One-sample and paired forms answer different questions, so the comparison and structure of the data must be specified.

Its result is interpreted under the test's assumptions and chosen significance level; statistical significance alone does not show that a difference is practically important.

CC0 1.0View versioned object

Tampering

overadjustment of a stable process in statistical process control

In statistical process control, tampering is adjusting a stable process in response to ordinary variation as though an unusual cause had appeared.

More about this term

Such adjustments can increase variation even when intended to move the next result toward a target.

A control chart can help distinguish expected variation from a signal that warrants investigation before changing the process.

CC0 1.0View versioned object

Tangibles

visible physical features in service-quality assessment

In service-quality assessment, tangibles are the visible physical features of a service setting, its equipment, and the appearance of personnel.

More about this term

A clean waiting area or well-kept equipment can shape a customer's impression of a service.

Those cues do not by themselves establish that the service is reliable, accurate, or responsive.

CC0 1.0View versioned object

Target

results monitoring and evaluation

A target states the result sought on a specified indicator, for a specified population or scope, by a specified time.

More about this term

It helps people plan and later assess progress.

Its value should be justified by the objective, starting conditions, context, and resources; the word target supplies no universal cutoff.

CC0 1.0View versioned object

Teaching quality

higher education
