In higher education, teaching quality is how well teaching practices support the intended learning in a particular course or setting.

More about this term

Relevant evidence may concern clarity, interaction, assignments, assessment, and learning; a single student rating does not settle the judgment.

CC0 1.0View versioned object

Technical characteristic

design-side response in a House of Quality

In a House of Quality, a technical characteristic is a property of the proposed product, service, or process that a team can specify or influence in response to customer requirements.

More about this term

It names a design-side “how” and should be observable or measurable enough to guide development. The customer requirement names the need-side “what.”

The characteristic is distinct from its technical target, which states a desired level. A matrix cell records an assessed link between the characteristic and a customer requirement, not proof of achieved performance.

CC0 1.0View versioned object

Technical debt

software engineering

Technical debt is future work or risk created when a software design or implementation choice makes a system harder to change, maintain, or operate.

More about this term

It may result from a deliberate shortcut or an overlooked consequence; the debt metaphor describes later burden, not a literal financial balance.

CC0 1.0View versioned object

Technical execution

artistic making and performance

In artistic making or performance, technical execution is how a maker or performer carries out the practical skills and operations involved in realizing a work.

More about this term

The relevant skills depend on the medium and aim; technical polish alone does not decide artistic merit, and some art does not require conventional craft proficiency.

CC0 1.0View versioned object

Technical target

desired level for a technical characteristic in a House of Quality

In a House of Quality, a technical target is a specified desired value, range, or level for a technical characteristic in a proposed design.

More about this term

It answers “how much” of that characteristic the design should achieve. A useful target names its measure or scale, units where applicable, and the relevant conditions.

Customer needs, feasibility, and comparisons may inform the choice of target. The target is a design aim; a later measurement is needed to determine whether the delivered offering reaches it.

CC0 1.0View versioned object

Test

specified examination of an item's response in quality engineering

In quality engineering, a test exposes an item to specified conditions and observes its response to assess a characteristic or requirement.

More about this term

The conditions, method, and expected result need to be stated for the finding to be interpretable.

The observed response provides evidence; comparing it with a requirement is a further judgment.

CC0 1.0View versioned object

Test-retest reliability

psychological and educational measurement

Test-retest reliability concerns the consistency of scores when the same people complete the same assessment again under conditions where the measured attribute is expected to remain stable.

More about this term

The interval matters: recall of earlier responses can inflate agreement, while real change in the attribute can reduce it.

CC0 1.0View versioned object

Testability

software systems and requirements

In software engineering, testability is how readily a system, component, or requirement can be checked against stated test criteria.

More about this term

A requirement is more testable when its expected result can be specified and a test can determine whether that result occurred.

CC0 1.0View versioned object

Testing

product or component assessment in quality engineering

In quality engineering, testing applies defined conditions or procedures to an item to obtain evidence about its characteristics or capabilities.

More about this term

A test may expose the item to physical, chemical, environmental, or operating conditions. It may be destructive or nondestructive.

The observed or measured result needs interpretation against a relevant requirement before a conformity judgment is made. Testing and inspection overlap, but they are not interchangeable in every use.

CC0 1.0View versioned object

Threat

potential risk source in reliability and security

In reliability and security analysis, a threat is a potential source of adverse effects on a system or its objectives.

More about this term

A threat is identified before its possible consequence occurs.

Name the source and the outcome it could cause; calling an already realized loss a threat obscures that distinction.

CC0 1.0View versioned object

Threshold

decision and classification boundary

A threshold separates regions to which different interpretations or rules apply.

More about this term

Its meaning is incomplete until the relevant variable, direction of comparison, boundary value, and consequence of crossing it are specified.

CC0 1.0View versioned object

Time

temporal reference of an observation or evaluative claim

In evaluation, time is the temporal reference for when something is observed, how long it lasts, or when a result is due.

More about this term

A claim should identify its observation point or interval and the period to which its conclusion applies.

A result from one occasion alone cannot establish stable performance over time.

CC0 1.0View versioned object

Time horizon

period considered in a decision or evaluation

A time horizon is the span of time over which a decision, forecast, or evaluation considers outcomes.

More about this term

State when the period begins and ends, or how long it lasts. A short horizon may reveal immediate costs and benefits while missing effects that emerge later.

The time horizon is part of the question being asked. It is not the same as a deadline for making the decision or finishing the work.

CC0 1.0View versioned object

Time to degree

higher education

Time to degree is the elapsed time from a specified starting point in a student's program to the award of the degree.

More about this term

State the starting point and student group, including full-time or part-time status. A figure calculated only for graduates does not describe those who left without a degree.

CC0 1.0View versioned object

Time-to-failure

elapsed operating or exposure time until an item's specified failure

Time-to-failure is the elapsed time from a specified starting point until an item first meets a defined failure condition.

More about this term

The clock and failure rule must be stated: calendar time, operating hours, and cycles can answer different questions.

If the observation ends while the item still works, its exact failure time is unknown rather than zero; the record is censored.

CC0 1.0View versioned object

Timeliness

suitability of delivery or availability time for an intended use

Timeliness is how well an action, service, or information occurs or becomes available when it is needed for its intended use.

More about this term

A delay matters when it impairs the use or outcome at issue; a fast response is not automatically timely if it arrives at the wrong moment.

The relevant time window depends on the task and recipient, as in urgent care or a report needed for a decision.

CC0 1.0View versioned object

Tolerance

permitted variation of an engineered characteristic

In engineering, a tolerance states how much variation in a characteristic is permitted between specified limits.

More about this term

The characteristic, unit, and limits must be clear before a measured value can be judged against it.

A value within tolerance may still differ from the target; being allowed is not the same as being optimal.

CC0 1.0View versioned object

Top event

specified unwanted outcome in fault tree analysis

In fault tree analysis, a top event is the specified unwanted system state or event that the analysis seeks to explain.

More about this term

It heads the tree; lower events and logic gates show combinations that could bring it about.

Choosing it sets the question and boundary for the analysis. A top event is the outcome under study, not itself an identified root cause.

CC0 1.0View versioned object

Total environmental quality management (TEQM)

environmental-management framework

Total environmental quality management (TEQM) is an approach that applies organization-wide quality-management thinking to environmental effects.

More about this term

It places environmental concerns at the center of decisions about activities and their inputs and outputs. The term names a particular framework; it is not a general label for every environmental-management system.

CC0 1.0View versioned object

Total quality control

integrated organizational quality approach

Total quality control (TQC) is an organization-wide approach that brings quality development, maintenance, and improvement together across functions.

More about this term

It treats quality as a coordinated responsibility throughout the organization rather than only a final inspection task.

The term names a management approach, not a single inspection method or numerical control limit.

CC0 1.0View versioned object

Total quality management (TQM)

organization-wide quality management approach

Total quality management (TQM) is an organization-wide approach that makes meeting customer needs and improving work processes a shared, continuing responsibility.

More about this term

It joins leadership, participation across roles, evidence about performance, and repeated problem solving. Statistical tools can help, but no single tool constitutes TQM.

Calling a program TQM describes an intended approach. Whether it works depends on how its practices are carried out and what results they produce in the organization’s setting.

CC0 1.0View versioned object

Traceability

metrological traceability of a measurement result

In metrology, traceability is the property of a measurement result that allows it to be related to a stated reference through a documented chain of comparisons.

More about this term

Each link in the chain contributes uncertainty that must be accounted for.

Traceability identifies how a result is connected to a reference; it does not alone show that the result is sufficiently accurate for a particular use.

CC0 1.0View versioned object

Traceability matrix

tabular map between requirements and related design or verification records

A traceability matrix is a table that records links between requirements and the design, implementation, tests, or other records that address them.

More about this term

It helps a team check coverage and see what may need review when a requirement or related artifact changes. The rows and columns should identify the linked items and the nature of each link.

A filled cell shows a recorded relationship; it does not by itself prove that the requirement was met. The supporting design or test evidence still needs examination.

CC0 1.0View versioned object

Trade-off

choice among competing design outcomes

A trade-off is a choice in which improving one valued outcome involves giving up some attainable level of another under specified constraints.

More about this term

In a House of Quality, a negative interaction between proposed characteristics can signal a possible trade-off. The mark is a reason to investigate the design choices, not proof that no better combination is possible.

A defensible trade-off states the alternatives, the outcomes affected, and the reasons for accepting one balance over another. A compromise is justified by its context, not by a universal matrix score.

CC0 1.0View versioned object

Transferability

qualitative research

In qualitative research, transferability is the potential for a finding to offer useful insight in a setting or situation beyond the one studied.

More about this term

It must be judged against the new purpose and context; a finding is not automatically applicable everywhere.

CC0 1.0View versioned object

Transparency

openness of public decisions and government activities

In public governance, transparency is the openness that lets people examine how government decisions are made and resources are used.

More about this term

It requires relevant information to be available in a form people can access and understand.

Transparency can enable scrutiny and participation, but disclosure alone does not establish that a decision was sound or accountable.

CC0 1.0View versioned object

Trauma-informed care

health and social-service delivery

Trauma-informed care is an approach to delivering services that recognizes how trauma can affect people and adapts care to support safety, trust, choice, and agency.

More about this term

It shapes the way services are provided and is distinct from treatment specifically designed to address trauma-related symptoms.

CC0 1.0View versioned object

Triangulation

empirical-research comparison of distinct evidence streams

In empirical research, triangulation compares evidence gathered through different methods or observers to examine a question from more than one vantage point.

More about this term

Agreement can strengthen a finding, while differences may reveal complementary aspects or a disagreement needing explanation.

The term does not require three datasets, and agreement by itself does not guarantee that a conclusion is true.

CC0 1.0View versioned object

True value

metrology

In metrology, a true value is a quantity value consistent with the definition of a specified quantity.

More about this term

It serves as an ideal reference for discussing measurement error, although a measurement generally cannot establish it exactly.

CC0 1.0View versioned object

Trueness

agreement of a measurement average with a reference

Measurement trueness is how closely the average of many repeated results agrees with an accepted reference value.

More about this term

It concerns systematic displacement of the average, rather than how tightly individual results cluster.

A single result does not by itself establish trueness.

CC0 1.0View versioned object

Trustworthiness

grounds for relying on a system to meet critical requirements

In systems engineering, trustworthiness is the extent to which a system warrants reliance on it to fulfill specified critical requirements under relevant conditions.

More about this term

Those requirements may concern safety, security, reliability, performance, or resilience, depending on the system and its use.

A claim of trustworthiness needs evidence for the relevant requirements; success on one attribute does not establish all the others.

CC0 1.0View versioned object

Type I error

incorrect rejection of a true null hypothesis

A Type I error occurs when a hypothesis test rejects a null hypothesis that is in fact true.

More about this term

The chosen significance level, α, bounds the probability of this error under the test's stated conditions.

It differs from a Type II error, which fails to reject a false null hypothesis.

CC0 1.0View versioned object

Type II error

failure to reject a false null hypothesis

A Type II error occurs when a hypothesis test fails to reject a null hypothesis that is in fact false.

More about this term

For a specified alternative, its probability is β, and the test's power is 1 − β.

Failing to reject the null hypothesis therefore does not establish that the null is true.

CC0 1.0View versioned object
U8 terms

Uncertainty

limits on knowledge or prediction

Uncertainty is a limit on what can be known or predicted about a specified state, claim, quantity, or outcome.

More about this term

It can arise from incomplete observations, variability, assumptions, or limits in a model. State what is uncertain and why; uncertainty about a measurement differs from uncertainty about the consequences of a decision.

A probability or range can express some uncertainties, but neither is always available or sufficient. The limits should travel with the claim or recommendation they affect.

CC0 1.0View versioned object

Uncertainty budget

measurement uncertainty

An uncertainty budget is a documented breakdown of the components contributing to a measurement's uncertainty and how their contributions are combined.

More about this term

It records the estimates and assumptions behind the reported uncertainty so they can be reviewed or updated when the measurement process changes.

CC0 1.0View versioned object

Unit of analysis

entity level about which a study draws conclusions

In a study, the unit of analysis is the kind of entity about which the analysis draws a conclusion, such as a person or project team.

More about this term

Choosing the unit determines the level at which cases are compared and findings are stated.

A study of the same setting can ask different questions of individuals and teams, so the unit should be explicit when interpreting a result.

CC0 1.0View versioned object

Upper control limit

statistical process control

An upper control limit is the upper statistical boundary on a control chart for values expected from a process showing only routine variation.

More about this term

A point above it can signal a process change that warrants investigation. The limit is based on process behavior and is not the same as a maximum acceptable specification.

CC0 1.0View versioned object

Usability

product or system use by specified users

Usability concerns how effectively, efficiently, and satisfactorily specified users can accomplish specified goals with a product or system in a stated context of use.

More about this term

The users, tasks, and setting therefore matter to any usability claim.

A product may perform its technical function while remaining difficult for its intended users to use.

CC0 1.0View versioned object

Use

application of an object, method, or finding for a purpose

Use is the application of an object, method, or finding for a purpose by someone in a setting.

More about this term

To judge whether something works in use, identify its users, purpose, and conditions.

Intended use states what was planned; actual use describes what people do.

CC0 1.0View versioned object

Use value

direct use or experience in benefit-cost analysis

In benefit-cost analysis, use value is the value a person derives from directly using or experiencing a good, service, or resource.

More about this term

It concerns the user's own benefit from that experience, which may be expressed through willingness to pay.

It is not identical to a market price, which need not capture the full value of a use.

CC0 1.0View versioned object

Utility

numerical representation of preferences in decision theory

In decision theory, utility is a numerical representation of how a decision maker ranks outcomes or choices under a specified model of preferences.

More about this term

A utility function assigns numbers so the model can compare alternatives, including uncertain ones when probabilities are also specified.

Utility numbers are model-dependent; they need not equal money or express a universal measure of human well-being.

CC0 1.0View versioned object
V22 terms

V-model

software development and testing lifecycle representation

The V-model is a software-development framework that pairs successive requirements and design stages with corresponding integration and testing activities.

More about this term

One side develops the system from requirements toward implementation; the other checks components, their integration, the whole system, and its fit for users.

Passing a component test alone does not establish that the assembled system meets its intended use.

CC0 1.0View versioned object

Validation

evidence-based confirmation for intended use

Validation is confirmation, using objective evidence, that requirements for a specified intended use or application have been fulfilled.

More about this term

It asks whether the object is suitable for that use under the conditions being considered. The intended use, users, and relevant conditions should therefore be explicit.

A system can meet its written specification and still fail validation if that specification misses what the intended use requires. Verification and validation need not have the same result.

CC0 1.0View versioned object

Validation process

medical-device design validation

In medical-device design, a validation process is a planned sequence for gathering and reviewing evidence that the device design meets user needs and its intended uses.

More about this term

It identifies intended uses, methods, and acceptance criteria, then records results and resolves discrepancies.

Verification against design inputs can contribute evidence, but it does not by itself show that the design meets user needs.

CC0 1.0View versioned object

Validation protocol

prospective plan for pharmaceutical process validation

A validation protocol is a prospective document that states how a specified validation study will be conducted and judged.

More about this term

For a pharmaceutical process, it identifies the scope, important parameters, tests and sampling, data to record, and acceptance criteria. Responsibilities and the basis for those criteria should be clear.

Completing and evaluating the study provides validation evidence; approving the protocol alone does not establish that the process performs reliably.

CC0 1.0View versioned object

Validity

deductive logic, test-score interpretation, and empirical research

Validity is the status or degree of warrant for a specified inference, interpretation, or use, judged by the rules relevant to that claim.

More about this term

The word has distinct technical senses:

In deductive logic, an argument is valid when no possible interpretation makes all its premises true and its conclusion false. This is a yes-or-no property of the inference.

In measurement, validity concerns how well evidence and theory support a particular interpretation of scores for a stated use. Calling a test simply “valid” leaves out the interpretation and use that need justification.

In empirical research, validity concerns whether conclusions are warranted by the study: for example, whether an observed effect can be attributed to an intervention and whether the conclusion applies in the intended setting.

CC0 1.0View versioned object

Validity argument

justification for a specified test-score interpretation and use

A validity argument is a reasoned case that evidence and assumptions support a specified interpretation or use of test results for a stated population and purpose.

More about this term

It connects each important inference to relevant evidence and explains why the proposed action follows. Possible counterevidence and limits matter because the same scores can be used for different purposes.

A folder of studies is not a validity argument unless the studies bear on the claims being made. New uses or populations can require a revised argument.

CC0 1.0View versioned object

Value

evaluative sense

In its evaluative sense, value is the significance something has under an account of what merits concern, appreciation, use, or pursuit.

More about this term

A useful value claim says what matters, to whom, in what setting, and why.

Evaluation research distinguishes factual description from a judgment that brings evidence and relevant values together.

CC0 1.0View versioned object

Value creation

benefits realized through customer use of a service offering

In a value-in-use account of services, value creation is the emergence of benefits as a customer uses an offering together with their own activities and resources.

More about this term

A provider can enable that use, but the offering alone does not guarantee the benefit.

What is valuable, and how much, can differ across customers and situations.

CC0 1.0View versioned object

Value for money

outcomes and benefits relative to resources in service evaluation

Value for money is a judgment about the benefits or outcomes obtained for the resources spent, assessed against relevant alternatives.

More about this term

It considers both what a service achieves and what it costs to achieve it.

The lowest-priced option may offer poor value if it delivers worse outcomes or fails an important quality requirement.

CC0 1.0View versioned object

Value proposition

customer-facing statement of an offering's benefits

A value proposition states the benefits an offering promises to a specified customer and why that offering merits consideration against available alternatives.

More about this term

It should identify the customer, the problem or desired outcome, and the difference the offering is expected to make.

The statement is a claim about prospective value; evidence of use and results is needed to show whether the benefit was realized.

CC0 1.0View versioned object

Value realization

project management

In project management, value realization occurs when project outputs lead to outcomes that stakeholders find beneficial.

More about this term

Delivering the specified output alone does not show that the intended benefit was achieved.

CC0 1.0View versioned object

Value-added

customer-useful transformation in process analysis

In process analysis, a value-added activity transforms an input into an output that an internal or external customer can use.

More about this term

The question is whether the step contributes to the output the customer needs, not merely whether it consumes labor or raises cost.

A necessary supporting step may still be classified separately from direct value-adding transformation in a particular process model.

CC0 1.0View versioned object

Value-stream mapping

visual analysis of a defined product or service flow

Value-stream mapping is a method for drawing the sequence of activities and flows involved in delivering a specified product or service.

More about this term

A map makes handoffs, waits, repeated work, and other possible sources of waste easier to inspect. It can guide questions about how the current process works and where change may help.

The map represents a defined scope and observation period; it does not prove that every step is wasteful or that a proposed change will improve the result.

CC0 1.0View versioned object

Variable

characteristic with differing values across cases or observations

In empirical research, a variable is a characteristic of the subject being studied that can take different values across cases or observations.

More about this term

Specify what counts as a case, how the characteristic is observed, and which values it can take.

The variable is the characteristic; one recorded value is an observation of it.

CC0 1.0View versioned object

Variance

statistical dispersion around a mean

Variance is a measure of numerical dispersion based on squared deviations from a mean.

More about this term

For a population, it divides the sum of those squared deviations by the population size. The usual sample variance used to estimate population variance divides by the sample size minus one.

Variance has squared units; standard deviation is its positive square root and uses the original unit. The population or sample basis should be stated when reporting a value.

CC0 1.0View versioned object

Variation

differences among process outputs or observations

In a process, variation consists of differences in a characteristic or output across units, conditions, or times.

More about this term

Some variation arises from recurring features of the process; other variation has a specific, unusual cause.

Variation alone does not say whether an output meets a requirement; that judgment needs a stated criterion.

CC0 1.0View versioned object

Verification

evidence-based confirmation of specified requirements

Verification is confirmation, using objective evidence, that specified requirements have been fulfilled.

More about this term

It asks whether the object or result meets the requirements being checked. The method and evidence must fit those requirements.

Passing verification does not alone show that the requirements suit the intended use. That further question belongs to validation.

CC0 1.0View versioned object

Version

identified state of an information item in configuration control

In configuration control, a version is an identifiable state of an item preserved or distinguished from its other states.

More about this term

A new version records a changed state so people can tell which content they are using and trace its history.

Branches may contain different versions developed from the same earlier state; a version identifier alone does not say that a change was approved for release.

CC0 1.0View versioned object

Visual management

visible process signals and response in lean work management

Visual management uses visible signals and displays to make a process's status, expected condition, and deviations easy for people doing the work to see.

More about this term

A display may show whether work is on schedule, supplies are available, or an action has an owner.

Its purpose includes timely response when a deviation appears; displaying information without acting on it does not complete that management practice.

CC0 1.0View versioned object

Visual quality

images and visual media

Visual quality is an appraisal of an image's visible presentation for a specified viewing purpose.

More about this term

It may involve color, texture, organization, and aesthetic response; visual complexity alone cannot settle the judgment.

CC0 1.0View versioned object

Voice of the customer

customer evidence used in QFD inquiry

In QFD, voice of the customer is information gathered about identified customers’ needs, expectations, and use of a product or service.

More about this term

It may include what customers say directly and what investigation reveals about needs they have not stated. Who was heard, in what setting, and through which method affects what the information can support.

A customer statement is evidence to interpret, not automatically a well-specified requirement. A team should test its translation of that information before using it to direct a design.

CC0 1.0View versioned object

Vulnerability

system susceptibility to harm from a risk source

For a system, vulnerability is its susceptibility to damage or loss of performance when exposed to a risk source or disruptive event.

More about this term

It depends on the particular system and threat being considered.

A hazard names a potential source of harm; vulnerability concerns how readily the exposed system may be affected.

CC0 1.0View versioned object
W10 terms

Waiver

authorized quality-management exception to a requirement

In quality management, a waiver is an authorized, bounded exception that permits departure from an otherwise applicable requirement.

More about this term

It should identify who authorized the departure, which product or process it covers, and when or after how much production it expires.

A waiver does not show that the original requirement was met; after it expires, that requirement applies again unless formally changed.

CC0 1.0View versioned object

Warrant

argument-analysis link between grounds and claim

In argument analysis, a warrant is the principle that explains why stated grounds support a claim.

More about this term

The grounds supply case-specific information; the warrant supplies the linking reason. It may be stated or left implicit, and making it explicit helps readers test whether the move to the claim is sound.

Some warrants are defeasible: a credible objection or changed circumstance can weaken the inference.

CC0 1.0View versioned object

Warranty

seller or maker commitment for a covered failure

A warranty is a seller’s or maker’s commitment to provide a stated remedy if a product fails under covered conditions.

More about this term

Its terms specify what is covered, for how long or under what use conditions, and whether the remedy is repair, replacement, compensation, or another stated response.

A warranty defines an obligation after a covered problem occurs; it does not establish that the product will not fail.

CC0 1.0View versioned object

Waste

non-value-adding activity in Lean improvement

In Lean improvement, waste is an activity that uses resources without creating value for the intended recipient.

More about this term

Waiting caused by missing information, equipment, or supplies is one possible form.

Whether an activity is waste depends on the value sought and the process being examined; time or cost alone does not settle the judgment.

CC0 1.0View versioned object

Weighting

relative influence of components in a combined result

Weighting assigns different relative influence to components used in a combined result or comparison.

More about this term

A weight states how much a component contributes under the chosen aggregation rule; it does not make the underlying evidence more trustworthy.

Changing weights can change a ranking, so the choice and its rationale should be visible.

CC0 1.0View versioned object

Well-being

how well life goes for a person

Well-being is how well a person's life goes for that person.

More about this term

Accounts of well-being differ over the importance of pleasure, fulfilled desires, health, relationships, and opportunities to function.

It is not identical to momentary happiness or to a moral judgment that the person is good.

CC0 1.0View versioned object

Willingness to pay

economic valuation of a specified benefit

Willingness to pay is the most money or purchasing power a person would give up to obtain a specified benefit under stated conditions.

More about this term

It expresses a tradeoff against other possible uses of that person's resources.

The stated amount depends on the benefit, circumstances, and resources available; it is not a context-free measure of the benefit's worth.

CC0 1.0View versioned object

Worker knowledge

workplace competence and improvement

Worker knowledge is the task, process, and situational understanding people bring to performing and improving their work.

More about this term

It may develop through study and practice. Knowledge is one part of competence, alongside experience, skills, and the conditions that let a worker apply them.

CC0 1.0View versioned object

Workmanship

execution of making, installing or finishing work

Workmanship is how well the work of making, installing, or finishing something is carried out.

More about this term

It is judged against applicable craft, design, and acceptance requirements for the work performed.

Workmanship concerns execution; it does not by itself establish that the chosen design or materials are suitable.

CC0 1.0View versioned object

Worth

broad evaluative and practical-decision use

In its broad evaluative use, worth is the value, merit, or importance attributed to something on stated grounds.

More about this term

In a practical decision, “Is it worth it?” asks whether the reasons to pursue or obtain something justify its effort, cost, risk, and forgone alternatives.

That question may call for judgment without yielding a single monetary answer.

CC0 1.0View versioned object
Y1 term

Yield

acceptable output share in a defined process

In a defined production or service process, yield is the share of input units that emerge as acceptable output under a stated counting rule.

More about this term

State the unit, process boundary, acceptance criteria, and whether reworked units count.

First-pass yield and final yield can differ when units are repaired or reworked before acceptance.

CC0 1.0View versioned object
Z1 term

Z-value

normal-distribution statistics

For a normally distributed quantity, a Z-value indicates how many standard deviations an observation lies above or below its mean.

More about this term

Compute it by subtracting the mean from the observation and dividing by a nonzero standard deviation. Positive values lie above the mean, negative values below it, and zero is at the mean.
